# Safeguarding Adults in Wales — Wales

Jurisdiction: Wales
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Wales practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/wales/safeguarding-adults-in-wales.html

# Safeguarding Adults in Wales

## Learning outcomes

Recognise the Welsh adult-at-risk framework, distinguish reporting from enquiries, and produce a clear record of concerns, participation, immediate action and follow-up.

## Three questions about an adult at risk

Section 126(1) concerns an adult experiencing or at risk of abuse or neglect, with care and support needs, who is unable to protect themselves from that abuse or neglect because of those needs. The needs do not have to be met by the authority already. Risk can justify attention before actual harm has occurred. Read the [Wales Safeguarding Procedures](https://safeguarding.wales/en/adu-i/adu-i-a2/a2-p2/).

## Reporting and enquiries are different responsibilities

The local authority's section 126(2) enquiry duty arises where it has reasonable cause to suspect an adult in its area is an adult at risk. Section 128 sets reporting duties for relevant partners. Record your role and the applicable duty rather than treating every practitioner as the authority making the enquiry decision. Refer to the [adult enquiry procedures](https://www.safeguarding.wales/en/adu-i/adu-i-a3pt1/) and [Volume 6 statutory guidance](https://www.gov.wales/sites/default/files/publications/2019-06/volume-6-handling-individual-cases-to-protect-adults-at-risk.pdf).

## A practical sequence

1. Address immediate danger and urgent health needs through the appropriate emergency service. Do not wait for a completed learning checklist.
2. Record the concern, source, time and observable impact. Separate direct observation, what someone said and your interpretation.
3. Speak with the adult in a way that supports safety and communication. Explore what they want, who they trust, and any pressure affecting their choices.
4. Follow the local reporting route, share relevant information securely, and confirm who received it. Keep an escalation route where a response is missing or the concern increases.
5. Contribute to agreed enquiries and protection planning within your role. Record the rationale, responsibilities, review and the adult's involvement.

## Consent, capacity and coercion

A wish not to involve services needs careful exploration and recording. It does not automatically settle whether information can or must be shared. Identify relevant duties, risks to others, confidentiality and data-protection requirements, with advice where needed. A capacity assessment answers a specific decision; it is not a blanket assessment of whether someone can “safeguard themselves”. Coercion and barriers to speaking freely also need attention.

## Self-neglect and organisational concerns

Investigate context: pain, loss, poverty, isolation, environmental barriers and previous experiences of services can matter. Do not make a threshold decision from a label alone. For concerns in an organisation, examine patterns across records, staffing, communication and other people potentially affected. A single service response may not address a wider pattern. Follow employer and regional procedures concerning practitioners or people in positions of trust.

## Worked learning example

Fictional example: Rhys needs help with meals and finances. A relative has moved in; Rhys appears anxious and has missed meals. Record what is known without assuming the relative is responsible. Arrange a safe opportunity for Rhys to speak, clarify immediate needs and consider the statutory elements. A report should explain why further enquiries may be needed, what Rhys wants and what has already been done. It should not claim abuse is proved when it is suspected.

## Recording check

Use the safeguarding prompt to document the three statutory elements, evidence and gaps, the adult's wishes, communication/advocacy needs, reporting duty considered, information shared, interim safety action and the responsible contact. Keep allegations and findings distinct. Revisit the plan when new facts or wishes emerge.

<!-- curriculum-expansion -->

## Further local practice detail

Section 126 of the Social Services and Well-being (Wales) Act 2014 concerns an adult experiencing or at risk of abuse or neglect, with care and support needs, who cannot protect themselves because of those needs. The authority’s reasonable-cause-to-suspect enquiry duty and relevant partners’ reporting duties are different.

A capacity finding is not a substitute for the adult-at-risk analysis. Coercion, dependence, practical barriers and the adult’s own desired outcomes need attention. Reporting, enquiries, service support and authority for any imposed intervention must be distinguished.

### Decision pathway

- Record evidence against the adult-at-risk elements and address immediate safety.
- Identify your reporting responsibility and the authority responsible for enquiries.
- Use the Wales Safeguarding Procedures and the applicable statutory guidance.
- Record participation, lawful sharing, accepted responsibilities and review of outcomes.

### Challenge and review in this pathway

Explain the local-authority and provider complaint processes and relevant advocacy or legal support. A safeguarding referral does not automatically authorise removal, treatment or management of finances. Check the law for the particular proposed action.

### Additional worked case

Fictional case: An adult understands a relative’s financial demands but relies on that person for meals and fears losing contact if they report.

Consider the protection criteria, dependency and safe ways to hear the adult. Arrange immediate practical help and the appropriate report or enquiries. Understanding the financial transaction does not by itself show that the adult can protect themselves.

Common error to avoid: Using capacity as the only safeguarding threshold or treating reporting and enquiries as the same duty.

### Sources for the expanded lesson

- [Welsh Act, adult-at-risk and enquiry provision](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/anaw/2014/4/section/126)
- [Wales Safeguarding Procedures: adult at risk](https://safeguarding.wales/en/adu-i/adu-i-a2/a2-p2/)
- [Adult protection statutory guidance, Volume 6](https://www.gov.wales/sites/default/files/publications/2019-06/volume-6-handling-individual-cases-to-protect-adults-at-risk.pdf)
- [adult enquiry procedures](https://www.safeguarding.wales/en/adu-i/adu-i-a3pt1/)

# Children, Families and Transitions — Wales

Jurisdiction: Wales
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Wales practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/wales/children-families-and-transitions.html

# Children, Families and Transitions

## Learning outcomes

Connect Welsh care/support, child protection, education and transition frameworks while keeping the child's account distinct from adult service concerns.

## Use the right framework for the question

The Social Services and Well-being (Wales) Act includes child assessment and support duties. Child-protection work also requires the relevant Children Act provisions and Welsh safeguarding guidance. Do not use England's Working Together document as the Wales procedure. Refer to [Welsh statutory guidance](https://socialcare.wales/resources-guidance/information-and-learning-hub/sswbact/statutory-guidance), including Working Together to Safeguard People Volume 5, and the [Wales Safeguarding Procedures](https://safeguarding.wales/).

Distinguish a child needing care and support, a child potentially at risk, a child looked after, and a young carer. Several frameworks can be relevant simultaneously. A service allocation or adult safeguarding referral does not remove the need to consider a child's circumstances separately.

## The child's lived experience

Describe daily life: meals, sleep, school, relationships, safety, care responsibilities and who the child turns to. Use developmentally appropriate communication and the child's preferred language. Notice discrepancies between adults' explanations and the child's account without assuming which is correct. Explain confidentiality and information sharing in a way the child can understand.

When an adult is unwell or support arrangements fail, ask who takes over tasks. A child who appears capable may still be carrying responsibilities with consequences for education, rest or relationships. Make the child's support needs visible rather than treating their help as part of an adult care package.

## ALN and Individual Development Plans

Wales uses the additional learning needs framework and Individual Development Plans. The ALN Code sets out duties for schools, further-education institutions, local authorities and NHS bodies. The legal definition, responsibility for a plan, timeframes and review/challenge routes must be checked for the learner's circumstances. An IDP is not an English EHCP with a different heading. [ALN Code and official IDP examples](https://www.gov.wales/additional-learning-needs-code).

## Transition is a coordinated process

Start by mapping what is changing and when: education, support provider, home, funding, consent/decision-making arrangements and professional contacts. Do not assume support continues unchanged on a birthday, or that it must automatically stop. Clarify the applicable assessment and planning duties, identify gaps and name who is resolving each one.

Ask what the young person wants their adult life to look like. Consider communication, relationships, transport, employment or learning, cultural identity and family support. Make separate space for carers' needs. Use a shared timeline with evidence of handover and a contingency if the next service is delayed.

## Family models and safeguarding

Models can help organise conversations and hypotheses; they do not replace legal analysis or the child's evidence. Check training, local adoption and whether a method is appropriate where there is coercion or unsafe family contact. The model finder suggests topics for supervision, not a national requirement or an automated plan.

## Worked learning example

Fictional example: Seren is 17, has learning and communication needs and is leaving school. Her parent assumes adult support and transport are already arranged. Identify current plans, named contacts, decisions still outstanding and Seren's own wishes. Ask what will happen on the first day without school transport. Record actual arrangements and unresolved responsibility rather than an optimistic statement that “transition is underway”.

## Recording check

Capture the child's account, family context, caring responsibilities, source of concerns, relevant frameworks, education-plan links, information shared, named actions and dates. Record disagreements, missing information and escalation arrangements. Keep cross-border placements and responsibility questions explicit in the handover.

<!-- curriculum-expansion -->

## Further local practice detail

Welsh care and support, child protection and education duties need to be mapped separately. The Social Services and Well-being (Wales) Act 2014 works alongside the Children Act framework and the Additional Learning Needs and Education Tribunal (Wales) Act 2018.

An Individual Development Plan (IDP) records additional learning needs and provision within the Welsh education framework. It does not replace a care and support plan or child-protection response. Welsh Government published further ALN decision-making guidance and example IDP forms in 2026; use these with the Code and statutory duties.

### Decision pathway

- Identify the child’s support and protection needs and the relevant Welsh statutory route.
- Hear the child and family with suitable language and communication support.
- Check who prepares and maintains the IDP and how education, health and social care contributions connect.
- Plan transition with named responsibilities and confirm actual acceptance by the next service.

### Challenge and review in this pathway

Disagreement about an ALN decision can involve the applicable reconsideration, disagreement-resolution and Education Tribunal for Wales routes. A social-care complaint follows a different process. Help the family identify the decision and remedy without allowing one dispute to halt other necessary support.

### Additional worked case

Fictional case: A young person has an IDP but no agreed adult support when leaving school, and each service assumes the plan guarantees the other’s provision.

Separate education duties from adult care assessment and service eligibility. Identify the young person’s goals, obtain named decisions and arrange a coordinated transition. The existence of an IDP does not establish that adult social-care support has been agreed.

Common error to avoid: Treating an education plan as a substitute for care assessment or a completed transition handover.

### Sources for the expanded lesson

- [ALN and Education Tribunal (Wales) Act 2018](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/anaw/2018/2/contents)
- [ALN decision-making and communication guidance](https://www.gov.wales/additional-learning-needs-aln-decision-making-and-communication-html)
- [Example IDP standard form, June 2026](https://www.gov.wales/individual-development-plan-idp-example-standard-form)
- [Welsh statutory guidance](https://socialcare.wales/resources-guidance/information-and-learning-hub/sswbact/statutory-guidance)
- [Wales Safeguarding Procedures](https://safeguarding.wales/)
- [ALN Code and official IDP examples](https://www.gov.wales/additional-learning-needs-code)

# Rights, Language and Recording — Wales

Jurisdiction: Wales
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Wales practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/wales/rights-language-and-recording.html

# 08 - Equality, Human Rights, and Recording

## Purpose

This module helps keep social work lawful, anti-oppressive, and defensible.

## Equality Act 2010

Protected characteristics include:

- age
- disability
- gender reassignment
- marriage and civil partnership
- pregnancy and maternity
- race
- religion or belief
- sex
- sexual orientation

Practice duties include:

- making reasonable adjustments
- avoiding direct and indirect discrimination
- recognising harassment and victimisation
- considering the Public Sector Equality Duty where relevant

## Reasonable Adjustments

Adjustments may include:

- accessible formats
- interpreter
- communication aids
- extra time
- quiet environment
- home visit
- involving a trusted person
- flexible appointments
- advocacy
- sensory adaptations
- accessible transport

Record adjustments offered and whether they worked.

## Human Rights Act

Commonly relevant rights:

- Article 2: right to life
- Article 3: freedom from torture, inhuman or degrading treatment
- Article 5: liberty and security
- Article 6: fair process
- Article 8: private and family life, home, and correspondence
- Article 14: non-discrimination in enjoyment of rights

Human rights analysis is not abstract. It helps answer:

- What right is engaged?
- Is interference lawful?
- Is there a legitimate aim?
- Is the action necessary and proportionate?
- Is there a less restrictive alternative?
- Has the person been involved?
- Are safeguards available?

## Anti-Oppressive Practice

Ask:

- How might racism, ableism, sexism, homophobia, transphobia, ageism, poverty, immigration status, trauma, or institutional mistrust shape this situation?
- Whose account is being believed most easily?
- Is the person being described in loaded language?
- Are services expecting the person to adapt to the system rather than adapting the system to the person?
- Is risk being overestimated because of stigma or underestimated because of familiarity?

## Culturally Responsive Practice

Do:

- ask, do not assume
- use interpreters
- recognise religious and cultural networks as possible strengths
- explore family roles without stereotyping
- understand migration, racism, asylum, and trauma contexts
- consider food, prayer, gender, modesty, grief, and end-of-life customs
- challenge harmful practice without condemning identity

## Good Recording

Good records are:

- accurate
- timely
- respectful
- evidence-led
- analytical
- clear about legal basis
- clear about the person's voice
- clear about disagreement
- clear about risk and protective factors
- clear about decisions and review

## Recording Formula

```text
What happened?
Who said what?
What did I observe?
What evidence supports this?
What does the person want?
What law/policy applies?
What options were considered?
What decision was made?
Why is it proportionate?
What happens next?
```

## Language to Avoid

Avoid:

- non-compliant
- attention-seeking
- manipulative
- difficult family
- refusing to engage
- lifestyle choice
- bed blocker
- failed placement
- challenging behaviour without context

Use:

- declined
- distressed
- disagreed
- unable to attend
- communication of unmet need
- pattern of self-neglect
- family disputes the plan
- placement is no longer meeting needs

## Defensible Decision-Making

A decision is more defensible when it shows:

- relevant law and policy were considered
- relevant information was gathered
- the person was involved
- capacity and consent were addressed
- risks and benefits were balanced
- less restrictive options were considered
- discrimination and human rights were considered
- reasons were recorded
- review or contingency was set

## Common Pitfalls

- Recording professional opinion as fact.
- Omitting the person's own words.
- Describing behaviour without context.
- Using vague risk phrases.
- Copying forward old assessments.
- Not explaining why options were rejected.
- Forgetting equality and communication needs.
- Recording "family agreed" without saying who, what authority they had, and whether the person agreed.


## Welsh language and participation

Make an active offer of Welsh-language support and record how the preference will be met in assessment, meetings, plans and review. Check the organisation's Welsh language standards and arrangements. Language can affect trust, emotional expression and the reliability of an assessment; it is not simply a document-translation task.

## Information sharing in Wales

Identify the purpose, lawful basis, people who need the information and the minimum relevant information. Consent is not always required to share safeguarding information, but there must be a lawful justification. Record the decision to share or not share and explain it to the person where appropriate and safe. Seek information-governance advice where the position is unclear. The ICO flags that its guidance is being reviewed following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025; check updates for live decisions.

## Practice exercise

Fictional case: an adult asks for Welsh-language meetings but the invitation and proposed support plan are in English. Their relative answers every question. Write three changes that would enable direct participation. Then record the difference between what the adult said, what the relative reported and your own analysis. Identify a review date and who will confirm that the communication changes worked.

## Wales sources

- [More than just words update](https://www.gov.wales/written-statement-update-more-just-words-2022-27)
- [ICO safeguarding information-sharing guidance](https://ico.org.uk/10steps)
- [Welsh social services codes](https://www.gov.wales/social-services-codes-practice)

<!-- curriculum-expansion -->

## Further local practice detail

The Human Rights Act 1998, Equality Act 2010, applicable data-protection law and Welsh-language duties engage different parts of a decision. More than just words promotes the Active Offer of Welsh-language care, recognising language as part of safe and effective support.

Distinguish a person’s language need and the organisation’s applicable Welsh-language standards from a general translation preference. Record how communication affects participation, consent, assessment and the reliability of evidence. A completed English form is not proof that the person could take part effectively.

### Decision pathway

- Ask and record language and communication needs and make the Active Offer practical.
- Identify the actual equality, human-rights and Welsh-language duties of the service.
- Check the purpose and lawful basis for information sharing, with appropriate limits.
- Explain access, correction, complaints and the relevant rights or language challenge route.

### Challenge and review in this pathway

A Welsh-language standards concern, a privacy complaint and a challenge to the care decision may require different bodies. Explain the organisation’s procedure and relevant external route. Address immediate access barriers while a complaint is considered.

### Additional worked case

Fictional case: A Welsh-speaking adult appears confused during an English assessment but communicates clearly when suitable Welsh-language support is arranged.

Revisit the evidence and any capacity or eligibility conclusions affected by the communication barrier. Record the support required for future contacts and the person’s account, rather than retaining an unsupported label of confusion.

Common error to avoid: Treating language access as cosmetic or using a communication barrier as evidence of incapacity.

### Sources for the expanded lesson

- [More than just words and the Active Offer](https://www.gov.wales/written-statement-update-more-just-words-2022-27)
- [Welsh Language (Wales) Measure 2011](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/mwa/2011/1/contents)
- [ICO safeguarding information-sharing guidance](https://ico.org.uk/10steps)
- [Welsh social services codes](https://www.gov.wales/social-services-codes-practice)

# Quick Reference — Wales

Jurisdiction: Wales
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Wales practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/wales/quick-reference.html

# Practice reference — Wales practice guide


Use alongside the full modules and current official sources. Each entry separates the local framework, action and review.


## Professional Foundations

Social Care Wales’s new Codes of Professional Practice took effect in July 2026. Use the current worker Code and distinguish it from the employer Code, local-authority procedures and statutory appointments. The professional framework applies across different settings, but the legal power for an intervention depends on the actual function.

A person’s preferred language and ability to participate belong in the first conversation, formulation and plan. Record how supervision, feedback and professional learning change practice rather than only listing completed training.


- Check the current Social Care Wales Code and the requirements of the actual role.
- Explain the legal or voluntary purpose of involvement and confidentiality limits.
- Make language, accessibility, power and service barriers visible in assessment.
- Distinguish a professional concern, service complaint and statutory decision challenge.


Social Care Wales addresses professional regulation; the local authority, provider and relevant statutory review bodies address different service decisions. Explain the route that can provide the remedy the person seeks.


- [New professional Codes, July 2026](https://socialcare.wales/news-stories/new-codes-of-professional-practice)
- [Social Care Wales worker Code](https://socialcare.wales/codes-of-practice-and-guidance/code-of-professional-practice-for-social-care-workers)
- [Practice guidance](https://socialcare.wales/codes-of-practice-and-guidance/practice-guidance-for-the-code-of-professional-practice)


## Care and Support in Wales

The Social Services and Well-being (Wales) Act 2014 separates adult, child and carer assessments in sections 19, 21 and 24. Part 4 and the eligibility regulations govern the next stage; the Part 5 charging decision is separate. Use the current Welsh assessment, meeting-needs, charging and advocacy Codes.

Eligibility requires the applicable needs-and-outcomes analysis and consideration of whether the person can meet those needs alone, with willing others or through accessible community services, or requires the authority’s involvement. A service that exists on a directory but cannot be accessed is not an established solution.


- Identify the correct assessment duty and explain the person’s outcomes and evidence of need.
- Apply the relevant Welsh eligibility regulations rather than a test imported from another system.
- Check participation barriers and the independent professional advocacy requirements.
- Record the support plan, separate charging decision, unmet needs and review or complaint route.


Ask for written reasons and the relevant local-authority review or complaints process. Consider independent advocacy where required to make participation effective. A disagreement over charges should not erase the needs assessment or interim support plan.


- [Social Services and Well-being (Wales) Act 2014](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/anaw/2014/4/contents)
- [Care and Support (Eligibility) (Wales) Regulations 2015](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/wsi/2015/1578/contents)
- [Assessment Code](https://www.gov.wales/assessing-care-and-support-needs-individuals-code-practice)
- [Advocacy Code](https://www.gov.wales/advocacy-services-code-practice)
- [Welsh codes collection](https://www.gov.wales/social-services-codes-practice)


## Mental Capacity Act 2005

The Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies to the specific decision and time. The person must be unable to decide because of an impairment or disturbance of mind or brain; inability concerns understanding, retaining, using or weighing relevant information, or communicating the decision. Support must be tried and an unwise choice is not itself incapacity.

An attorney, deputy, advance decision and a professional acting under the Act have different roles and limits. A best-interests decision should preserve participation and consider wishes, feelings, beliefs, values and less restrictive options. It does not itself answer every deprivation-of-liberty or mental-health authority question.


- Specify the decision and record support and evidence against the relevant abilities.
- Explain the causal connection to impairment if concluding that capacity is lacking.
- Check any attorney, deputy or advance decision and the scope of its authority.
- Record best-interests reasoning, consultation, disagreement and the appropriate challenge route.


The Court of Protection deals with relevant disputes and decisions. Consider statutory advocacy requirements and specialist advice where serious disagreement or liberty issues arise. A relative’s agreement should not substitute for the required legal analysis.


- [Mental Capacity Act 2005](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2005/9/contents)
- [MCA Code of Practice](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/mental-capacity-act-code-of-practice)
- [Welsh DoLS guidance and forms](https://www.gov.wales/mental-capacity-act-deprivation-liberty-guidance-and-forms)


## DoLS and Deprivation of Liberty

The Supreme Court’s June 2026 judgment requires the liberty analysis to distinguish the Article 5 consent question from domestic decision-making capacity. The old two-part checklist should not be used as the sole answer. Mere acquiescence does not establish valid consent.

Where required, the hospital or care-home DoLS route and community Court of Protection arrangements have different scope. The actual restrictions, the person’s understanding and wishes, the authorisation and the care or treatment decisions should remain separate in the record.


- Record the actual setting, restrictions, duration and response to a wish to leave.
- Use current judgment and Welsh guidance with specialist advice on the applicable legal test.
- Check the correct authorisation route, representation, conditions and review.
- Explore less restrictive alternatives and act on objections or changed circumstances.


Explain the representative, advocacy and court challenge arrangements that apply. An existing authorisation should be reviewed through the responsible process; do not simply remove safeguards on the basis of a changed summary or training slide.


- [Supreme Court judgment summary and case](https://supremecourt.uk/cases/press-summary/uksc-2025-0042)
- [Welsh regulator statement on liberty judgment](https://www.careinspectorate.wales/supreme-court-judgment-deprivation-liberty)
- [Welsh DoLS guidance and forms](https://www.gov.wales/mental-capacity-act-deprivation-liberty-guidance-and-forms)


## Mental Health in Wales

Use the Mental Health Act 1983 with the Welsh Code of Practice and commenced amendments. The Mental Health (Wales) Measure 2010 adds distinct duties concerning primary mental-health support, care coordination and planning, reassessment of eligible former service users and advocacy. It is not simply another detention route.

Part 2 care and treatment planning concerns outcomes, services, responsibilities and review. Part 3 provides a direct reassessment route for eligible former secondary-service users, subject to its conditions. New mental-health reform provisions must be checked for commencement before changing operational procedures.


- Identify the exact assessment, detention, treatment or Measure duty involved.
- Use the Welsh Code and current statutory forms and commencement information.
- For care planning, record outcomes, named services, responsibilities and review.
- Explain reassessment and advocacy rights appropriate to the person’s eligibility and status.


The Mental Health Review Tribunal for Wales and other statutory review routes address particular detention questions. Measure care planning and reassessment are separate rights. Explain which process addresses the person’s concern and how to obtain support or legal advice.


- [Welsh Mental Health Act Code](https://www.gov.wales/mental-health-act-1983-code-practice)
- [Mental Health (Wales) Measure 2010](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/mwa/2010/7/contents)
- [Current Welsh explanation of Measure activity](https://www.gov.wales/mental-health-wales-measure-2010-june-2026-html)
- [Mental Health Act 2025 first commencement regulations](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/385/contents)
- [Senedd research overview](https://research.senedd.wales/research-articles/devolution-and-health-in-wales-part-2-mental-health-organ-donation-and-nurse-staffing/)
- [Part 3 information](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/mwa/2010/7/part/3)
- [Government reform collection](https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/mental-health-bill-2025)


## Safeguarding Adults in Wales

Section 126 of the Social Services and Well-being (Wales) Act 2014 concerns an adult experiencing or at risk of abuse or neglect, with care and support needs, who cannot protect themselves because of those needs. The authority’s reasonable-cause-to-suspect enquiry duty and relevant partners’ reporting duties are different.

A capacity finding is not a substitute for the adult-at-risk analysis. Coercion, dependence, practical barriers and the adult’s own desired outcomes need attention. Reporting, enquiries, service support and authority for any imposed intervention must be distinguished.


- Record evidence against the adult-at-risk elements and address immediate safety.
- Identify your reporting responsibility and the authority responsible for enquiries.
- Use the Wales Safeguarding Procedures and the applicable statutory guidance.
- Record participation, lawful sharing, accepted responsibilities and review of outcomes.


Explain the local-authority and provider complaint processes and relevant advocacy or legal support. A safeguarding referral does not automatically authorise removal, treatment or management of finances. Check the law for the particular proposed action.


- [Welsh Act, adult-at-risk and enquiry provision](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/anaw/2014/4/section/126)
- [Wales Safeguarding Procedures: adult at risk](https://safeguarding.wales/en/adu-i/adu-i-a2/a2-p2/)
- [Adult protection statutory guidance, Volume 6](https://www.gov.wales/sites/default/files/publications/2019-06/volume-6-handling-individual-cases-to-protect-adults-at-risk.pdf)
- [adult enquiry procedures](https://www.safeguarding.wales/en/adu-i/adu-i-a3pt1/)


## Children, Families and Transitions

Welsh care and support, child protection and education duties need to be mapped separately. The Social Services and Well-being (Wales) Act 2014 works alongside the Children Act framework and the Additional Learning Needs and Education Tribunal (Wales) Act 2018.

An Individual Development Plan (IDP) records additional learning needs and provision within the Welsh education framework. It does not replace a care and support plan or child-protection response. Welsh Government published further ALN decision-making guidance and example IDP forms in 2026; use these with the Code and statutory duties.


- Identify the child’s support and protection needs and the relevant Welsh statutory route.
- Hear the child and family with suitable language and communication support.
- Check who prepares and maintains the IDP and how education, health and social care contributions connect.
- Plan transition with named responsibilities and confirm actual acceptance by the next service.


Disagreement about an ALN decision can involve the applicable reconsideration, disagreement-resolution and Education Tribunal for Wales routes. A social-care complaint follows a different process. Help the family identify the decision and remedy without allowing one dispute to halt other necessary support.


- [ALN and Education Tribunal (Wales) Act 2018](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/anaw/2018/2/contents)
- [ALN decision-making and communication guidance](https://www.gov.wales/additional-learning-needs-aln-decision-making-and-communication-html)
- [Example IDP standard form, June 2026](https://www.gov.wales/individual-development-plan-idp-example-standard-form)
- [Welsh statutory guidance](https://socialcare.wales/resources-guidance/information-and-learning-hub/sswbact/statutory-guidance)
- [Wales Safeguarding Procedures](https://safeguarding.wales/)
- [ALN Code and official IDP examples](https://www.gov.wales/additional-learning-needs-code)


## Rights, Language and Recording

The Human Rights Act 1998, Equality Act 2010, applicable data-protection law and Welsh-language duties engage different parts of a decision. More than just words promotes the Active Offer of Welsh-language care, recognising language as part of safe and effective support.

Distinguish a person’s language need and the organisation’s applicable Welsh-language standards from a general translation preference. Record how communication affects participation, consent, assessment and the reliability of evidence. A completed English form is not proof that the person could take part effectively.


- Ask and record language and communication needs and make the Active Offer practical.
- Identify the actual equality, human-rights and Welsh-language duties of the service.
- Check the purpose and lawful basis for information sharing, with appropriate limits.
- Explain access, correction, complaints and the relevant rights or language challenge route.


A Welsh-language standards concern, a privacy complaint and a challenge to the care decision may require different bodies. Explain the organisation’s procedure and relevant external route. Address immediate access barriers while a complaint is considered.


- [More than just words and the Active Offer](https://www.gov.wales/written-statement-update-more-just-words-2022-27)
- [Welsh Language (Wales) Measure 2011](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/mwa/2011/1/contents)
- [ICO safeguarding information-sharing guidance](https://ico.org.uk/10steps)
- [Welsh social services codes](https://www.gov.wales/social-services-codes-practice)

# Templates and Checklists — Wales

Jurisdiction: Wales
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Wales practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/wales/templates-and-checklists.html

# Wales recording templates

Use these ten structures to practise recording facts, analysis, the person’s perspective and agreed action. Download an individual prompt or the full collection below. They are learning aids, not statutory forms. Do not put identifiable case details in this browser.

## Care and support assessment

1. Person’s account, language and communication
2. What matters: outcomes and changes sought
3. Strengths, relationships, environment and barriers
4. Care and support needs and evidence
5. Support for participation and advocacy
6. Carer position, willingness and separate assessment
7. Immediate needs and protective action
8. Eligibility analysis under Welsh regulations and Code
9. Options, agreed plan, responsibilities and contingency
10. Charging or financial assessment addressed separately
11. Disagreements, reasons, review date and challenge route

[Practice source](https://www.gov.wales/social-services-codes-practice)

## Carer support assessment

1. Carer’s own account and desired outcomes
2. Nature and impact of caring, including work, study and wellbeing
3. Willingness and ability to continue: do not presume
4. Current support and unmet support needs
5. Language, participation and advocacy
6. Assessment and eligibility analysis
7. Support options, contingency and emergency contacts
8. Agreed actions, responsible people and review

[Practice source](https://www.gov.wales/social-services-codes-practice)

## Decision-specific capacity

1. Exact decision and time
2. Reason to assess and relevant impairment or disturbance
3. All practicable communication and decision support
4. Relevant information and realistic options
5. Person’s responses: understand, retain, use or weigh, communicate
6. How any inability results from impairment or disturbance
7. Evidence for conclusion and uncertainties
8. Can the decision wait? Review trigger and date
9. Next action and separate best interests process if required

[Practice source](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/mental-capacity-act-code-of-practice)

## Best interests decision

1. Decision, capacity finding and decision-maker
2. Attorney/deputy/advance decision: validity and scope
3. Person’s participation, wishes, feelings, beliefs and values
4. Relevant circumstances and prospect of regaining capacity
5. People consulted and their views
6. Options, benefits, burdens and less restrictive alternatives
7. Decision, rationale and unresolved disagreement
8. Separate authority for restraint or deprivation of liberty where relevant
9. Implementation, challenge route and review

[Practice source](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/mental-capacity-act-code-of-practice)

## Adult safeguarding: Wales

1. Immediate safety or emergency response
2. Factual concern, source, timing and evidence preserved
3. Section 126 adult-at-risk criteria: analysis not just a tick
4. Adult’s account, desired outcomes, communication and advocacy
5. Safe contact, coercion and capacity questions
6. Reporting under Welsh procedures and relevant section 128 duty
7. Local authority enquiries and multi-agency responsibilities
8. Information-sharing purpose, lawful justification and recipients
9. Protection plan, person responsible, timescale and review
10. Reasons for decisions and escalation of unresolved concerns

[Practice source](https://safeguarding.wales/)

## Liberty and restriction review

1. Setting, age and actual care arrangements
2. Restrictions: type, intensity, duration and effects
3. Person’s wishes, feelings, objection and support to express them
4. Consent analysis under current law distinct from domestic capacity
5. Current June 2026 judgment and Welsh guidance checked
6. Less restrictive options considered
7. DoLS, court or other legal route: advice and reasons
8. Existing authorisation scope and conditions
9. Representation, rights to challenge and urgent actions
10. Review date and changes requiring earlier review

[Practice source](https://www.careinspectorate.wales/supreme-court-judgment-deprivation-liberty)

## Mental health interface discussion

1. Immediate safety, person’s account and communication needs
2. Purpose of proposed intervention
3. Clinical team and AMHP involvement
4. Less restrictive support and alternatives
5. Welsh Code and current statutory provision checked
6. MHA/MCA/DoLS interface and reasons for proposed route
7. Physical treatment considered separately
8. Advocacy, rights information, family or carer involvement
9. Care coordination, discharge and aftercare questions
10. Responsibilities, escalation and review

[Practice source](https://www.gov.wales/mental-health-act-1983-code-practice)

## Child, family and transition planning

1. Child or young person’s own words and aspirations
2. Language, communication and participation
3. Immediate safeguarding concerns and Welsh procedure
4. Family strengths, support needs and young carer considerations
5. ALN/IDP, education, health and care planning links
6. Decisions and capacity framework where applicable
7. Named coordinator, services and cross-border questions
8. Actions before transition and continuity arrangements
9. Carer support, disagreements and advocacy
10. Review with the young person: dates and accountable people

[Practice source](https://www.gov.wales/additional-learning-needs-code)

## Reflective supervision

1. Anonymised learning situation and your role
2. Facts separated from reports and assumptions
3. Person’s perspective and what influenced your judgement
4. Competing hypotheses and contrary evidence
5. Relevant Welsh sources and dates checked
6. Power, language, equality and ethical tensions
7. What went well and what needs to change
8. Feedback and discussion with manager
9. Action, evidence of impact and next review

[Practice source](https://socialcare.wales/codes-of-practice-and-guidance/practice-guidance-for-the-code-of-professional-practice)

## Chronology and analysis

1. Date/time of event and date information received
2. Event, source and direct or reported evidence
3. Person’s account and impact
4. Action and rationale at the time
5. Patterns, protective factors and alternative explanations
6. Missing or contradictory evidence
7. Current risk and proportionate action
8. Responsible person, deadline and review

[Practice source](https://safeguarding.wales/)

# Wales printable practice tools

Ten downloadable prompts cover care and support, carers, capacity, best interests, safeguarding, liberty, mental health, transition, supervision and chronology. Every file identifies Wales and its source.

## Using a prompt

1. Choose the relevant topic; more than one may apply.
2. Practise with a fictional case.
3. Identify unanswered questions and current-source checks.
4. Review your reasoning in supervision.
5. Use your organisation’s approved records for actual casework.

Print this section or download the text files below. The complete written structures are also in Recording Templates.


## Downloadable prompt text

### Care and support assessment

```text
Care and support assessment
Wales practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Social Services and Well-being (Wales) Act 2014 separates adult, child and carer assessments in sections 19, 21 and 24. Part 4 and the eligibility regulations govern the next stage; the Part 5 charging decision is separate. Use the current Welsh assessment, meeting-needs, charging and advocacy Codes.

Eligibility requires the applicable needs-and-outcomes analysis and consideration of whether the person can meet those needs alone, with willing others or through accessible community services, or requires the authority’s involvement. A service that exists on a directory but cannot be accessed is not an established solution.

Local pathway:
Identify the correct assessment duty and explain the person’s outcomes and evidence of need.
Apply the relevant Welsh eligibility regulations rather than a test imported from another system.
Check participation barriers and the independent professional advocacy requirements.
Record the support plan, separate charging decision, unmet needs and review or complaint route.

Recording prompts:
1. Daily-life evidence, fluctuation and desired outcomes
Notes:

2. The service, eligibility test and decision-maker
Notes:

3. Carer willingness and separately identified needs
Notes:

4. Funding, charges, decisions and reasons
Notes:

5. Start dates, unmet needs, contingency and challenge route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Ask for written reasons and the relevant local-authority review or complaints process. Consider independent advocacy where required to make participation effective. A disagreement over charges should not erase the needs assessment or interim support plan.

Sources:
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/anaw/2014/4/contents
```

### Decision-specific capacity

```text
Decision-specific capacity
Wales practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies to the specific decision and time. The person must be unable to decide because of an impairment or disturbance of mind or brain; inability concerns understanding, retaining, using or weighing relevant information, or communicating the decision. Support must be tried and an unwise choice is not itself incapacity.

An attorney, deputy, advance decision and a professional acting under the Act have different roles and limits. A best-interests decision should preserve participation and consider wishes, feelings, beliefs, values and less restrictive options. It does not itself answer every deprivation-of-liberty or mental-health authority question.

Local pathway:
Specify the decision and record support and evidence against the relevant abilities.
Explain the causal connection to impairment if concluding that capacity is lacking.
Check any attorney, deputy or advance decision and the scope of its authority.
Record best-interests reasoning, consultation, disagreement and the appropriate challenge route.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, options and time at which it is needed
Notes:

2. Communication support and observed responses
Notes:

3. Applicable legal test and evidence for each element
Notes:

4. Representative’s document, scope and decision standard
Notes:

5. Wishes, disagreement, review and any urgent action
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The Court of Protection deals with relevant disputes and decisions. Consider statutory advocacy requirements and specialist advice where serious disagreement or liberty issues arise. A relative’s agreement should not substitute for the required legal analysis.

Sources:
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2005/9/contents
https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/mental-capacity-act-code-of-practice
https://www.gov.wales/mental-capacity-act-deprivation-liberty-guidance-and-forms
```

# Practice Scenarios — Wales

Jurisdiction: Wales
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Wales practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/wales/practice-scenarios.html

# Scenario Workouts — Wales practice guide


All cases are fictional learning exercises. Explain your evidence and reasoning before reading the discussion.


## Professional Foundations

A worker uses an old professional-code handout and an English-only assessment despite a request for Welsh-language support.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Use the current Code, arrange appropriate communication and revisit any assessment conclusions affected by the barrier. Link the change to supervision and feedback from the person.


## Care and Support in Wales

An authority says community support meets a need, but the only advertised group has no accessible transport or available places.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Check actual availability and accessibility in the eligibility reasoning. Revisit whether authority involvement is required, record the unmet need and agree interim action. A directory listing alone does not demonstrate that the outcome can be achieved.


## Mental Capacity Act 2005

An adult refuses a proposed care arrangement after explaining its benefits and drawbacks, while relatives consider the choice too risky.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Explore the reasoning and support needs without treating disagreement as incapacity. If capacity is lacking, identify the exact authority and best-interests process. Keep the person’s wishes and any liberty issue separately recorded.


## DoLS and Deprivation of Liberty

A resident is quiet during meetings but repeatedly packs a bag and asks staff to take them home.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Use appropriate communication to understand the request and record how staff respond. Review actual restrictions and consent evidence with the responsible specialist. Calm presentation does not settle the legal question or remove the need to support a challenge.


## Mental Health in Wales

An eligible former secondary-service user reports deterioration and is told that only a new GP referral can lead to assessment.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Check the Part 3 conditions and explain the direct reassessment route where applicable. Arrange an appropriate response to urgent need and record responsibility and follow-up. Do not confuse reassessment rights with a guarantee of a particular service.


## Safeguarding Adults in Wales

An adult understands a relative’s financial demands but relies on that person for meals and fears losing contact if they report.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Consider the protection criteria, dependency and safe ways to hear the adult. Arrange immediate practical help and the appropriate report or enquiries. Understanding the financial transaction does not by itself show that the adult can protect themselves.


## Children, Families and Transitions

A young person has an IDP but no agreed adult support when leaving school, and each service assumes the plan guarantees the other’s provision.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Separate education duties from adult care assessment and service eligibility. Identify the young person’s goals, obtain named decisions and arrange a coordinated transition. The existence of an IDP does not establish that adult social-care support has been agreed.


## Rights, Language and Recording

A Welsh-speaking adult appears confused during an English assessment but communicates clearly when suitable Welsh-language support is arranged.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Revisit the evidence and any capacity or eligibility conclusions affected by the communication barrier. Record the support required for future contacts and the person’s account, rather than retaining an unsupported label of confusion.

# About Us — Wales

Jurisdiction: Wales
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Wales practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/wales/about-us.html

# About Us

Daily Mindset Moments CIC is the organisation behind this learning resource. It was founded by Raymond Hill, founder and social worker, with a focus on practical technology that reduces pressure, supports clearer thinking, and helps people turn complex work into usable systems.

This Social Worker Resource reflects that mission. It is designed to help social workers, students, newly qualified social workers, managers, safeguarding practitioners, and care professionals learn key legal frameworks in a more structured, calm, and usable way.

## Our Mission

The mission of Daily Mindset Moments is to build practical digital tools with human purpose. The work is centred on helping people, businesses, families, communities, and professionals do more with less pressure.

The aim is not to replace human judgement. It is to give people better systems, clearer information, and more space for care, creativity, decision-making, and meaningful human connection.

For social work, that matters. Good tools should make legal literacy, reflective practice, safeguarding thinking, recording, supervision, and learning easier to access without taking the human voice out of the work.

## Why This Resource Exists

Social work law and guidance can feel heavy when it is scattered across legislation, statutory guidance, codes of practice, policy updates, and local procedures. This resource brings the major frameworks into one structured learning space.

It is built to support:

- clear learning routes through Welsh care and support law, Mental Capacity Act, DoLS, Mental Health Act, safeguarding, transitions, equality, human rights, and recording;
- practical case analysis that keeps the person, their rights, and their outcomes at the centre;
- confident supervision, reflective learning, newly qualified development, and practice conversations;
- safer decision-making by encouraging practitioners to check current law, guidance, local policy, and legal advice.

This resource is not legal advice. It is a learning and practice-support tool.

## Daily Mindset Moments Ecosystem

Daily Mindset Moments CIC connects AI software, wellbeing, care, learning, business support, and community connection through a growing ecosystem of websites and product brands.

| Website | Focus | What it supports |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Daily Mindset Moments](https://www.daily-mindset-moments.com) | AI software studio with a social mission | Practical AI products, automation, digital platforms, and responsible technology for business, care, wellbeing, learning, and communities. |
| [Amplify You](https://www.amplify-you.ai) | AI marketing automation | Campaign planning, content ideas, captions, publishing workflows, analytics, and clearer brand visibility. |
| [Vent It Out](https://www.vent-it-out.org) | Mental wellbeing | Reflection, mood tracking, voice journalling, safety planning, affirmations, and routes to support. |
| [Grace Companion](https://www.grace-companion.com) | Compassionate care technology | Support for families, older people, routines, reassurance, prompts, and daily connection. |
| [Nexus Historia](https://www.nexus-historia.co.uk) | Interactive education | Alternate histories, timelines, story worlds, scenario generation, and creative learning. |
| [My Civic Circles](https://mycivic-circles.com) | Community networking | Venue discovery, professional meetups, and trusted local and global connections. |

## Responsible Technology

Daily Mindset Moments is built around the idea that useful technology should be practical, explainable, privacy-aware, and led by human judgement.

The products are shaped around:

- human review where decisions affect trust, care, safety, or reputation;
- accessible design that reduces confusion and cognitive load;
- responsible use of AI where the person remains in control;
- practical outcomes such as time saved, clearer communication, better access, and reduced avoidable strain;
- reinvesting success into wider access to useful AI coaching, skills, and development tools.

## Raymond Hill

Raymond Hill is the founder of Daily Mindset Moments CIC and a social worker. His work combines social work values, lived understanding of pressure and cognitive load, and practical AI product development.

The aim is to create tools that feel usable in real life: calm enough to learn from, structured enough to support decision-making, and human enough to keep care, rights, relationships, and dignity at the centre.

# Privacy Policy — Wales

# Privacy Policy

Last updated: 8 September 2026.

This privacy policy explains how the Ultimate Social Worker Resource handles information when you use this website.

## Who Runs This Resource

Daily Mindset Moments CIC is the data controller for personal information collected through this website. It is founded by Raymond Hill, founder and social worker.

Main website: [www.daily-mindset-moments.com](https://www.daily-mindset-moments.com)

Privacy contact: [info@daily-mindset-moments.com](mailto:info@daily-mindset-moments.com)

## What This Website Stores Locally

The learning resource uses your browser's local storage to remember:

- your selected practice location;
- which sections you have marked as read, separately for each location;
- your confidence ratings for learning sections;
- reflections you save and unfinished form text saved automatically as you type, separately for each location.

This information stays on your device and is not sent to Daily Mindset Moments CIC by the learning resource.

It should remain after a normal page refresh. It may disappear if you clear browser site data, use private browsing, change device or browser, or if a workplace device resets browser storage.

You can clear it by clearing your browser site data for this website.

Do not save names, addresses, dates of birth, case numbers, or identifiable case information in the CPD and reflection log. The CPD log is a local drafting tool only. It does not send CPD to Social Care Wales or to Daily Mindset Moments CIC. Use the export or Print / Save as PDF option if you need to keep a copy.

## Contact Form Information

If you use the Contact Us form, the information you enter is processed through Netlify Forms and made available to authorised people at Daily Mindset Moments CIC so that we can respond to and manage your enquiry. This may include:

- your name;
- your email address;
- your organisation;
- your enquiry type;
- your message;
- your consent to be contacted about the enquiry.

We use this information only to respond to and manage the enquiry. The form is optional and asks for your agreement to be contacted; this is our lawful basis for processing the enquiry. We do not use an enquiry for marketing unless you separately ask us to do so or give separate consent.

Netlify Forms provides the form-processing service. Netlify and its service providers may process data in countries outside the UK; where a restricted transfer is involved, the provider's applicable data-transfer safeguards apply. You can read [Netlify's privacy policy](https://www.netlify.com/privacy/).

We retain contact-form enquiries for up to 12 months after the last meaningful contact, unless a longer period is necessary to manage an ongoing relationship or meet a legal obligation. We then delete or anonymise them.

Only send information that is appropriate for a business, learning, partnership, or general enquiry.

Do not send confidential case information or personal data about people using services.

## Your Data Rights

Subject to the circumstances, you can ask to access, correct, erase, restrict, or object to our use of your personal information. You may withdraw your consent to be contacted about an enquiry at any time. To make a request, email [info@daily-mindset-moments.com](mailto:info@daily-mindset-moments.com).

You can also complain to the [Information Commissioner's Office](https://ico.org.uk/make-a-complaint/).

## External Links

This website links to Daily Mindset Moments CIC and related product websites. Those websites may have their own privacy notices, cookies, analytics, forms, and terms.

External websites linked from this resource include:

- [Daily Mindset Moments](https://www.daily-mindset-moments.com)
- [Amplify You](https://www.amplify-you.ai)
- [Vent It Out](https://www.vent-it-out.org)
- [Grace Companion](https://www.grace-companion.com)
- [Nexus Historia](https://www.nexus-historia.co.uk)
- [My Civic Circles](https://mycivic-circles.com)

## Learning Content

This resource is for learning and practice support. It does not require an account, and it does not ask you to upload case records or personal documents.

## Contact

For privacy-related questions, use the Contact Us page or visit [www.daily-mindset-moments.com](https://www.daily-mindset-moments.com).

# Terms of Service — Wales

Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/wales/terms-of-service.html

# Terms of Service

Last updated: 8 September 2026.

These terms explain how the Ultimate Social Worker Resource may be used.

## Purpose of This Resource

This website is a structured learning and practice-support resource for social workers, students, newly qualified social workers, managers, safeguarding practitioners, care coordinators, and related professionals.

It is designed to support learning around Welsh care and support law, Mental Capacity Act, DoLS, Mental Health Act, safeguarding, transitions, equality, human rights, recording, and reflective practice.

## Content Review Date

The Wales source check was completed on 8 September 2026. Independent Welsh practitioner review has not been completed. This date is a source-check note, not a guarantee that every law, guidance document, policy position, or external link remains current after that date.

Users should always verify current legislation, statutory guidance, codes of practice, local policy, and legal advice before relying on the resource in live practice.

## Not Legal Advice

This resource is not legal advice. It does not replace:

- current legislation;
- statutory guidance;
- codes of practice;
- court judgments;
- local authority policy;
- employer procedures;
- legal services advice;
- supervision or management oversight.

For live cases, always check current law, local procedures, legal advice, and supervision.

## Professional Responsibility

Users remain responsible for their own professional judgement, recording, decision-making, escalation, and compliance with their employer's policies and professional standards.

The resource is intended to support thinking, not to make decisions on behalf of practitioners.

## Acceptable Use

You must not use this website to:

- upload or submit confidential case information;
- share identifiable information about people using services;
- treat the content as a substitute for legal advice;
- copy the resource in a way that misrepresents its source;
- use the contact form for spam, abusive messages, or unlawful purposes.

## Contact Form

The Contact Us form is for business, learning, partnership, feedback, and general enquiries. Do not submit confidential case details or personal data about people using services.

The form is handled through Netlify Forms. Website form notifications should be sent to info@daily-mindset-moments.com.

## Local Learning Tools

The route finder, glossary, flashcards, confidence tracker, printable prompts, and CPD reflection log are learning tools. They support thinking and reflection, but they do not make professional or legal decisions.

Do not enter identifiable case information into the CPD reflection log or any free-text field intended for learning notes.

The Wales reflection log supports private learning and manager discussion in the Social Care Wales context. It does not submit records to the regulator or confirm compliance with registration requirements. Check current Social Care Wales guidance for your circumstances.

CPD drafts are stored locally in the user's browser. They should remain after a normal refresh, but they may be lost if browser storage is cleared, private browsing is used, workplace systems reset storage, or the user changes device or browser. Users should export or print/save a PDF copy before relying on the CPD log as a record.

## External Websites

This website links to external websites operated by Daily Mindset Moments CIC and related product brands. External websites may have their own terms, privacy policies, and contact processes.

## Changes

The resource may be updated over time to improve structure, content, links, wording, or legal accuracy. Users should always check the date of the content and verify current law and guidance before relying on it.

## Ownership and Attribution

This resource is built by Daily Mindset Moments CIC. Raymond Hill is the founder and a social worker.

# Learning Map — Scotland — Scotland

Jurisdiction: Scotland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Scotland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/scotland/learning-map.html

# Learning Map — Scotland

## A sequence for study

1. [Professional Foundations](/?jurisdiction=scotland&resource=foundations#learningWorkspace): Professional role, ethics, competence, supervision and accountable decisions.
2. [Social Care and Support](/?jurisdiction=scotland&resource=care-support#learningWorkspace): Needs, strengths, access to support, family responsibilities and service planning.
3. [Decision-Making and Capacity](/?jurisdiction=scotland&resource=mca#learningWorkspace): Decision support, consent and the authority for someone else to decide.
4. [Restrictions and Liberty](/?jurisdiction=scotland&resource=dols#learningWorkspace): Restrictions, legal authority, less restrictive options and review.
5. [Mental Health](/?jurisdiction=scotland&resource=mha#learningWorkspace): Mental-health support, crisis response, treatment and rights.
6. [Adult Safeguarding](/?jurisdiction=scotland&resource=safeguarding#learningWorkspace): Abuse, neglect, coercion, safe enquiry and the appropriate protective response.
7. [Children, Families and Transitions](/?jurisdiction=scotland&resource=children#learningWorkspace): Child participation, family support, child protection and transitions.
8. [Rights, Culture and Recording](/?jurisdiction=scotland&resource=rights#learningWorkspace): Participation, privacy, cultural safety and clear recording.

## Put learning into practice

Choose one fictional scenario. Record what is known, the person’s perspective and what still needs checking. Open the source library before answering a legal question. Use supervision to test alternative explanations and a reflection to record the next action.

# Case Route Finder — Scotland — Scotland

Jurisdiction: Scotland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Scotland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/scotland/case-route-finder.html

# Case Route Finder — Scotland

## Use the route finder

Select the concerns that fit a fictional case. More than one framework may be relevant. Open each suggested module and its sources; the tool selects learning topics and does not decide a legal threshold.

## Compare the routes

Separate support needs, decision-making, mental-health intervention, protective reporting and restrictions. Record the question each route answers, the source you checked and who needs to provide further advice.


## Route questions

### Care or carer support needs

Which needs and outcomes belong to the person and to carers?

Assess personal outcomes and explain which community-care duty and eligibility policy are being applied. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### A decision-specific capacity question

What is the precise decision and why is ability to decide questioned?

Identify the decision and use communication support before concluding that the adult cannot act or decide. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Restrictions or liberty concerns

What restrictions actually operate and how do they affect the person?

Describe the actual restrictions and the person’s responses, including attempted departures and staff interventions. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Mental health support or compulsion questions

What is the purpose of each proposed intervention?

Identify whether emergency detention, short-term detention or an application for a compulsory treatment order is proposed. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Abuse, neglect or safeguarding concerns

How can the person be heard safely and privately?

Refer concerns on the basis of the available evidence; a referrer need not prove that all criteria are met. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### A child, young carer or transition issue

What does the child say or show about safety and daily life?

Use the child’s account and daily-life evidence alongside family strengths and protection concerns. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Language, participation or recording concerns

What makes participation accessible for this person?

Identify the actual decision and the public body or service responsible for it. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Professional learning or supervision

What is the purpose and limit of your role?

Explain your SSSC role, employer and the purpose of involvement; check any specialist appointment required for the work. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.
