# Printable Tools — Scotland

## Download and use the tools

The ten prompts cover eight practice topics, supervision and checking sources. Use them individually or export the collection from [Templates and Checklists](/?jurisdiction=scotland&resource=templates#learningWorkspace).

## Before sharing

Check that the location is Scotland, use anonymised or fictional information, and keep personal learning notes separate from service records. These prompts help organise reasoning; they do not establish legal authority or meet a regulator’s submission requirements automatically.


## Downloadable prompt text

### Professional Foundations

```text
Professional Foundations
Scotland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Scottish Social Services Council (SSSC) Codes of Practice apply to workers and employers. The revised Codes took effect on 1 May 2024. Professional registration and employer procedures serve different purposes: an employer can allocate work but cannot confer a statutory appointment or qualification that a particular function requires.

Identify the responsible local authority, Health and Social Care Partnership, NHS service or voluntary organisation. Integration does not remove the need to identify who is exercising a duty, holding a record or making a funding decision. The SSSC regulates the workforce; the Care Inspectorate regulates registered care services.

Local pathway:
Explain your SSSC role, employer and the purpose of involvement; check any specialist appointment required for the work.
Use an outcomes conversation to connect daily living, relationships, poverty and service barriers to an assessment.
Take a conflict between resources and assessed need to supervision with evidence and a proposed response.
Link continuous professional learning to feedback and a change in practice, using the current SSSC requirements.

Recording prompts:
1. Your role and the legal or professional framework
Notes:

2. The person’s outcomes and communication preferences
Notes:

3. Evidence, competing explanations and missing perspectives
Notes:

4. Power, boundaries and any conflict of interest
Notes:

5. Agreed action, supervision, feedback and review
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Use the employer’s complaints process for a service decision and the SSSC route for a concern about a registered worker’s fitness to practise. Explain that these address different questions. A complaint to a regulator does not automatically review a funding decision.

Sources:
https://www.sssc.uk.com/standards/codes-of-practice/

```

### Social Care and Support

```text
Social Care and Support
Scotland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Community care sits across the Social Work (Scotland) Act 1968, the Social Care (Self-directed Support) (Scotland) Act 2013 and the Carers (Scotland) Act 2016. Identify the relevant assessment duty and local eligibility policy. A budget calculation is a different step from identifying the person’s needs.

The 2025 statutory SDS guidance describes four options: a direct payment; support selected by the person and arranged through the authority or an agreed third party; support selected and arranged by the authority with the person; or a combination. Discuss the choices rather than treating one option as the default.

Local pathway:
Assess personal outcomes and explain which community-care duty and eligibility policy are being applied.
Offer and explain the four SDS options, including practical assistance with managing the chosen arrangement.
Consider an adult carer support plan or young carer statement separately from the cared-for person’s assessment.
Record the support budget, any charging decision, agreed provision and how unmet needs will be escalated.

Recording prompts:
1. Daily-life evidence, fluctuation and desired outcomes
Notes:

2. The service, eligibility test and decision-maker
Notes:

3. Carer willingness and separately identified needs
Notes:

4. Funding, charges, decisions and reasons
Notes:

5. Start dates, unmet needs, contingency and challenge route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Ask for the authority’s written reasons and information about reconsideration or complaints when assessment, eligibility or provision is disputed. Use the current SDS and carers guidance for the particular issue. Independent advocacy and accessible information can make participation effective.

Sources:
https://www.gov.scot/publications/statutory-guidance-accompany-social-care-self-directed-support-scotland-act-2013-updated-2025/
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2013/1/contents
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2016/9/contents

```

### Decision-Making and Capacity

```text
Decision-Making and Capacity
Scotland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 (AWI) provides different routes for welfare, property and treatment decisions. Its principles require benefit that cannot reasonably be achieved without intervention, the least restrictive option, attention to the adult’s wishes, consultation with relevant people, and encouragement of the adult’s skills.

For the matter in question, AWI incapacity concerns inability to act, decide, communicate or understand a decision, or remember it, because of mental disorder or inability to communicate caused by physical disability. A communication difficulty that human or mechanical assistance can resolve does not itself satisfy the definition. A welfare attorney, guardian or person holding an intervention order has only the powers actually conferred. A financial appointment does not provide general welfare authority.

Local pathway:
Identify the decision and use communication support before concluding that the adult cannot act or decide.
Apply the AWI principles to the proposed intervention and describe the benefit sought.
Read any power of attorney or court order and check scope, activation and limits.
For medical treatment, check the Part 5 certification and treatment framework with the responsible clinician; do not treat a social-work assessment as clinical authorisation.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, options and time at which it is needed
Notes:

2. Communication support and observed responses
Notes:

3. Applicable legal test and evidence for each element
Notes:

4. Representative’s document, scope and decision standard
Notes:

5. Wishes, disagreement, review and any urgent action
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Disagreement about a proxy, treatment or a court order requires the relevant AWI route, not simply a majority vote at a meeting. The Mental Welfare Commission provides rights information; the Office of the Public Guardian and sheriff court have different functions depending on the issue.

Sources:
https://www.gov.scot/publications/adults-with-incapacity-act-principles/
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2000/4/contents
https://www.mwcscot.org.uk/looking-help/your-rights

```

### Restrictions and Liberty

```text
Restrictions and Liberty
Scotland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Scottish restrictions require analysis under the applicable welfare, mental-health and human-rights framework. There is no English hospital/care-home authorisation scheme to copy. AWI welfare guardianship or an intervention order may be relevant, but the wording and lawful scope of a particular order matter.

Distinguish agreement to support, authority for a welfare decision and the legal justification for actual confinement. Where arrangements may engage Article 5, obtain current advice about the applicable legal test and route. A service’s description of a placement as voluntary does not resolve what happens if the person wants to leave.

Local pathway:
Describe the actual restrictions and the person’s responses, including attempted departures and staff interventions.
Identify whether the proposed authority is an AWI order, a mental-health measure or another lawful route.
Read the exact powers and seek specialist advice where confinement or disputed authority is involved.
Arrange a less restrictive plan, independent support and a named review of necessity and objections.

Recording prompts:
1. Each restriction, setting, duration and actual effect
Notes:

2. The person’s wishes, understanding and objections
Notes:

3. Legal authority, decision-maker, limits and conditions
Notes:

4. Alternatives tried and the evidence about necessity
Notes:

5. Representation, review date, expiry and challenge
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Use the court or tribunal route appropriate to the actual measure. The Mental Welfare Commission can advise about rights and concerns. A welfare order and a compulsory mental-health order should not be described as interchangeable, and neither removes the need to review everyday restrictions.

Sources:
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2000/4/contents
https://www.mwcscot.org.uk/looking-help/your-rights

```

### Mental Health

```text
Mental Health
Scotland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Mental Health (Care and Treatment) (Scotland) Act 2003 provides emergency, short-term and longer-term compulsory routes, with amendments including the Mental Health (Scotland) Act 2015. A Mental Health Officer (MHO) has a specific statutory role; being a social worker does not itself confer that appointment.

For a compulsory treatment order, the criteria concern mental disorder, available treatment, significant risk without treatment, significantly impaired decision-making ability about medical treatment because of the disorder, and necessity. The exact criteria differ between routes. Significantly impaired decision-making ability is not simply another name for the AWI incapacity test.

Local pathway:
Identify whether emergency detention, short-term detention or an application for a compulsory treatment order is proposed.
Map evidence to that route’s criteria, including the contribution of voluntary and community alternatives.
Identify the responsible medical professionals, MHO and Mental Health Tribunal for Scotland functions.
Separate psychiatric treatment safeguards from the authority for unrelated physical healthcare.

Recording prompts:
1. Mental and physical health evidence and the person’s account
Notes:

2. The local criteria and voluntary alternatives considered
Notes:

3. Separate authority for transport, admission and treatment
Notes:

4. Required notices, advocacy, representation and review
Notes:

5. Continuity, discharge responsibilities and crisis plan
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain access to independent advocacy, the named-person arrangements that apply, legal representation and tribunal review. Particular treatments have additional safeguards. Use the Mental Welfare Commission rights guidance and the actual order when explaining the person’s position.

Sources:
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2003/13/contents
https://www.mwcscot.org.uk/looking-help/your-rights
https://www.mwcscot.org.uk/node/510

```

### Adult Safeguarding

```text
Adult Safeguarding
Scotland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Adult Support and Protection (Scotland) Act 2007 concerns adults aged 16 or over meeting all three criteria: inability to safeguard their own wellbeing, property, rights or interests; risk of harm; and greater vulnerability to harm because of disability, mental disorder, illness or physical or mental infirmity. Capacity is not a separate gateway requirement.

The council’s inquiry duty, investigative powers and protection orders are distinct. The three criteria are not an eligibility test for ordinary support. A finding that this Act is not the appropriate route should lead to consideration of other available help, rather than automatic case closure.

Local pathway:
Refer concerns on the basis of the available evidence; a referrer need not prove that all criteria are met.
Consider each criterion explicitly in council inquiries and revisit it as circumstances change.
Identify the council officer’s role, partner-agency responsibilities and any need for police involvement.
Apply the Act’s benefit and least restrictive principles, consider advocacy and distinguish support from compulsory powers.

Recording prompts:
1. Concern, source, chronology and the adult’s own account
Notes:

2. Immediate safety and a safe communication method
Notes:

3. The local reporting threshold, recipient and timing
Notes:

4. Consent, coercion and information-sharing basis
Notes:

5. Accepted responsibilities, outcomes and follow-up
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The 2022 Code explains participation, consent and the safeguards around investigations and protection measures. Seek the relevant legal advice before coercive action; a protection concern does not confer unlimited entry, removal or treatment powers.

Sources:
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2007/10/contents
https://www.gov.scot/publications/adult-support-protection-scotland-act-2007-guidance-general-practice/pages/2/

```

### Children, Families and Transitions

```text
Children, Families and Transitions
Scotland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Children (Scotland) Act 1995 and Children’s Hearings (Scotland) Act 2011 provide important duties and compulsory-measure routes. GIRFEC is the national practice framework for coordinated support. Its SHANARRI wellbeing indicators organise enquiry; they do not replace the legal grounds and safeguards for a compulsory measure.

A child’s plan and a lead professional can coordinate services. Referral to the Children’s Reporter and decisions in the hearings system are separate from an ordinary support meeting. Explain which process is being used, why, and how the child and family can participate.

Local pathway:
Use the child’s account and daily-life evidence alongside family strengths and protection concerns.
Apply GIRFEC and current national child-protection guidance without treating a wellbeing concern as automatic compulsory authority.
Identify whether local-authority support, a protection response or a referral to the Reporter is required.
Plan transitions with education, health and adult services, verifying actual acceptance and continuing responsibilities.

Recording prompts:
1. Child’s account, communication and daily-life evidence
Notes:

2. Harm, strengths, needs and alternative explanations
Notes:

3. Reporting duty, recipient and action taken
Notes:

4. Family participation, culture and legal authority
Notes:

5. Named plan, education/health links and transition dates
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Children should receive accessible explanations and appropriate advocacy or legal support for the process affecting them. The UNCRC (Incorporation) (Scotland) Act 2024 adds duties within its statutory scope; check that scope rather than describing every public decision as covered in the same way.

Sources:
https://www.gov.scot/policies/girfec/
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1995/36/contents
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2011/1/contents

```

### Rights, Culture and Recording

```text
Rights, Culture and Recording
Scotland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Scottish practice engages the Human Rights Act 1998, Equality Act 2010 and the applicable UK data-protection framework, alongside local statutory duties. The SSSC Codes provide professional expectations; they do not replace the legal basis for an intervention or disclosure.

The UNCRC (Incorporation) (Scotland) Act 2024 strengthens children’s rights within its defined scope. Identify the source of the public function and the statutory limits before asserting that a particular action breaches its compatibility duty. Participation and accessible explanations remain essential to a reasoned assessment.

Local pathway:
Identify the actual decision and the public body or service responsible for it.
Consider equality barriers and reasonable adjustments in assessment, communication and service access.
For information sharing, identify the applicable lawful basis and any additional condition for sensitive data; distinguish confidentiality from data protection.
Record reasons, alternatives and disagreement, and explain the organisation’s access, correction and complaints routes.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, affected rights and responsible organisation
Notes:

2. Accessibility, culture and participation arrangements
Notes:

3. Disclosure purpose, legal basis, recipient and limits
Notes:

4. Evidence, alternatives, reasons and disagreement
Notes:

5. Access, correction, complaints and review route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
A service complaint, a data-protection complaint and a court or tribunal challenge have different purposes and timescales. Help the person identify the remedy they seek and obtain advice on the relevant route; an internal review does not necessarily preserve a separate legal deadline.

Sources:
https://www.gov.scot/policies/human-rights/childrens-rights/
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2010/15/contents
https://www.sssc.uk.com/standards/codes-of-practice/

```

# Practice Scenarios — Scotland — Scotland

Jurisdiction: Scotland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Scotland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/scotland/practice-scenarios.html

# Scenario Workouts — Scotland practice guide


All cases are fictional learning exercises. Explain your evidence and reasoning before reading the discussion.


## Professional Foundations — Scotland

A worker is asked to close a referral because a family has missed two appointments. The person says bus fares and caring duties prevented attendance.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Test the access barrier before concluding that support is unwanted. Offer a workable contact method, clarify the person’s outcomes and record the referral decision and its reasons. In supervision, distinguish a resource pressure from evidence about need and willingness.


## Social Care and Support — Scotland

An adult wants assistance to attend evening activities, while a parent asks the authority to arrange all daytime support.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Explore the adult’s outcomes and whether a combination of SDS options would fit. Establish what the parent is willing to do and any need for a separate carer plan. Confirm actual evening provision, management support and costs before describing the package as agreed.


## Decision-Making and Capacity — Scotland

A man can choose his meals and visitors but struggles to understand a proposed sale of his home. His sister holds a welfare power of attorney.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Keep the property decision distinct from daily choices and welfare matters. Provide accessible financial information and check the document’s powers. Do not let the welfare appointment stand in for financial authority. Explain which advice or court process is needed if the sale remains necessary and authority is missing.


## Restrictions and Liberty — Scotland

A supported-living service locks the front door at night and says a guardian agreed to the placement. The adult repeatedly asks to leave.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Obtain the order and distinguish placement powers from the measures staff enforce. Record the adult’s wishes, actual ability to leave and alternatives such as staffing or environmental changes. Escalate the legal basis of confinement promptly and arrange support to challenge it; family approval is insufficient reasoning.


## Mental Health — Scotland

A person experiencing severe mental distress declines admission but accepts daily support and an urgent medical review at home.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Assess whether the proposed community support is real and sufficient, and compare it with the relevant statutory criteria. Record the person’s reasoning and the MHO’s assessment. Do not substitute disagreement with the recommended treatment for evidence of significantly impaired decision-making ability or necessity.


## Adult Safeguarding — Scotland

A 61-year-old understands their bank account but depends on a neighbour who takes their money and controls access to shopping.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Do not reject the concern because the adult can explain the transactions. Explore dependency, coercion and ability to safeguard their interests against the three criteria. Arrange a safe conversation, practical access to essentials and the appropriate council and police response.


## Children, Families and Transitions — Scotland

A 15-year-old misses school to support an ill parent and says they want to stay at home but need help.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Explore the young person’s safety, education and caring responsibilities. Coordinate support and consider a young carer statement. Establish whether there is evidence requiring a protection or Reporter route, while avoiding a conclusion that school absence alone settles that question.


## Rights, Culture and Recording — Scotland

A deaf parent is offered only telephone appointments and is then described as failing to engage with a family assessment.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Arrange suitable communication support, correct the inaccurate inference and reassess the effect of the service barrier. Record the parent’s preferred method, the adjustment agreed and responsibility for providing it. Review the assessment outcome in light of the earlier exclusion.

## How to verify a rule

Identify territorial scope, current consolidated text, amendments and commencement, then the applicable statutory guidance and service procedure. An enactment announcement or portal is not proof that every provision is in force.

# About Us — Scotland

## About this resource

Daily Mindset Moments CIC, founded by Raymond Hill, provides this structured social-work learning resource. It supports students, practitioners and supervisors with modules, fictional exercises, source links and private reflections.

## Scotland context

This guide separates the learning material for Scotland from the other practice locations. Shared theories support enquiry; laws, professional requirements and service pathways must be checked locally. Read the source library for scope and editorial status.

# Privacy Policy — Scotland

## Learning stored on your device

The app stores your selected location, reading progress, confidence, saved reflections and unfinished reflection fields in this browser. Records are separated by location. They are not submitted to a professional body. Export or print a copy before clearing browser data or changing devices.

## Website enquiries

If you use the contact form, the details you submit are sent to the website’s form service and operator. Do not send confidential case information. External source websites have their own privacy policies.

## Your records

Use Delete reflection to remove saved entries. Clearing this site’s browser storage removes local progress and notes. Contact [Daily Mindset Moments CIC](mailto:info@daily-mindset-moments.com) about information sent through an enquiry.


---

# Terms of Service — Scotland — Scotland

Jurisdiction: Scotland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Scotland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/scotland/terms-of-service.html

# Terms of Service — Scotland

## Purpose and scope

The Scotland guide is an educational resource for learning and supervision. It does not provide individual legal advice, determine a case outcome or certify professional competence. Use current official sources and the procedures applicable to your role.

## Responsible use

Practice scenarios are fictional. Downloads are learning prompts, not statutory forms. Do not enter identifiable case details into reflections or enquiries. Your browser stores local notes; export your own copy if you need a durable record.

## Sources and corrections

External sources may change. The source library records editorial scope; inclusion of a link or model does not imply endorsement by its publisher. Send corrections with the relevant source and section title through the contact route.

# Start Here — Northern Ireland — Northern Ireland

Jurisdiction: Northern Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Northern Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/northern-ireland/start-here-northern-ireland.html

# Start Here — Northern Ireland

## Your Northern Ireland learning guide

Use the location selector to choose among twelve separate guides. Your reading progress, confidence and reflections are stored separately for each location.

## Start learning

Read [Professional Foundations](/?jurisdiction=northern-ireland&resource=foundations#learningWorkspace), choose a topic from [Learning Map](/?jurisdiction=northern-ireland&resource=map#learningWorkspace), then practise with [Practice Scenarios](/?jurisdiction=northern-ireland&resource=scenarios#learningWorkspace). Test recall with flashcards and use the reflection log to identify a specific next action.

## Scope

Eight modules, forty flashcards, a glossary, eight fictional scenarios and ten recording prompts support revision and supervision. This is a final learning-guide release. It is not an exhaustive account of law, a statutory form or a regulator-approved training programme. The source library explains how to check the applicable version and local route.

# Learning Map — Northern Ireland — Northern Ireland

Jurisdiction: Northern Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Northern Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/northern-ireland/learning-map.html

# Learning Map — Northern Ireland

## A sequence for study

1. [Professional Foundations](/?jurisdiction=northern-ireland&resource=foundations#learningWorkspace): Professional role, ethics, competence, supervision and accountable decisions.
2. [Social Care and Support](/?jurisdiction=northern-ireland&resource=care-support#learningWorkspace): Needs, strengths, access to support, family responsibilities and service planning.
3. [Decision-Making and Capacity](/?jurisdiction=northern-ireland&resource=mca#learningWorkspace): Decision support, consent and the authority for someone else to decide.
4. [Restrictions and Liberty](/?jurisdiction=northern-ireland&resource=dols#learningWorkspace): Restrictions, legal authority, less restrictive options and review.
5. [Mental Health](/?jurisdiction=northern-ireland&resource=mha#learningWorkspace): Mental-health support, crisis response, treatment and rights.
6. [Adult Safeguarding](/?jurisdiction=northern-ireland&resource=safeguarding#learningWorkspace): Abuse, neglect, coercion, safe enquiry and the appropriate protective response.
7. [Children, Families and Transitions](/?jurisdiction=northern-ireland&resource=children#learningWorkspace): Child participation, family support, child protection and transitions.
8. [Rights, Culture and Recording](/?jurisdiction=northern-ireland&resource=rights#learningWorkspace): Participation, privacy, cultural safety and clear recording.

## Put learning into practice

Choose one fictional scenario. Record what is known, the person’s perspective and what still needs checking. Open the source library before answering a legal question. Use supervision to test alternative explanations and a reflection to record the next action.

# Case Route Finder — Northern Ireland — Northern Ireland

Jurisdiction: Northern Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Northern Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/northern-ireland/case-route-finder.html

# Case Route Finder — Northern Ireland

## Use the route finder

Select the concerns that fit a fictional case. More than one framework may be relevant. Open each suggested module and its sources; the tool selects learning topics and does not decide a legal threshold.

## Compare the routes

Separate support needs, decision-making, mental-health intervention, protective reporting and restrictions. Record the question each route answers, the source you checked and who needs to provide further advice.


## Route questions

### Care or carer support needs

Which needs and outcomes belong to the person and to carers?

Describe the person’s needs and desired outcomes, including fluctuation and the effect of unavailable support. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### A decision-specific capacity question

What is the precise decision and why is ability to decide questioned?

Identify the proposed act and confirm that the provision being relied on is commenced for that purpose. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Restrictions or liberty concerns

What restrictions actually operate and how do they affect the person?

Describe actual arrangements and obtain evidence about the person’s wishes, understanding and objections. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Mental health support or compulsion questions

What is the purpose of each proposed intervention?

Identify voluntary support and whether an assessment or treatment detention route is actually being considered. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Abuse, neglect or safeguarding concerns

How can the person be heard safely and privately?

Identify abuse, exploitation or neglect and the adult’s ability to protect themselves in their actual circumstances. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### A child, young carer or transition issue

What does the child say or show about safety and daily life?

Record the child’s account, daily experience, harm concerns and support needs. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Language, participation or recording concerns

What makes participation accessible for this person?

Identify the relevant equality law and public-authority duty for the actual decision. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Professional learning or supervision

What is the purpose and limit of your role?

Explain the purpose of contact, professional role and confidentiality limits in accessible language. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

# Learning Flashcards — Northern Ireland — Northern Ireland

Jurisdiction: Northern Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Northern Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/northern-ireland/learning-flashcards.html

# Learning Flashcards — Northern Ireland practice guide


Answer before revealing the response in the interactive workspace. These cards accompany the full local modules.


## Professional Foundations — Northern Ireland


### Which local framework anchors this topic in Northern Ireland practice guide?

The Northern Ireland Social Care Council (NISCC) Standards of Conduct and Practice provide the professional framework for registered social workers. Distinguish those standards from the procedures of a Health and Social Care (HSC) Trust and from powers available only to a specifically trained or appointed practitioner.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

HSC Trusts provide important health and social-care functions; the Regulation and Quality Improvement Authority (RQIA) has a separate service-regulation role. Identify the actual decision-maker and employer. A concern about a worker’s professional conduct, a provider’s quality and a Trust’s care decision may need different responses.


### What are the key local actions?

Explain the purpose of contact, professional role and confidentiality limits in accessible language. Identify the HSC Trust, provider and any statutory appointment relevant to the task. Use supervision to test how poverty, disability, trauma or barriers to services influence the formulation. Link learning and feedback to the current NISCC registration and professional-development requirements.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

Explain the relevant Trust or provider complaint route and when a concern about a registered worker belongs with NISCC. Give the person a clear account of who can address the outcome they seek; professional regulation does not itself arrange a care package.


### What common error should you avoid?

Treating “the Trust decided” as sufficient explanation without identifying the decision, authority and reasons.


## Social Care and Support — Northern Ireland


### Which local framework anchors this topic in Northern Ireland practice guide?

An HSC Trust needs assessment is the starting point for community support. The Health and Personal Social Services (Northern Ireland) Order 1972 and the Carers and Direct Payments Act (Northern Ireland) 2002 form part of the legal map. Establish the particular duty, Trust criteria and service being requested.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

Direct payments can allow an eligible person to arrange assessed support. Discuss the option during assessment, including consent, the ability to manage it with support, permitted use and employer responsibilities. A carer’s own assessment concerns their caring role and needs; it does not replace the assessment of the person receiving care.


### What are the key local actions?

Describe the person’s needs and desired outcomes, including fluctuation and the effect of unavailable support. Ask the Trust to explain the assessment and eligibility decisions separately from costs and provision. Offer a carer’s assessment where the relevant conditions are met, including consideration of young carers. Compare arranged services with direct payments and confirm that the proposed support can actually be delivered.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

Request reasons, reassessment where circumstances change and the appropriate Trust complaint or review route. Record interim arrangements and unmet needs while a decision is disputed. NI Direct explains access, carers’ assessments and direct payments, with links to local services.


### What common error should you avoid?

Confusing the carer’s support with services for the cared-for person, or describing an unpaid family arrangement as an agreed funded plan.


## Decision-Making and Capacity — Northern Ireland


### Which local framework anchors this topic in Northern Ireland practice guide?

The Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 is only partly commenced. Phase 1 covers research and specified deprivation-of-liberty and money-and-valuables provisions. Do not apply the whole Act as though it were already the general framework for every treatment or welfare decision.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

Within the operative framework, the assessment is decision-specific, with support before a conclusion of incapacity. The inability must result from impairment or disturbance of the mind or brain. Test understanding, retaining information for the decision, appreciating its relevance and using and weighing it, and communicating the choice. Record how any failed ability affects this decision, rather than relying on a diagnosis. The principles address capacity and best interests. Formal assessments and other statutory functions have training and qualification requirements. A nominated person must be consulted in the relevant process; the role does not confer general substitute decision-making authority.


### What are the key local actions?

Identify the proposed act and confirm that the provision being relied on is commenced for that purpose. Specify the decision and provide practical support before applying the relevant capacity test. Check whether the required assessment must be completed by a suitably qualified and trained person. Record the person’s wishes, consultation and the actual legal basis for any decision taken without their own consent.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

For phase-1 deprivation-of-liberty decisions, check the Review Tribunal route and safeguards in the current Code, forms and interim guidance. For another type of decision, obtain advice about the applicable law rather than extending phase-1 powers by analogy.


### What common error should you avoid?

Assuming full commencement or treating the nominated person as a universal decision-maker.


## Restrictions and Liberty — Northern Ireland


### Which local framework anchors this topic in Northern Ireland practice guide?

The operative deprivation-of-liberty provisions of the Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 require the relevant assessments, authorisation and safeguards. Setting, age, purpose and the applicable mental-health or children’s framework must be established before selecting a route.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

The Department of Health states that the Supreme Court judgment of 2 June 2026 changed the previous approach to defining deprivation of liberty. Interim guidance is available while the Code and other material are reviewed. Read that guidance with current Trust specialist advice; an older training slide is not sufficient evidence of the current legal test.


### What are the key local actions?

Describe actual arrangements and obtain evidence about the person’s wishes, understanding and objections. Consult the current interim guidance before deciding whether the arrangements amount to deprivation of liberty. Use the appropriate trained assessors, Trust process and current forms where an authorisation is required. Keep capacity, best interests, authorisation, consultation and challenge arrangements separately recorded.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

Identify the nominated person, advocacy or representation required and the person’s access to the Review Tribunal. Check expiry, review and changed circumstances. Do not remove an existing safeguard solely because a judgment or guidance has changed without the responsible legal review.


### What common error should you avoid?

Treating an old definition, a completed form or family approval as a complete legal analysis.


## Mental Health — Northern Ireland


### Which local framework anchors this topic in Northern Ireland practice guide?

The Mental Health (Northern Ireland) Order 1986 remains relevant alongside the partly commenced capacity legislation. Assessment and treatment routes have their own criteria and professional roles. For admission for assessment, the Order includes mental disorder of a nature or degree warranting detention for assessment and the relevant substantial likelihood of serious physical harm.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

An approved social worker has specific training and functions. The medical recommendation, application and hospital processes should be distinguished. A general referral to mental-health services is not a compulsory admission application.


### What are the key local actions?

Identify voluntary support and whether an assessment or treatment detention route is actually being considered. Check the current Order, evidence for the particular criteria and the authorised professional’s role. Keep the partly commenced capacity framework and any separate physical-treatment decision distinct. Explain the person’s status and arrange rights information, support and review under the applicable route.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

The Review Tribunal and the relevant hospital discharge or review processes address detention questions. Help the person obtain advice and understand how to challenge the measure. Confirm which rules apply to their specific admission status and documents.


### What common error should you avoid?

Assuming the 2016 capacity legislation has replaced every mental-health admission provision.


## Adult Safeguarding — Northern Ireland


### Which local framework anchors this topic in Northern Ireland practice guide?

The regional policy Adult Safeguarding: Prevention and Protection in Partnership distinguishes an adult at risk of harm from an adult in need of protection. It considers personal characteristics and life circumstances, with HSC Trust and PSNI roles according to the concern. It is not a general power to compel an adult to accept services.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

The Adult Protection Bill is a reform to monitor, not a source of powers to assume are already operational. The Assembly’s legislative tracker must be checked for passage and any subsequent Act and commencement before applying a new duty.


### What are the key local actions?

Identify abuse, exploitation or neglect and the adult’s ability to protect themselves in their actual circumstances. Use the organisation’s safeguarding arrangements and refer protection concerns to the appropriate HSC Trust route. Contact PSNI where the circumstances require a police response, distinguishing criminal investigation from the support plan. Establish the lawful basis for information sharing and for any proposed intervention without agreement.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

Use the policy’s participation and proportionate-response approach, together with the applicable consent, capacity and legal safeguards. Explain the Trust or provider complaint process and obtain specialist advice if a coercive intervention is proposed.


### What common error should you avoid?

Treating a safeguarding policy as a detention power or treating a proposed Bill as commenced law.


## Children, Families and Transitions — Northern Ireland


### Which local framework anchors this topic in Northern Ireland practice guide?

The Children (Northern Ireland) Order 1995 provides the main framework for children in need, family support and protective court processes. Co-operating to Safeguard Children and Young People supplies the regional policy framework. The HSC Trust’s children’s services and PSNI have different responsibilities.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

Assessment and family support should be distinguished from a protection investigation or court order. A family meeting cannot create powers of removal or determine legal parental responsibility. Check the child’s position and the relevant authority for accommodation, contact and treatment decisions.


### What are the key local actions?

Record the child’s account, daily experience, harm concerns and support needs. Use the current regional policy and Trust referral procedure for a child-protection concern. Identify who holds parental responsibility and any court order affecting the proposed decision. Coordinate education, health and family support and plan transitions before a service ends.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

Explain the particular assessment, protection or court process, including how the child and family can participate, obtain advocacy or legal advice and raise disagreement. Do not promise confidentiality that conflicts with a necessary safeguarding response.


### What common error should you avoid?

Allowing an internal discussion or a parent’s request for secrecy to replace the required protection response.


## Rights, Culture and Recording — Northern Ireland


### Which local framework anchors this topic in Northern Ireland practice guide?

Northern Ireland has its own equality laws. The Equality Act 2010 does not apply. Identify the relevant disability, sex, race, religious or political discrimination provision and the setting it covers. Section 75 of the Northern Ireland Act 1998 places equality-of-opportunity and good-relations duties on designated public authorities.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

The Human Rights Act and applicable UK data-protection law also matter, but they answer different questions. A public authority’s equality scheme does not by itself establish permission to disclose a person’s health information.


### What are the key local actions?

Identify the relevant equality law and public-authority duty for the actual decision. Arrange accessible communication and consider the applicable reasonable-adjustment obligations. Establish the purpose and legal basis of sharing, including the treatment of sensitive information. Record the person’s account, alternatives, reasons, disagreement and the route for correction or challenge.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

The Equality Commission for Northern Ireland provides information on discrimination and routes to challenge. Distinguish a service complaint, an equality-scheme concern and legal proceedings; obtain timely advice because different limits and remedies apply.


### What common error should you avoid?

Copying an equality test from another legal system or equating identical treatment with accessible participation.

Work through each topic using its official sources, then complete the case and recording exercise.

## Pathway activities

### Professional Foundations

Explain the purpose of contact, professional role and confidentiality limits in accessible language. Work through the fictional case and explain: Treating “the Trust decided” as sufficient explanation without identifying the decision, authority and reasons.

### Social Care and Support

Describe the person’s needs and desired outcomes, including fluctuation and the effect of unavailable support. Work through the fictional case and explain: Confusing the carer’s support with services for the cared-for person, or describing an unpaid family arrangement as an agreed funded plan.

### Decision-Making and Capacity

Identify the proposed act and confirm that the provision being relied on is commenced for that purpose. Work through the fictional case and explain: Assuming full commencement or treating the nominated person as a universal decision-maker.

### Restrictions and Liberty

Describe actual arrangements and obtain evidence about the person’s wishes, understanding and objections. Work through the fictional case and explain: Treating an old definition, a completed form or family approval as a complete legal analysis.

### Mental Health

Identify voluntary support and whether an assessment or treatment detention route is actually being considered. Work through the fictional case and explain: Assuming the 2016 capacity legislation has replaced every mental-health admission provision.

### Adult Safeguarding

Identify abuse, exploitation or neglect and the adult’s ability to protect themselves in their actual circumstances. Work through the fictional case and explain: Treating a safeguarding policy as a detention power or treating a proposed Bill as commenced law.

### Children, Families and Transitions

Record the child’s account, daily experience, harm concerns and support needs. Work through the fictional case and explain: Allowing an internal discussion or a parent’s request for secrecy to replace the required protection response.

### Rights, Culture and Recording

Identify the relevant equality law and public-authority duty for the actual decision. Work through the fictional case and explain: Copying an equality test from another legal system or equating identical treatment with accessible participation.

# Practice Glossary — Northern Ireland — Northern Ireland

Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/northern-ireland/practice-glossary.html

# Practice Glossary — Northern Ireland practice guide

Use each definition with its linked full lesson and official sources.

## Professional Foundations

The Northern Ireland Social Care Council (NISCC) Standards of Conduct and Practice provide the professional framework for registered social workers. Distinguish those standards from the procedures of a Health and Social Care (HSC) Trust and from powers available only to a specifically trained or appointed practitioner.

## Social Care and Support

An HSC Trust needs assessment is the starting point for community support. The Health and Personal Social Services (Northern Ireland) Order 1972 and the Carers and Direct Payments Act (Northern Ireland) 2002 form part of the legal map. Establish the particular duty, Trust criteria and service being requested.

## Decision-Making and Capacity

The Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 is only partly commenced. Phase 1 covers research and specified deprivation-of-liberty and money-and-valuables provisions. Do not apply the whole Act as though it were already the general framework for every treatment or welfare decision.

## Restrictions and Liberty

The operative deprivation-of-liberty provisions of the Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 require the relevant assessments, authorisation and safeguards. Setting, age, purpose and the applicable mental-health or children’s framework must be established before selecting a route.

## Mental Health

The Mental Health (Northern Ireland) Order 1986 remains relevant alongside the partly commenced capacity legislation. Assessment and treatment routes have their own criteria and professional roles. For admission for assessment, the Order includes mental disorder of a nature or degree warranting detention for assessment and the relevant substantial likelihood of serious physical harm.

## Adult Safeguarding

The regional policy Adult Safeguarding: Prevention and Protection in Partnership distinguishes an adult at risk of harm from an adult in need of protection. It considers personal characteristics and life circumstances, with HSC Trust and PSNI roles according to the concern. It is not a general power to compel an adult to accept services.

## Children, Families and Transitions

The Children (Northern Ireland) Order 1995 provides the main framework for children in need, family support and protective court processes. Co-operating to Safeguard Children and Young People supplies the regional policy framework. The HSC Trust’s children’s services and PSNI have different responsibilities.

## Rights, Culture and Recording

Northern Ireland has its own equality laws. The Equality Act 2010 does not apply. Identify the relevant disability, sex, race, religious or political discrimination provision and the setting it covers. Section 75 of the Northern Ireland Act 1998 places equality-of-opportunity and good-relations duties on designated public authorities.

## Northern Ireland Social Care Council (NISCC)

The professional body identified for this guide. Check its remit and the requirements that apply to your role.

## Advocacy

Support to express views, understand choices and participate; statutory entitlements depend on the local framework.

## CPD

Continuing professional development: learning, reflection and evidence of improvement.

## Consent

Agreement to a specific action; check the applicable requirements for information, voluntariness and ability to consent.

## Coercion

Pressure or control that can affect expressed wishes and freedom to act.

## Eligibility

The criteria for a particular service or programme; distinct from a description of need.

## Capacity

Ability to make the relevant decision under the applicable legal framework; avoid a global label.

## Representative

Someone with a defined support or decision-making role; verify the source and scope of authority.

## Proportionality

A reasoned comparison of intended benefit, burdens, rights and alternatives.

## Cultural safety

Attention to power, identity and the person’s experience of a service, informed by their preferences.

## Data minimisation

Using or sharing only information needed for an identified lawful purpose.

## Confidentiality

Protecting information while understanding and explaining lawful exceptions.

## Safeguarding referral

Communicating a concern to the appropriate agency; confirm the applicable route and follow-up.

## Professional supervision

Structured discussion of decisions, ethics, skills, wellbeing and accountability.

## Formulation

A reasoned account connecting evidence and possible explanations to a plan.

## Family network

Relationships that may offer support; availability, safety and willingness need assessment.

## Transition

Planned change between services or life stages, with continuity and named responsibilities.

## Contingency

An agreed response if risks increase or the preferred plan cannot operate.

## Review

A planned check of outcomes, changing circumstances and whether actions remain appropriate.

## Least restrictive option

An option that can achieve the purpose with less interference in rights and freedom.

# Theory Into Practice — Northern Ireland — Northern Ireland

Jurisdiction: Northern Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Northern Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/northern-ireland/theory-into-practice-northern-ireland.html

# Theory Into Practice — Northern Ireland

## Build a testable explanation

Use the theory finder to generate alternative explanations for a fictional case. Compare what each lens notices about relationships, environment, power, trauma and strengths. Record evidence that would support or challenge your explanation.

## Use models thoughtfully

Theories are shared learning lenses, not country-specific statutory rules. Their inclusion does not imply official adoption in Northern Ireland. Check suitability, training requirements, cultural context and the person’s account before applying a method.


## Interactive theory lenses

### Ecological Systems Theory

Person, family, housing, community, services, poverty, policy, culture, and environment.

Hypothesis: The presenting issue may be shaped by pressures around the person, not only by individual behaviour or choice.

- What changed in the environment before the concern escalated?
- Which systems are supporting the person, and which are adding pressure?
- Would risk reduce if housing, income, access, care, or community support changed?

### Strengths-Based Practice

Capabilities, identity, relationships, community, culture, hope, and what is already working.

Hypothesis: The person may have protective strategies or relationships that are hidden by a risk-heavy professional account.

- What has helped the person survive or cope so far?
- Who does the person trust, and what role could they safely play?
- Which strengths are real evidence, and which are optimistic assumptions?

### Trauma-Informed Practice

Safety, trust, choice, collaboration, empowerment, shame, threat responses, and control.

Hypothesis: Behaviour that looks like refusal, avoidance, anger, or disengagement may be a survival response to trauma, coercion, loss, or fear.

- What might feel unsafe or controlling from the person's perspective?
- What helps the person feel more choice and predictability?
- How can we avoid repeating patterns of powerlessness?

### Attachment Theory

Trust, separation, dependency, rejection, fear, care-seeking, and relationship patterns.

Hypothesis: Responses to professionals or carers may reflect previous experiences of care, loss, abandonment, or unsafe relationships.

- How does the person respond when support increases, reduces, or changes?
- Are there patterns of clinging, pushing away, testing, mistrust, or fear?
- What relationship approach is consistent, boundaried, and safe?

### Systems and Family Theory

Roles, rules, communication, repeated patterns, conflict, care dynamics, and network effects.

Hypothesis: The concern may be maintained by relationship patterns, family roles, service responses, or network conflict.

- Who gains or loses if the current pattern changes?
- What role has each person been placed in or taken on?
- How do professional responses affect the family or network pattern?

### Anti-Oppressive and Anti-Discriminatory Practice

Power, oppression, racism, disability, class, gender, sexuality, culture, age, stigma, and access.

Hypothesis: The presenting issue may be intensified by structural inequality, professional power, discrimination, or inaccessible services.

- What barriers has the person faced before we became involved?
- Whose account is being treated as most credible, and why?
- What reasonable adjustments, cultural humility, or advocacy are needed?

### Crisis Theory

Immediate stress, narrowed options, temporary disequilibrium, coping capacity, and stabilisation.

Hypothesis: The person or family may be temporarily overwhelmed and need stabilisation before longer-term planning is realistic.

- What immediate event or loss has exceeded usual coping?
- What needs to happen in the next 24 to 72 hours?
- What can wait until safety, sleep, food, medication, or support is more stable?

### Life Course Theory

Transitions, cumulative disadvantage, ageing, identity, loss, timing, and turning points.

Hypothesis: Current risk or distress may connect to earlier life events, cumulative exclusion, transition, bereavement, or changing identity.

- What transitions or losses are happening now?
- How has cumulative disadvantage shaped options and trust?
- What strengths, relationships, or identities from earlier life still matter?

### Task-Centred Practice

Specific problems, agreed goals, small steps, roles, review, and measurable change.

Hypothesis: The person may benefit from breaking an overwhelming issue into concrete, negotiated tasks with clear review.

- What problem does the person most want to work on first?
- What is the smallest useful next step?
- Who will do what, by when, and how will we know it helped?

# Children and Family Practice Models — Northern Ireland

## Compare approaches to children and families

Use the model finder to explore enquiry, family relationships, support and safety planning. Begin with the child’s account and daily experience; distinguish observed evidence from adult interpretation.

## Local application

These shared models are educational examples, not a list of officially approved Northern Ireland programmes. Check training, licensing, local adoption and cultural suitability. A model never replaces the applicable reporting duty or legal threshold.


## Model finder

### Signs of Safety

Child protection mapping, danger statements, safety goals, family network work, scaling, and safety planning.

### Signs of Wellbeing, Success, and Belonging

Family support, children in care, permanency, reunification, stability, identity, and belonging work.

### Family Safeguarding

Whole-family child protection where parental domestic abuse, mental health, substance misuse, trauma, or adult needs affect child safety.

### Contextual Safeguarding

Extra-familial harm, exploitation, peer group risk, school, neighbourhood, online spaces, and adolescent safeguarding.

### Family Group Conferencing

Family-led planning, kinship care, safety planning, pre-proceedings, reunification, and support network building.

### Systemic Practice

Family patterns, repeated cycles, communication, roles, meaning, conflict, and relationship-based formulation.

### Motivational Interviewing

Ambivalence, parental engagement, adolescent risk, substance use, resistance, and behaviour change conversations.

### Solution-Focused Practice

Goal-setting, exceptions, scaling, strengths, future-focused planning, and building on small signs of progress.

### PACE and DDP-Informed Practice

Children affected by trauma, attachment disruption, care experience, shame, mistrust, and blocked trust.

### Safe and Together

Domestic abuse-informed child welfare, perpetrator pattern mapping, protective parent strengths, and child impact.

### Graded Care Profile 2

Neglect assessment, evidence-based care mapping, physical care, safety, love and esteem, and developmental care.

### Restorative Practice

Repair, accountability, family meetings, school relationships, conflict, shame, and shared problem-solving.

# Professional Foundations — Northern Ireland — Northern Ireland

Jurisdiction: Northern Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Northern Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/northern-ireland/professional-foundations.html

# Professional Foundations — Northern Ireland

## Learning outcomes

Explain your professional role, distinguish an ethical concern from a statutory power, and turn a formulation into an accountable plan.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

The Northern Ireland Social Care Council (NISCC) Standards of Conduct and Practice provide the professional framework for registered social workers. Distinguish those standards from the procedures of a Health and Social Care (HSC) Trust and from powers available only to a specifically trained or appointed practitioner.

HSC Trusts provide important health and social-care functions; the Regulation and Quality Improvement Authority (RQIA) has a separate service-regulation role. Identify the actual decision-maker and employer. A concern about a worker’s professional conduct, a provider’s quality and a Trust’s care decision may need different responses.

## From information to a professional formulation

A chronology says what happened. A formulation explains how the available evidence, the person's experience and their environment might connect. Start with the person's desired change. Map relationships, housing, income, health, discrimination and service barriers alongside individual strengths. A missed appointment may reflect fear, inaccessible transport or an unsafe household; it does not establish unwillingness to engage.

Use at least two possible explanations for a difficult situation. State what evidence supports each and what would challenge it. A strengths approach should identify actual resources the person can use, with their agreement. It should not turn an absent service into an assumed family responsibility. A trauma-informed conversation offers predictability, choice and control over pace while keeping necessary enquiries clear.

## Boundaries and supervision

Explain who employs you, the purpose of contact, how information will be used and the limits of confidentiality. Separate an invitation to accept support from an action the law permits without agreement. Ask for supervision when an instruction conflicts with professional duties or exceeds your authority. Record the issue, advice, action and unresolved concern; merely recording that a manager agreed does not explain the decision.

For a learning reflection, choose one decision you influenced. Describe what the person said, your initial assumption, what changed your understanding and what you will do differently. Seek feedback about the effect on the person, rather than counting training attendance as evidence of improved practice.

## Apply the local pathway

- Explain the purpose of contact, professional role and confidentiality limits in accessible language.
- Identify the HSC Trust, provider and any statutory appointment relevant to the task.
- Use supervision to test how poverty, disability, trauma or barriers to services influence the formulation.
- Link learning and feedback to the current NISCC registration and professional-development requirements.

## Rights, challenge and review

Explain the relevant Trust or provider complaint route and when a concern about a registered worker belongs with NISCC. Give the person a clear account of who can address the outcome they seek; professional regulation does not itself arrange a care package.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A family receives different explanations from a Trust worker and a commissioned provider about why visits have reduced.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Establish who changed the assessed plan and who changed delivery. Obtain the recorded decision and reasons, hear the person’s experience and address immediate unmet needs. Escalate the appropriate assessment or contract issue instead of referring every complaint to the professional regulator.

### Common error to avoid

Treating “the Trust decided” as sufficient explanation without identifying the decision, authority and reasons.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Your role and the legal or professional framework
- The person’s outcomes and communication preferences
- Evidence, competing explanations and missing perspectives
- Power, boundaries and any conflict of interest
- Agreed action, supervision, feedback and review

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [NISCC Standards and Guidance](https://niscc.info/standards-and-guidance/)

# Social Care and Support — Northern Ireland — Northern Ireland

Jurisdiction: Northern Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Northern Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/northern-ireland/social-care-and-support-northern-ireland.html

# Social Care and Support — Northern Ireland

## Learning outcomes

Map assessment, eligibility, funding and delivery separately; include family support without assuming it; explain the local route for challenging a decision.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

An HSC Trust needs assessment is the starting point for community support. The Health and Personal Social Services (Northern Ireland) Order 1972 and the Carers and Direct Payments Act (Northern Ireland) 2002 form part of the legal map. Establish the particular duty, Trust criteria and service being requested.

Direct payments can allow an eligible person to arrange assessed support. Discuss the option during assessment, including consent, the ability to manage it with support, permitted use and employer responsibilities. A carer’s own assessment concerns their caring role and needs; it does not replace the assessment of the person receiving care.

## Assess daily life, not just a list of services

Begin with what a good day would look like. Explore washing, dressing, nutrition, medicines, mobility, home safety, relationships, work or education and community participation. Ask about variation: what happens at night, on a bad day or when a regular supporter is unavailable? Establish what the person can do with appropriate equipment, accessible information or a different environment. Do not confuse performing a task once during a visit with being able to do it reliably in daily life.

Speak with family supporters about willingness, practical ability and sustainability. Their account belongs alongside the person's account, not in place of it. Record support that is actually offered and its limits. An adult child working overnight is not an available overnight care service. Where views differ, describe the disagreement and its consequences for the proposed plan.

## Turn the assessment into a deliverable plan

Keep four decisions visible: the needs identified; the applicable eligibility decision; the funding or charging decision; and the service that will actually start. A referral, waiting-list entry or funding approval is not proof that support has begun. Obtain the person's understanding of costs and responsibilities before recording agreement.

For each outcome, identify an action, a responsible service or person and a review trigger. Include what happens if the worker does not arrive, the person declines support, a carer becomes unavailable or needs change. Record unmet needs and interim arrangements explicitly. A budget dispute should not disappear into a description of the person as difficult or unrealistic.

## Apply the local pathway

- Describe the person’s needs and desired outcomes, including fluctuation and the effect of unavailable support.
- Ask the Trust to explain the assessment and eligibility decisions separately from costs and provision.
- Offer a carer’s assessment where the relevant conditions are met, including consideration of young carers.
- Compare arranged services with direct payments and confirm that the proposed support can actually be delivered.

## Rights, challenge and review

Request reasons, reassessment where circumstances change and the appropriate Trust complaint or review route. Record interim arrangements and unmet needs while a decision is disputed. NI Direct explains access, carers’ assessments and direct payments, with links to local services.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A disabled parent needs morning assistance. Their teenager is missing school to help, and a relative suggests using the parent’s benefits to pay informally.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Assess the parent’s support needs and the impact on the young person. Consider Trust-arranged care or an eligible direct-payment arrangement with proper support. Clarify funding and employment responsibilities; do not assume the child can continue filling a gap in services.

### Common error to avoid

Confusing the carer’s support with services for the cared-for person, or describing an unpaid family arrangement as an agreed funded plan.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Daily-life evidence, fluctuation and desired outcomes
- The service, eligibility test and decision-maker
- Carer willingness and separately identified needs
- Funding, charges, decisions and reasons
- Start dates, unmet needs, contingency and challenge route

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [Arranging health and social care](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/arranging-health-and-social-care)
- [Direct payments for care](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/direct-payments-care)
- [Carers and Direct Payments Act (Northern Ireland) 2002](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/nia/2002/6/contents)

# Decision-Making and Capacity — Northern Ireland — Northern Ireland

Jurisdiction: Northern Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Northern Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/northern-ireland/mental-capacity-act-northern-ireland-2016.html

# Decision-Making and Capacity — Northern Ireland

## Learning outcomes

Identify the precise decision, provide practical decision support, apply the local capacity or consent framework and verify a representative’s authority.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

The Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 is only partly commenced. Phase 1 covers research and specified deprivation-of-liberty and money-and-valuables provisions. Do not apply the whole Act as though it were already the general framework for every treatment or welfare decision.

Within the operative framework, the assessment is decision-specific, with support before a conclusion of incapacity. The inability must result from impairment or disturbance of the mind or brain. Test understanding, retaining information for the decision, appreciating its relevance and using and weighing it, and communicating the choice. Record how any failed ability affects this decision, rather than relying on a diagnosis. The principles address capacity and best interests. Formal assessments and other statutory functions have training and qualification requirements. A nominated person must be consulted in the relevant process; the role does not confer general substitute decision-making authority.

## Start with the decision and the support

Write the decision as a question the person could answer: accepting a particular treatment, choosing accommodation or authorising a financial transaction. These questions may engage different laws and decision-makers. A diagnosis, cognitive score or disagreement with professionals is not a complete capacity assessment. Describe the ability relevant to this decision and the evidence for any concern.

Prepare information about the real options, including doing nothing where relevant. Use an interpreter, accessible material, communication aids and suitable timing. Address pain, fatigue, sensory impairment, medication effects and anxiety. Ask the person to explain their understanding in their own way; repeating professional phrases is not the only way to demonstrate understanding. Record what support was tried and its effect, rather than simply writing that all support was offered.

## Keep authority and the decision itself separate

A relative may provide valuable information without holding authority to decide. Obtain the actual appointment, agreement, court order or statutory basis being relied upon. Check the decisions it covers, conditions, whether it is operative and whether another person has priority. Authority over property does not automatically include healthcare or accommodation.

Where a representative can lawfully act, identify the decision standard they must apply locally. Explore the person's wishes, values, previous statements and present participation. Record a disagreement rather than converting it into apparent agreement. Consider whether a reversible interim option allows more support or recovery before an irreversible decision. If authority remains disputed, obtain the appropriate clinical or legal advice and arrange the applicable review; a multidisciplinary meeting cannot create missing legal powers.

## Apply the local pathway

- Identify the proposed act and confirm that the provision being relied on is commenced for that purpose.
- Specify the decision and provide practical support before applying the relevant capacity test.
- Check whether the required assessment must be completed by a suitably qualified and trained person.
- Record the person’s wishes, consultation and the actual legal basis for any decision taken without their own consent.

## Rights, challenge and review

For phase-1 deprivation-of-liberty decisions, check the Review Tribunal route and safeguards in the current Code, forms and interim guidance. For another type of decision, obtain advice about the applicable law rather than extending phase-1 powers by analogy.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A hospital team asks a nominated person to sign consent for an unrelated operation because a deprivation-of-liberty assessment has been completed.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Separate the operation from the liberty arrangements. Check the patient’s ability to decide about that treatment and the applicable consent law. The nominated-person role and a liberty assessment do not provide a general consent signature for another intervention.

### Common error to avoid

Assuming full commencement or treating the nominated person as a universal decision-maker.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Decision, options and time at which it is needed
- Communication support and observed responses
- Applicable legal test and evidence for each element
- Representative’s document, scope and decision standard
- Wishes, disagreement, review and any urgent action

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [Mental Capacity Act: implementation and current guidance](https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/topics/mental-capacity-act)
- [Mental Capacity Act FAQs](https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/articles/mental-capacity-act-faqs)
- [Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/nia/2016/18/contents)
