# Restrictions and Liberty — Northern Ireland — Northern Ireland

Jurisdiction: Northern Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Northern Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/northern-ireland/deprivation-of-liberty-northern-ireland.html

# Restrictions and Liberty — Northern Ireland

## Learning outcomes

Describe actual restrictions, identify the setting-specific legal authority, test alternatives and make representation and review practical.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

The operative deprivation-of-liberty provisions of the Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 require the relevant assessments, authorisation and safeguards. Setting, age, purpose and the applicable mental-health or children’s framework must be established before selecting a route.

The Department of Health states that the Supreme Court judgment of 2 June 2026 changed the previous approach to defining deprivation of liberty. Interim guidance is available while the Code and other material are reviewed. Read that guidance with current Trust specialist advice; an older training slide is not sufficient evidence of the current legal test.

## Describe what happens in everyday life

Look beyond the label used by the service. Describe locked doors, staff responses to a request to leave, supervision, physical interventions, isolation, medication used to control behaviour and restrictions on visitors, money or communication. State when each measure operates, who applies it, its duration and its cumulative effect. Distinguish a person's preferred routine from a rule enforced by staff.

Hear the person privately with suitable communication support. An absence of verbal objection is not a complete account of their wishes. Distress, repeated requests to go home or avoiding a particular worker may require further enquiry. Family agreement is relevant information but should not be treated as a substitute for the authority required by law.

## Connect necessity to a less restrictive plan

Identify the concrete harm a measure is intended to prevent. Explore environmental changes, pain relief, meaningful activity, different staffing, communication and practical support. Record which options were tried, their effects and why another option is proposed. Provider convenience or an unsigned risk assessment should not become the explanation for an ongoing restriction.

Separate emergency action from a continuing arrangement. An urgent response needs its own factual justification and follow-up; it should not silently become a standing plan. Check the scope of any order or authorisation, applicable conditions, expiry and who must review it. The person needs an accessible explanation and a usable way to object, obtain independent help and challenge the arrangement. Assign responsibility for acting on an objection rather than merely documenting it at the next routine meeting.

## Apply the local pathway

- Describe actual arrangements and obtain evidence about the person’s wishes, understanding and objections.
- Consult the current interim guidance before deciding whether the arrangements amount to deprivation of liberty.
- Use the appropriate trained assessors, Trust process and current forms where an authorisation is required.
- Keep capacity, best interests, authorisation, consultation and challenge arrangements separately recorded.

## Rights, challenge and review

Identify the nominated person, advocacy or representation required and the person’s access to the Review Tribunal. Check expiry, review and changed circumstances. Do not remove an existing safeguard solely because a judgment or guidance has changed without the responsible legal review.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A care setting continues to use an old checklist after June 2026 and says its completed form proves all arrangements are lawful.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Review the actual restrictions and the source version used. Ask the Trust’s MCA team to apply the current guidance and determine any required reassessment or authorisation. Continue meeting immediate care and participation duties while resolving the legal position.

### Common error to avoid

Treating an old definition, a completed form or family approval as a complete legal analysis.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Each restriction, setting, duration and actual effect
- The person’s wishes, understanding and objections
- Legal authority, decision-maker, limits and conditions
- Alternatives tried and the evidence about necessity
- Representation, review date, expiry and challenge

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [Interim guidance on the Mental Capacity Act (NI) 2016](https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/publications/interim-guidance-mental-capacity-act-ni-2016)
- [Mental Capacity Act FAQs](https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/articles/mental-capacity-act-faqs)

Editorial expansion: 8 September 2026. The sources support the distinctions taught here; check their current text, amendments, commencement and applicable local procedure before operational use. Independent practitioner review has not been recorded.

# Mental Health — Northern Ireland — Northern Ireland

Jurisdiction: Northern Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Northern Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/northern-ireland/mental-health-northern-ireland.html

# Mental Health — Northern Ireland

## Learning outcomes

Distinguish voluntary care, compulsory assessment, detention and treatment; connect the local criteria to evidence and explain the person’s review rights.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

The Mental Health (Northern Ireland) Order 1986 remains relevant alongside the partly commenced capacity legislation. Assessment and treatment routes have their own criteria and professional roles. For admission for assessment, the Order includes mental disorder of a nature or degree warranting detention for assessment and the relevant substantial likelihood of serious physical harm.

An approved social worker has specific training and functions. The medical recommendation, application and hospital processes should be distinguished. A general referral to mental-health services is not a compulsory admission application.

## Assess the crisis in context

Attend to urgent physical health and immediate safety while creating space for the person's account. Explore sleep, medication, substance use, pain, relationships, housing, financial pressure and previous helpful or harmful experiences of services. Cultural or spiritual expression should be understood in context. Use an appropriate interpreter and ask which supporters the person wants involved.

Describe behaviour and its consequences rather than relying on labels such as non-compliant or high risk. Distinguish what you observed, what somebody reported and the inference being drawn. Consider information that challenges the proposed compulsory route as carefully as information that supports it. The existence of a legal power does not establish that its conditions are met in this case.

## Separate each intervention

Transport, assessment, admission, psychiatric treatment and treatment of an unrelated physical condition can involve different authorities. Check the exact route, the professional authorised to exercise it, required documentation and its time limits. Do not use a single statement that the person is detained to explain every intervention. Document attempts to arrange voluntary or less restrictive support and whether those services are actually available.

Rights information should be understandable at the time and revisited when the person can engage more fully. Explain independent support, legal representation and the applicable review process. During discharge planning, identify housing, medicines, follow-up, family responsibilities and crisis contacts. Confirm who accepts responsibility for each task. A person should not leave with an apparently complete plan consisting only of referrals that no receiving service has accepted.

## Apply the local pathway

- Identify voluntary support and whether an assessment or treatment detention route is actually being considered.
- Check the current Order, evidence for the particular criteria and the authorised professional’s role.
- Keep the partly commenced capacity framework and any separate physical-treatment decision distinct.
- Explain the person’s status and arrange rights information, support and review under the applicable route.

## Rights, challenge and review

The Review Tribunal and the relevant hospital discharge or review processes address detention questions. Help the person obtain advice and understand how to challenge the measure. Confirm which rules apply to their specific admission status and documents.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A person declines admission after an argument at home but agrees to a same-day assessment and support from a trusted friend.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Explore the immediate safety evidence, physical health and whether voluntary arrangements are workable. Ask the authorised professionals to assess the actual statutory criteria if compulsion is proposed. Refusal of the first offer is not itself the required harm analysis.

### Common error to avoid

Assuming the 2016 capacity legislation has replaced every mental-health admission provision.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Mental and physical health evidence and the person’s account
- The local criteria and voluntary alternatives considered
- Separate authority for transport, admission and treatment
- Required notices, advocacy, representation and review
- Continuity, discharge responsibilities and crisis plan

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [Mental Health (Northern Ireland) Order 1986](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/nisi/1986/595/contents)
- [Mental health services and support](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/mental-health-services-and-support)

Editorial expansion: 8 September 2026. The sources support the distinctions taught here; check their current text, amendments, commencement and applicable local procedure before operational use. Independent practitioner review has not been recorded.

# Adult Safeguarding — Northern Ireland — Northern Ireland

Jurisdiction: Northern Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Northern Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/northern-ireland/adult-safeguarding-northern-ireland.html

# Adult Safeguarding — Northern Ireland

## Learning outcomes

Recognise abuse, neglect and coercion; choose the correct local reporting route; connect immediate protection to the adult’s wishes and continuing support.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

The regional policy Adult Safeguarding: Prevention and Protection in Partnership distinguishes an adult at risk of harm from an adult in need of protection. It considers personal characteristics and life circumstances, with HSC Trust and PSNI roles according to the concern. It is not a general power to compel an adult to accept services.

The Adult Protection Bill is a reform to monitor, not a source of powers to assume are already operational. The Assembly’s legislative tracker must be checked for passage and any subsequent Act and commencement before applying a new duty.

## Enquire safely and proportionately

Start with immediate danger and the safest way to communicate. A private conversation may reveal concerns that cannot be expressed in front of a relative, carer or staff member. Check whether telephone calls, letters or messages could expose the person to retaliation. Use independent communication support where a proposed interpreter may have a conflict of interest.

Record the nature of the concern, its source, the person's own words and any observed injuries, living conditions or financial issues. Distinguish a disclosure, a suspicion and a confirmed finding. Do not wait to conduct your own investigation before acting on a reporting duty. Equally, avoid leading questions or repeated interviewing that may distress the person or compromise another agency's investigation.

## Combine protection with participation

Ask what the person wants to change and what they fear might happen after a report. Assess coercion, dependency and practical barriers alongside decision-making ability. A person may understand a risk yet be unable to obtain food, leave safely or resist somebody controlling their money. Support, reporting and authority to impose an intervention are separate questions.

Agree what information needs sharing, with whom and on what legal basis. Where sharing is required or justified without consent, record the reason and explain it to the person when safe and appropriate. Make a plan for immediate needs, follow-up contact and responsibility between agencies. A referral does not establish that somebody has accepted the concern. Confirm receipt, escalate unresolved danger and review whether the action has improved safety in the person's own terms.

## Apply the local pathway

- Identify abuse, exploitation or neglect and the adult’s ability to protect themselves in their actual circumstances.
- Use the organisation’s safeguarding arrangements and refer protection concerns to the appropriate HSC Trust route.
- Contact PSNI where the circumstances require a police response, distinguishing criminal investigation from the support plan.
- Establish the lawful basis for information sharing and for any proposed intervention without agreement.

## Rights, challenge and review

Use the policy’s participation and proportionate-response approach, together with the applicable consent, capacity and legal safeguards. Explain the Trust or provider complaint process and obtain specialist advice if a coercive intervention is proposed.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: An isolated adult says a neighbour takes their pension but fears losing the only person who buys groceries.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Arrange a safe conversation and practical alternatives for food and contact. Assess the protection concern and report through the relevant Trust and police routes as appropriate. A refusal of one intervention does not remove the need to explore coercion, dependency and a safer support plan.

### Common error to avoid

Treating a safeguarding policy as a detention power or treating a proposed Bill as commenced law.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Concern, source, chronology and the adult’s own account
- Immediate safety and a safe communication method
- The local reporting threshold, recipient and timing
- Consent, coercion and information-sharing basis
- Accepted responsibilities, outcomes and follow-up

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [Adult safeguarding policy and documents](https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/publications/adult-safeguarding-prevention-and-protection-partnership-key-documents)
- [Assembly legislation tracker](https://www.niassembly.gov.uk/assembly-business/legislation/2022-2027-mandate/primary-legislation-bills-22-27-mandate/)

Editorial expansion: 8 September 2026. The sources support the distinctions taught here; check their current text, amendments, commencement and applicable local procedure before operational use. Independent practitioner review has not been recorded.

# Children, Families and Transitions — Northern Ireland — Northern Ireland

Jurisdiction: Northern Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Northern Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/northern-ireland/children-families-and-safeguarding-northern-ireland.html

# Children, Families and Transitions — Northern Ireland

## Learning outcomes

Separate family support from protection powers, apply the local reporting duty, involve the child and coordinate education, health and transition planning.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

The Children (Northern Ireland) Order 1995 provides the main framework for children in need, family support and protective court processes. Co-operating to Safeguard Children and Young People supplies the regional policy framework. The HSC Trust’s children’s services and PSNI have different responsibilities.

Assessment and family support should be distinguished from a protection investigation or court order. A family meeting cannot create powers of removal or determine legal parental responsibility. Check the child’s position and the relevant authority for accommodation, contact and treatment decisions.

## Understand the child’s daily experience

Use age-appropriate communication, observation and accessible material. Ask about ordinary routines, trusted adults, worries, food, sleep, school and relationships. Record the child's words separately from adult interpretations. For a baby or a child who does not use speech, describe interactions and behaviour without claiming to know a view they have not expressed.

Assess harm, strengths and the practical conditions affecting care. Poverty, inaccessible services or overcrowded housing may require material help; they should not automatically be treated as evidence of parental indifference. At the same time, a family's strengths do not remove the need to act on a protection concern. Explore the experience of siblings and whether a proposed protective adult can actually provide the support being described.

## Keep support and compulsory intervention clear

Explain your role, the concern, confidentiality limits and the next step in language the family can understand. Establish the local reporting threshold and receiving authority. A practice model can organise enquiry but cannot determine a statutory threshold or authorise removal. Where you disagree with a decision, identify the evidence and use the relevant escalation process without delaying necessary immediate action.

Plan with education, health, disability and community services, identifying each person's responsibility. For a young person approaching adulthood, address accommodation, income, healthcare, relationships, education or work and decision support before a service ends. Confirm eligibility and acceptance by adult services rather than assuming that a childhood plan transfers automatically. Preserve cultural, family and community relationships in ways consistent with the child's safety and wishes.

## Apply the local pathway

- Record the child’s account, daily experience, harm concerns and support needs.
- Use the current regional policy and Trust referral procedure for a child-protection concern.
- Identify who holds parental responsibility and any court order affecting the proposed decision.
- Coordinate education, health and family support and plan transitions before a service ends.

## Rights, challenge and review

Explain the particular assessment, protection or court process, including how the child and family can participate, obtain advocacy or legal advice and raise disagreement. Do not promise confidentiality that conflicts with a necessary safeguarding response.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A child tells a school worker they are frightened to return home. The parent asks for the conversation to remain within school.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Listen without leading questions, record the child’s words and assess immediate safety. Follow the relevant Trust and police referral arrangements where required. Explain confidentiality limits safely and establish who will act before the child leaves the setting.

### Common error to avoid

Allowing an internal discussion or a parent’s request for secrecy to replace the required protection response.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Child’s account, communication and daily-life evidence
- Harm, strengths, needs and alternative explanations
- Reporting duty, recipient and action taken
- Family participation, culture and legal authority
- Named plan, education/health links and transition dates

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [Children (Northern Ireland) Order 1995](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/nisi/1995/755/contents)
- [Co-operating to safeguard children and young people](https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/publications/co-operating-safeguard-children-and-young-people-northern-ireland)

Editorial expansion: 8 September 2026. The sources support the distinctions taught here; check their current text, amendments, commencement and applicable local procedure before operational use. Independent practitioner review has not been recorded.

# Rights, Culture and Recording — Northern Ireland — Northern Ireland

Jurisdiction: Northern Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Northern Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/northern-ireland/rights-participation-and-recording-northern-ireland.html

# Rights, Culture and Recording — Northern Ireland

## Learning outcomes

Connect rights to an actual service decision, distinguish privacy from absolute secrecy and write a record that makes reasons and disagreement visible.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

Northern Ireland has its own equality laws. The Equality Act 2010 does not apply. Identify the relevant disability, sex, race, religious or political discrimination provision and the setting it covers. Section 75 of the Northern Ireland Act 1998 places equality-of-opportunity and good-relations duties on designated public authorities.

The Human Rights Act and applicable UK data-protection law also matter, but they answer different questions. A public authority’s equality scheme does not by itself establish permission to disclose a person’s health information.

## Make rights practical

Identify the decision affecting the person: access to an assessment, a restriction, a disclosure, an inaccessible meeting or a refusal of support. Ask which right or duty is engaged and which organisation is responsible. A statement that a plan is rights-based does not explain whether the person could participate or how the effect on them was weighed.

Arrange interpretation, accessible formats and communication support suited to the person. Ask about cultural identity, discrimination and the supporters they wish to involve. Do not infer these preferences from appearance, surname or language. Consider whether a seemingly neutral rule disadvantages someone because of disability or another protected characteristic, and what accommodation or adjustment is available under the applicable law.

## Make disclosure and recording accountable

Identify the purpose, recipient and legal basis before sharing personal information. Determine whether the organisation is covered by health, public-sector, private-sector or another confidentiality regime. Consent is not the only possible basis for disclosure, but an organisational request is not a legal basis by itself. Share the information relevant to the permitted purpose and record any limits or objection.

A useful record separates observation, the person's account, information from others, analysis and action. Write what evidence led to the conclusion, which alternatives were considered and why a particular option was chosen. Preserve disagreement respectfully and correct factual errors through the appropriate process. Explain how the person can request access, seek correction, complain or obtain an independent review. Store learning reflections without identifiable case details and use approved systems for professional records.

## Apply the local pathway

- Identify the relevant equality law and public-authority duty for the actual decision.
- Arrange accessible communication and consider the applicable reasonable-adjustment obligations.
- Establish the purpose and legal basis of sharing, including the treatment of sensitive information.
- Record the person’s account, alternatives, reasons, disagreement and the route for correction or challenge.

## Rights, challenge and review

The Equality Commission for Northern Ireland provides information on discrimination and routes to challenge. Distinguish a service complaint, an equality-scheme concern and legal proceedings; obtain timely advice because different limits and remedies apply.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A service offers an assessment in an inaccessible building and says its policy treats every applicant identically.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Identify the disability-related barrier and the applicable adjustment duty. Offer an accessible arrangement and revisit any adverse inference caused by the failed appointment. Record the change and how the person can challenge the earlier decision.

### Common error to avoid

Copying an equality test from another legal system or equating identical treatment with accessible participation.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Decision, affected rights and responsible organisation
- Accessibility, culture and participation arrangements
- Disclosure purpose, legal basis, recipient and limits
- Evidence, alternatives, reasons and disagreement
- Access, correction, complaints and review route

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [Equality laws in Northern Ireland](https://equalityni.org/equality-laws-ni)
- [Section 75 and equality schemes](https://equalityni.org/public-authorities/section-75)
- [Northern Ireland Act 1998, section 75](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1998/47/section/75)

# Quick Reference — Northern Ireland — Northern Ireland

Jurisdiction: Northern Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Northern Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/northern-ireland/quick-reference.html

# Practice reference — Northern Ireland practice guide


Use alongside the full modules and current official sources. Each entry separates the local framework, action and review.


## Professional Foundations — Northern Ireland

The Northern Ireland Social Care Council (NISCC) Standards of Conduct and Practice provide the professional framework for registered social workers. Distinguish those standards from the procedures of a Health and Social Care (HSC) Trust and from powers available only to a specifically trained or appointed practitioner.

HSC Trusts provide important health and social-care functions; the Regulation and Quality Improvement Authority (RQIA) has a separate service-regulation role. Identify the actual decision-maker and employer. A concern about a worker’s professional conduct, a provider’s quality and a Trust’s care decision may need different responses.


- Explain the purpose of contact, professional role and confidentiality limits in accessible language.
- Identify the HSC Trust, provider and any statutory appointment relevant to the task.
- Use supervision to test how poverty, disability, trauma or barriers to services influence the formulation.
- Link learning and feedback to the current NISCC registration and professional-development requirements.


Explain the relevant Trust or provider complaint route and when a concern about a registered worker belongs with NISCC. Give the person a clear account of who can address the outcome they seek; professional regulation does not itself arrange a care package.


- [NISCC Standards and Guidance](https://niscc.info/standards-and-guidance/)


## Social Care and Support — Northern Ireland

An HSC Trust needs assessment is the starting point for community support. The Health and Personal Social Services (Northern Ireland) Order 1972 and the Carers and Direct Payments Act (Northern Ireland) 2002 form part of the legal map. Establish the particular duty, Trust criteria and service being requested.

Direct payments can allow an eligible person to arrange assessed support. Discuss the option during assessment, including consent, the ability to manage it with support, permitted use and employer responsibilities. A carer’s own assessment concerns their caring role and needs; it does not replace the assessment of the person receiving care.


- Describe the person’s needs and desired outcomes, including fluctuation and the effect of unavailable support.
- Ask the Trust to explain the assessment and eligibility decisions separately from costs and provision.
- Offer a carer’s assessment where the relevant conditions are met, including consideration of young carers.
- Compare arranged services with direct payments and confirm that the proposed support can actually be delivered.


Request reasons, reassessment where circumstances change and the appropriate Trust complaint or review route. Record interim arrangements and unmet needs while a decision is disputed. NI Direct explains access, carers’ assessments and direct payments, with links to local services.


- [Arranging health and social care](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/arranging-health-and-social-care)
- [Direct payments for care](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/direct-payments-care)
- [Carers and Direct Payments Act (Northern Ireland) 2002](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/nia/2002/6/contents)


## Decision-Making and Capacity — Northern Ireland

The Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 is only partly commenced. Phase 1 covers research and specified deprivation-of-liberty and money-and-valuables provisions. Do not apply the whole Act as though it were already the general framework for every treatment or welfare decision.

Within the operative framework, the assessment is decision-specific, with support before a conclusion of incapacity. The inability must result from impairment or disturbance of the mind or brain. Test understanding, retaining information for the decision, appreciating its relevance and using and weighing it, and communicating the choice. Record how any failed ability affects this decision, rather than relying on a diagnosis. The principles address capacity and best interests. Formal assessments and other statutory functions have training and qualification requirements. A nominated person must be consulted in the relevant process; the role does not confer general substitute decision-making authority.


- Identify the proposed act and confirm that the provision being relied on is commenced for that purpose.
- Specify the decision and provide practical support before applying the relevant capacity test.
- Check whether the required assessment must be completed by a suitably qualified and trained person.
- Record the person’s wishes, consultation and the actual legal basis for any decision taken without their own consent.


For phase-1 deprivation-of-liberty decisions, check the Review Tribunal route and safeguards in the current Code, forms and interim guidance. For another type of decision, obtain advice about the applicable law rather than extending phase-1 powers by analogy.


- [Mental Capacity Act: implementation and current guidance](https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/topics/mental-capacity-act)
- [Mental Capacity Act FAQs](https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/articles/mental-capacity-act-faqs)
- [Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/nia/2016/18/contents)

- Describe actual arrangements and obtain evidence about the person’s wishes, understanding and objections.
- Consult the current interim guidance before deciding whether the arrangements amount to deprivation of liberty.
- Use the appropriate trained assessors, Trust process and current forms where an authorisation is required.
- Keep capacity, best interests, authorisation, consultation and challenge arrangements separately recorded.


Identify the nominated person, advocacy or representation required and the person’s access to the Review Tribunal. Check expiry, review and changed circumstances. Do not remove an existing safeguard solely because a judgment or guidance has changed without the responsible legal review.

- [Mental Capacity Act FAQs](https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/articles/mental-capacity-act-faqs)

- Coordinate education, health and family support and plan transitions before a service ends.


Explain the particular assessment, protection or court process, including how the child and family can participate, obtain advocacy or legal advice and raise disagreement. Do not promise confidentiality that conflicts with a necessary safeguarding response.


- [Children (Northern Ireland) Order 1995](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/nisi/1995/755/contents)
- [Co-operating to safeguard children and young people](https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/publications/co-operating-safeguard-children-and-young-people-northern-ireland)


## Rights, Culture and Recording — Northern Ireland

Northern Ireland has its own equality laws. The Equality Act 2010 does not apply. Identify the relevant disability, sex, race, religious or political discrimination provision and the setting it covers. Section 75 of the Northern Ireland Act 1998 places equality-of-opportunity and good-relations duties on designated public authorities.

The Human Rights Act and applicable UK data-protection law also matter, but they answer different questions. A public authority’s equality scheme does not by itself establish permission to disclose a person’s health information.


- Identify the relevant equality law and public-authority duty for the actual decision.
- Arrange accessible communication and consider the applicable reasonable-adjustment obligations.
- Establish the purpose and legal basis of sharing, including the treatment of sensitive information.
- Record the person’s account, alternatives, reasons, disagreement and the route for correction or challenge.


The Equality Commission for Northern Ireland provides information on discrimination and routes to challenge. Distinguish a service complaint, an equality-scheme concern and legal proceedings; obtain timely advice because different limits and remedies apply.


- [Equality laws in Northern Ireland](https://equalityni.org/equality-laws-ni)
- [Section 75 and equality schemes](https://equalityni.org/public-authorities/section-75)
- [Northern Ireland Act 1998, section 75](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1998/47/section/75)

### Professional Foundations

```text
Professional Foundations
Northern Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Northern Ireland Social Care Council (NISCC) Standards of Conduct and Practice provide the professional framework for registered social workers. Distinguish those standards from the procedures of a Health and Social Care (HSC) Trust and from powers available only to a specifically trained or appointed practitioner.

HSC Trusts provide important health and social-care functions; the Regulation and Quality Improvement Authority (RQIA) has a separate service-regulation role. Identify the actual decision-maker and employer. A concern about a worker’s professional conduct, a provider’s quality and a Trust’s care decision may need different responses.

Local pathway:
Explain the purpose of contact, professional role and confidentiality limits in accessible language.
Identify the HSC Trust, provider and any statutory appointment relevant to the task.
Use supervision to test how poverty, disability, trauma or barriers to services influence the formulation.
Link learning and feedback to the current NISCC registration and professional-development requirements.

Recording prompts:
1. Your role and the legal or professional framework
Notes:

2. The person’s outcomes and communication preferences
Notes:

3. Evidence, competing explanations and missing perspectives
Notes:

4. Power, boundaries and any conflict of interest
Notes:

5. Agreed action, supervision, feedback and review
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain the relevant Trust or provider complaint route and when a concern about a registered worker belongs with NISCC. Give the person a clear account of who can address the outcome they seek; professional regulation does not itself arrange a care package.

Sources:
https://niscc.info/standards-and-guidance/

```

### Social Care and Support

```text
Social Care and Support
Northern Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
An HSC Trust needs assessment is the starting point for community support. The Health and Personal Social Services (Northern Ireland) Order 1972 and the Carers and Direct Payments Act (Northern Ireland) 2002 form part of the legal map. Establish the particular duty, Trust criteria and service being requested.

Direct payments can allow an eligible person to arrange assessed support. Discuss the option during assessment, including consent, the ability to manage it with support, permitted use and employer responsibilities. A carer’s own assessment concerns their caring role and needs; it does not replace the assessment of the person receiving care.

Local pathway:
Describe the person’s needs and desired outcomes, including fluctuation and the effect of unavailable support.
Ask the Trust to explain the assessment and eligibility decisions separately from costs and provision.
Offer a carer’s assessment where the relevant conditions are met, including consideration of young carers.
Compare arranged services with direct payments and confirm that the proposed support can actually be delivered.

Recording prompts:
1. Daily-life evidence, fluctuation and desired outcomes
Notes:

2. The service, eligibility test and decision-maker
Notes:

3. Carer willingness and separately identified needs
Notes:

4. Funding, charges, decisions and reasons
Notes:

5. Start dates, unmet needs, contingency and challenge route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Request reasons, reassessment where circumstances change and the appropriate Trust complaint or review route. Record interim arrangements and unmet needs while a decision is disputed. NI Direct explains access, carers’ assessments and direct payments, with links to local services.

Sources:
https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/arranging-health-and-social-care
https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/direct-payments-care
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/nia/2002/6/contents

```

### Decision-Making and Capacity

```text
Decision-Making and Capacity
Northern Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 is only partly commenced. Phase 1 covers research and specified deprivation-of-liberty and money-and-valuables provisions. Do not apply the whole Act as though it were already the general framework for every treatment or welfare decision.

Within the operative framework, the assessment is decision-specific, with support before a conclusion of incapacity. The inability must result from impairment or disturbance of the mind or brain. Test understanding, retaining information for the decision, appreciating its relevance and using and weighing it, and communicating the choice. Record how any failed ability affects this decision, rather than relying on a diagnosis. The principles address capacity and best interests. Formal assessments and other statutory functions have training and qualification requirements. A nominated person must be consulted in the relevant process; the role does not confer general substitute decision-making authority.

Local pathway:
Identify the proposed act and confirm that the provision being relied on is commenced for that purpose.
Specify the decision and provide practical support before applying the relevant capacity test.
Check whether the required assessment must be completed by a suitably qualified and trained person.
Record the person’s wishes, consultation and the actual legal basis for any decision taken without their own consent.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, options and time at which it is needed
Notes:

2. Communication support and observed responses
Notes:

3. Applicable legal test and evidence for each element
Notes:

4. Representative’s document, scope and decision standard
Notes:

5. Wishes, disagreement, review and any urgent action
Notes:

Challenge and review:
For phase-1 deprivation-of-liberty decisions, check the Review Tribunal route and safeguards in the current Code, forms and interim guidance. For another type of decision, obtain advice about the applicable law rather than extending phase-1 powers by analogy.

Sources:
https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/topics/mental-capacity-act
https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/articles/mental-capacity-act-faqs
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/nia/2016/18/contents

```

### Restrictions and Liberty

```text
Restrictions and Liberty
Northern Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The operative deprivation-of-liberty provisions of the Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 require the relevant assessments, authorisation and safeguards. Setting, age, purpose and the applicable mental-health or children’s framework must be established before selecting a route.

The Department of Health states that the Supreme Court judgment of 2 June 2026 changed the previous approach to defining deprivation of liberty. Interim guidance is available while the Code and other material are reviewed. Read that guidance with current Trust specialist advice; an older training slide is not sufficient evidence of the current legal test.

Local pathway:
Describe actual arrangements and obtain evidence about the person’s wishes, understanding and objections.
Consult the current interim guidance before deciding whether the arrangements amount to deprivation of liberty.
Use the appropriate trained assessors, Trust process and current forms where an authorisation is required.
Keep capacity, best interests, authorisation, consultation and challenge arrangements separately recorded.

Recording prompts:
1. Each restriction, setting, duration and actual effect
Notes:

2. The person’s wishes, understanding and objections
Notes:

3. Legal authority, decision-maker, limits and conditions
Notes:

4. Alternatives tried and the evidence about necessity
Notes:

5. Representation, review date, expiry and challenge
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Identify the nominated person, advocacy or representation required and the person’s access to the Review Tribunal. Check expiry, review and changed circumstances. Do not remove an existing safeguard solely because a judgment or guidance has changed without the responsible legal review.

Sources:
https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/publications/interim-guidance-mental-capacity-act-ni-2016
https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/articles/mental-capacity-act-faqs

```

### Mental Health

```text
Mental Health
Northern Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Mental Health (Northern Ireland) Order 1986 remains relevant alongside the partly commenced capacity legislation. Assessment and treatment routes have their own criteria and professional roles. For admission for assessment, the Order includes mental disorder of a nature or degree warranting detention for assessment and the relevant substantial likelihood of serious physical harm.

An approved social worker has specific training and functions. The medical recommendation, application and hospital processes should be distinguished. A general referral to mental-health services is not a compulsory admission application.

Local pathway:
Identify voluntary support and whether an assessment or treatment detention route is actually being considered.
Check the current Order, evidence for the particular criteria and the authorised professional’s role.
Keep the partly commenced capacity framework and any separate physical-treatment decision distinct.
Explain the person’s status and arrange rights information, support and review under the applicable route.

Recording prompts:
1. Mental and physical health evidence and the person’s account
Notes:

2. The local criteria and voluntary alternatives considered
Notes:

3. Separate authority for transport, admission and treatment
Notes:

4. Required notices, advocacy, representation and review
Notes:

5. Continuity, discharge responsibilities and crisis plan
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The Review Tribunal and the relevant hospital discharge or review processes address detention questions. Help the person obtain advice and understand how to challenge the measure. Confirm which rules apply to their specific admission status and documents.

Sources:
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/nisi/1986/595/contents
https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/mental-health-services-and-support

```

### Adult Safeguarding

```text
Adult Safeguarding
Northern Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The regional policy Adult Safeguarding: Prevention and Protection in Partnership distinguishes an adult at risk of harm from an adult in need of protection. It considers personal characteristics and life circumstances, with HSC Trust and PSNI roles according to the concern. It is not a general power to compel an adult to accept services.

The Adult Protection Bill is a reform to monitor, not a source of powers to assume are already operational. The Assembly’s legislative tracker must be checked for passage and any subsequent Act and commencement before applying a new duty.

Local pathway:
Identify abuse, exploitation or neglect and the adult’s ability to protect themselves in their actual circumstances.
Use the organisation’s safeguarding arrangements and refer protection concerns to the appropriate HSC Trust route.
Contact PSNI where the circumstances require a police response, distinguishing criminal investigation from the support plan.
Establish the lawful basis for information sharing and for any proposed intervention without agreement.

Recording prompts:
1. Concern, source, chronology and the adult’s own account
Notes:

2. Immediate safety and a safe communication method
Notes:

3. The local reporting threshold, recipient and timing
Notes:

4. Consent, coercion and information-sharing basis
Notes:

5. Accepted responsibilities, outcomes and follow-up
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Use the policy’s participation and proportionate-response approach, together with the applicable consent, capacity and legal safeguards. Explain the Trust or provider complaint process and obtain specialist advice if a coercive intervention is proposed.

Sources:
https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/publications/adult-safeguarding-prevention-and-protection-partnership-key-documents
https://www.niassembly.gov.uk/assembly-business/legislation/2022-2027-mandate/primary-legislation-bills-22-27-mandate/

```

### Children, Families and Transitions

```text
Children, Families and Transitions
Northern Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Children (Northern Ireland) Order 1995 provides the main framework for children in need, family support and protective court processes. Co-operating to Safeguard Children and Young People supplies the regional policy framework. The HSC Trust’s children’s services and PSNI have different responsibilities.

Assessment and family support should be distinguished from a protection investigation or court order. A family meeting cannot create powers of removal or determine legal parental responsibility. Check the child’s position and the relevant authority for accommodation, contact and treatment decisions.

Local pathway:
Record the child’s account, daily experience, harm concerns and support needs.
Use the current regional policy and Trust referral procedure for a child-protection concern.
Identify who holds parental responsibility and any court order affecting the proposed decision.
Coordinate education, health and family support and plan transitions before a service ends.

Recording prompts:
1. Child’s account, communication and daily-life evidence
Notes:

2. Harm, strengths, needs and alternative explanations
Notes:

3. Reporting duty, recipient and action taken
Notes:

4. Family participation, culture and legal authority
Notes:

5. Named plan, education/health links and transition dates
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain the particular assessment, protection or court process, including how the child and family can participate, obtain advocacy or legal advice and raise disagreement. Do not promise confidentiality that conflicts with a necessary safeguarding response.
```

# Practice Scenarios — Northern Ireland — Northern Ireland

Jurisdiction: Northern Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Northern Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/northern-ireland/practice-scenarios.html

# Scenario Workouts — Northern Ireland practice guide


All cases are fictional learning exercises. Explain your evidence and reasoning before reading the discussion.


## Professional Foundations — Northern Ireland

A family receives different explanations from a Trust worker and a commissioned provider about why visits have reduced.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Establish who changed the assessed plan and who changed delivery. Obtain the recorded decision and reasons, hear the person’s experience and address immediate unmet needs. Escalate the appropriate assessment or contract issue instead of referring every complaint to the professional regulator.


## Social Care and Support — Northern Ireland

A disabled parent needs morning assistance. Their teenager is missing school to help, and a relative suggests using the parent’s benefits to pay informally.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Assess the parent’s support needs and the impact on the young person. Consider Trust-arranged care or an eligible direct-payment arrangement with proper support. Clarify funding and employment responsibilities; do not assume the child can continue filling a gap in services.


## Decision-Making and Capacity — Northern Ireland

A hospital team asks a nominated person to sign consent for an unrelated operation because a deprivation-of-liberty assessment has been completed.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Separate the operation from the liberty arrangements. Check the patient’s ability to decide about that treatment and the applicable consent law. The nominated-person role and a liberty assessment do not provide a general consent signature for another intervention.


## Restrictions and Liberty — Northern Ireland

A care setting continues to use an old checklist after June 2026 and says its completed form proves all arrangements are lawful.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Review the actual restrictions and the source version used. Ask the Trust’s MCA team to apply the current guidance and determine any required reassessment or authorisation. Continue meeting immediate care and participation duties while resolving the legal position.


## Mental Health — Northern Ireland

A person declines admission after an argument at home but agrees to a same-day assessment and support from a trusted friend.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Explore the immediate safety evidence, physical health and whether voluntary arrangements are workable. Ask the authorised professionals to assess the actual statutory criteria if compulsion is proposed. Refusal of the first offer is not itself the required harm analysis.


## Adult Safeguarding — Northern Ireland

An isolated adult says a neighbour takes their pension but fears losing the only person who buys groceries.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Arrange a safe conversation and practical alternatives for food and contact. Assess the protection concern and report through the relevant Trust and police routes as appropriate. A refusal of one intervention does not remove the need to explore coercion, dependency and a safer support plan.


## Children, Families and Transitions — Northern Ireland

A child tells a school worker they are frightened to return home. The parent asks for the conversation to remain within school.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Listen without leading questions, record the child’s words and assess immediate safety. Follow the relevant Trust and police referral arrangements where required. Explain confidentiality limits safely and establish who will act before the child leaves the setting.


## Rights, Culture and Recording — Northern Ireland

A service offers an assessment in an inaccessible building and says its policy treats every applicant identically.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Identify the disability-related barrier and the applicable adjustment duty. Offer an accessible arrangement and revisit any adverse inference caused by the failed appointment. Record the change and how the person can challenge the earlier decision.

## How to verify a rule

Identify territorial scope, current consolidated text, amendments and commencement, then the applicable statutory guidance and service procedure. An enactment announcement or portal is not proof that every provision is in force.

# About Us — Northern Ireland

## About this resource

Daily Mindset Moments CIC, founded by Raymond Hill, provides this structured social-work learning resource. It supports students, practitioners and supervisors with modules, fictional exercises, source links and private reflections.

## Northern Ireland context

This guide separates the learning material for Northern Ireland from the other practice locations. Shared theories support enquiry; laws, professional requirements and service pathways must be checked locally. Read the source library for scope and editorial status.

# Contact Us — Northern Ireland

## Feedback and corrections

Contact [Daily Mindset Moments CIC](mailto:info@daily-mindset-moments.com) with the selected location, section title, source URL and a description of the correction. The contact form below is for website enquiries.

## Keep enquiries appropriate

Do not include identifiable case information. This website is not an emergency or casework reporting service. Use the responsible local agency, employer and emergency services for urgent or live practice concerns.

# Privacy Policy — Northern Ireland — Northern Ireland

Jurisdiction: Northern Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Northern Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/northern-ireland/privacy-policy.html

# Privacy Policy — Northern Ireland

## Learning stored on your device

The app stores your selected location, reading progress, confidence, saved reflections and unfinished reflection fields in this browser. Records are separated by location. They are not submitted to a professional body. Export or print a copy before clearing browser data or changing devices.

## Website enquiries

If you use the contact form, the details you submit are sent to the website’s form service and operator. Do not send confidential case information. External source websites have their own privacy policies.

## Your records

Use Delete reflection to remove saved entries. Clearing this site’s browser storage removes local progress and notes. Contact [Daily Mindset Moments CIC](mailto:info@daily-mindset-moments.com) about information sent through an enquiry.

# Terms of Service — Northern Ireland — Northern Ireland

Jurisdiction: Northern Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Northern Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/northern-ireland/terms-of-service.html

# Terms of Service — Northern Ireland

## Purpose and scope

The Northern Ireland guide is an educational resource for learning and supervision. It does not provide individual legal advice, determine a case outcome or certify professional competence. Use current official sources and the procedures applicable to your role.

## Responsible use

Practice scenarios are fictional. Downloads are learning prompts, not statutory forms. Do not enter identifiable case details into reflections or enquiries. Your browser stores local notes; export your own copy if you need a durable record.

## Sources and corrections

External sources may change. The source library records editorial scope; inclusion of a link or model does not imply endorsement by its publisher. Send corrections with the relevant source and section title through the contact route.

# Start Here — Ireland — Ireland

Jurisdiction: Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/ireland/start-here-ireland.html

# Start Here — Ireland

## Your Ireland learning guide

Use the location selector to choose among twelve separate guides. Your reading progress, confidence and reflections are stored separately for each location.

## Start learning

Read [Professional Foundations](/?jurisdiction=ireland&resource=foundations#learningWorkspace), choose a topic from [Learning Map](/?jurisdiction=ireland&resource=map#learningWorkspace), then practise with [Practice Scenarios](/?jurisdiction=ireland&resource=scenarios#learningWorkspace). Test recall with flashcards and use the reflection log to identify a specific next action.

## Scope

Eight modules, forty flashcards, a glossary, eight fictional scenarios and ten recording prompts support revision and supervision. This is a final learning-guide release. It is not an exhaustive account of law, a statutory form or a regulator-approved training programme. The source library explains how to check the applicable version and local route.

# Learning Map — Ireland — Ireland

Jurisdiction: Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/ireland/learning-map.html

# Learning Map — Ireland

## A sequence for study

1. [Professional Foundations](/?jurisdiction=ireland&resource=foundations#learningWorkspace): Professional role, ethics, competence, supervision and accountable decisions.
2. [Social Care and Support](/?jurisdiction=ireland&resource=care-support#learningWorkspace): Needs, strengths, access to support, family responsibilities and service planning.
3. [Decision-Making and Capacity](/?jurisdiction=ireland&resource=mca#learningWorkspace): Decision support, consent and the authority for someone else to decide.
4. [Restrictions and Liberty](/?jurisdiction=ireland&resource=dols#learningWorkspace): Restrictions, legal authority, less restrictive options and review.
5. [Mental Health](/?jurisdiction=ireland&resource=mha#learningWorkspace): Mental-health support, crisis response, treatment and rights.
6. [Adult Safeguarding](/?jurisdiction=ireland&resource=safeguarding#learningWorkspace): Abuse, neglect, coercion, safe enquiry and the appropriate protective response.
7. [Children, Families and Transitions](/?jurisdiction=ireland&resource=children#learningWorkspace): Child participation, family support, child protection and transitions.
8. [Rights, Culture and Recording](/?jurisdiction=ireland&resource=rights#learningWorkspace): Participation, privacy, cultural safety and clear recording.

## Put learning into practice

Choose one fictional scenario. Record what is known, the person’s perspective and what still needs checking. Open the source library before answering a legal question. Use supervision to test alternative explanations and a reflection to record the next action.

# Case Route Finder — Ireland — Ireland

Jurisdiction: Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/ireland/case-route-finder.html

# Case Route Finder — Ireland

## Use the route finder

Select the concerns that fit a fictional case. More than one framework may be relevant. Open each suggested module and its sources; the tool selects learning topics and does not decide a legal threshold.

## Compare the routes

Separate support needs, decision-making, mental-health intervention, protective reporting and restrictions. Record the question each route answers, the source you checked and who needs to provide further advice.


## Route questions

### Care or carer support needs

Which needs and outcomes belong to the person and to carers?

Identify daily-living needs and which HSE service or other body is responsible for the requested support. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### A decision-specific capacity question

What is the precise decision and why is ability to decide questioned?

State the precise decision and provide accessible information and communication support. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Restrictions or liberty concerns

What restrictions actually operate and how do they affect the person?

Describe what happens if the person asks to leave and record their will and preferences. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Mental health support or compulsion questions

What is the purpose of each proposed intervention?

Check the commencement record and current MHC operational guidance before choosing forms, criteria or time limits. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Abuse, neglect or safeguarding concerns

How can the person be heard safely and privately?

Identify the concern and safe contact arrangements, including coercion and dependency. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### A child, young carer or transition issue

What does the child say or show about safety and daily life?

Establish whether you are a mandated person and whether the concern meets the statutory reporting threshold. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Language, participation or recording concerns

What makes participation accessible for this person?

Identify the right or equality duty engaged by the actual service decision. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Professional learning or supervision

What is the purpose and limit of your role?

Confirm your professional role, competence and any specialist authority needed. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.
