The Children First Act 2015 creates reporting obligations for mandated persons; the Child Care Act 1991 supplies important child-welfare and protection functions. Tusla’s Children First guidance distinguishes the statutory harm threshold from other reasonable welfare concerns that should still be reported through the appropriate route.

For mandated reporting, harm includes assault, ill-treatment or neglect seriously affecting or likely seriously to affect health, development or welfare, and sexual abuse. Apply the guidance for the category and circumstances, including its specific provisions on disclosures. Do not require proof before considering reasonable grounds.


- Establish whether you are a mandated person and whether the concern meets the statutory reporting threshold.
- Report to Tusla through the correct process; follow emergency arrangements where a child is in immediate danger.
- Record the child’s words, the facts supporting the concern and what was reported.
- Coordinate family support, education and health, keeping any court or protection authority distinct.


Explain the assessment or protection process and how the child and family can participate and obtain support or legal advice. A concern below the mandated threshold can still warrant a welfare report; the threshold is not a reason to ignore other needs.


- [Tusla mandated reporting thresholds](https://www.tusla.ie/children-first/mandated-persons/what-are-the-thresholds-for-making-a-mandated-report/)
- [Children First guidance and legislation](https://www.tusla.ie/children-first/children-first-guidance-and-legislation/)
- [Children First Act 2015](https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2015/act/36/enacted/en/html)


## Rights, Culture and Recording — Ireland

The Equal Status Acts, constitutional rights, the European Convention on Human Rights Act 2003 and the Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission Act 2014 form part of the rights map. The public-sector equality and human-rights duty requires public bodies to integrate equality and rights into their functions.

GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 govern personal-data processing alongside professional confidentiality and sector-specific duties. Identify the controller, purpose, lawful basis and any additional condition for sensitive data. A request from another agency does not itself establish permission to send a full record.


- Identify the right or equality duty engaged by the actual service decision.
- Consider accessibility, discrimination and the person’s preferred cultural and communication support.
- Document the legal basis and necessary scope of a disclosure, including consent or another applicable basis.
- Explain access, correction and the relevant service, equality or data-protection complaint route.


IHREC provides public-sector duty guidance; the Data Protection Commission addresses data-protection matters. A service complaint or legal challenge may be needed for the underlying decision. Help the person identify the remedy and obtain advice within the applicable time limits.


- [Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission Act 2014: public bodies](https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2014/act/25/section/42/enacted/en/html)
- [Data Protection Act 2018](https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2018/act/7/enacted/en/html)
- [CORU social-worker Code](https://www.coru.ie/files-codes-of-conduct/swrb-code-of-professional-conduct-and-ethics-for-social-workers.pdf)

### Professional Foundations

```text
Professional Foundations
Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
CORU’s Social Workers Registration Board Code of Professional Conduct and Ethics is the professional anchor. Use the social-worker Code, rather than assuming that material for another CORU profession sets identical obligations. Registration, competence, confidentiality, professional boundaries and continuing learning need to be considered alongside the statutory function being performed.

HSE services, Tusla, local authorities and voluntary providers have different remits. Establish whether the task concerns adult health and support, child protection, housing or another service, and identify who holds the decision-making responsibility.

Local pathway:
Confirm your professional role, competence and any specialist authority needed.
Explain the purpose of involvement and how the person can influence assessment and planning.
Separate the person’s wishes and evidence from organisational assumptions about risk or resources.
Use the current CORU CPD guidance to turn supervision and feedback into demonstrable learning.

Notes:

4. Power, boundaries and any conflict of interest
Notes:

5. Agreed action, supervision, feedback and review
Notes:

Challenge and review:
A service complaint and a CORU fitness-to-practise concern address different issues. Help the person find the route relevant to the outcome they want, including the responsible organisation’s complaints and review processes.
```

### Social Care and Support

```text
Social Care and Support
Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Map the actual HSE, disability, housing, income-support or nursing-home scheme. HSE Home Support for older people provides assistance with everyday tasks following assessment; it is generally directed to people aged 65 or over, with some younger people also eligible. The published service is free, but an assessment and funding decision must still be followed through to delivery.

Home Support, disability services and the Nursing Homes Support Scheme are distinct routes. Do not describe one approval as covering all care settings or assume that the rules for nursing-home financial support apply to home support.

Local pathway:
Identify daily-living needs and which HSE service or other body is responsible for the requested support.
Use the relevant application and needs-assessment process, including discharge coordination if the person is in hospital.
Separate the allocation of support from service availability, start dates and any other scheme’s financial assessment.
Include family willingness, respite needs and a contingency if provision is delayed.

Recording prompts:
1. Daily-life evidence, fluctuation and desired outcomes
Notes:

2. The service, eligibility test and decision-maker
Notes:

3. Carer willingness and separately identified needs
Notes:

4. Funding, charges, decisions and reasons
Notes:

5. Start dates, unmet needs, contingency and challenge route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Ask the responsible service for the assessment outcome, reasons and review or complaint route. HSE’s Home Support guidance explains applications and local contacts. Where more than one scheme is involved, track each decision and its challenge route separately.

Sources:
https://www2.hse.ie/services/home-support-service/home-support-service-for-older-people/
```

### Decision-Making and Capacity

```text
Decision-Making and Capacity
Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act 2015, as amended, uses a functional, decision- and time-specific approach. Presume capacity, provide support and consider understanding, retention, use or weighing of relevant information, and communication. The person’s will and preferences are central to the statutory approach.

Decision-making assistants, co-decision-makers and court-appointed decision-making representatives have different functions. Enduring powers of attorney and advance healthcare directives require their own checks. The Decision Support Service (DSS) registers or supervises relevant arrangements and provides Codes; it does not itself become the person’s decision-maker.

Local pathway:
State the precise decision and provide accessible information and communication support.
Use the DSS capacity-assessment Code and record evidence against the relevant functional abilities.
Read the actual agreement, registration or court order and verify what the supporter or representative can do.
Check whether an applicable advance healthcare directive or other arrangement governs the healthcare decision.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, options and time at which it is needed
Notes:

2. Communication support and observed responses
Notes:

3. Applicable legal test and evidence for each element
Notes:

4. Representative’s document, scope and decision standard
Notes:

5. Wishes, disagreement, review and any urgent action
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Use the appropriate DSS complaint or court route for concerns about arrangements or representatives. A disagreement about treatment may require clinical and legal advice under the HSE Consent Policy. Distinguish support to decide from authority to decide for someone.

Sources:
https://www.decisionsupportservice.ie/resources/codes-practice/code-practice-supporting-decision-making-and-assessing-capacity
https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2015/act/64/enacted/en/html
https://www.decisionsupportservice.ie/resources/guidance-materials

```

### Restrictions and Liberty

```text
Restrictions and Liberty
Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Constitutional liberty and the applicable consent and mental-health law must be considered where a person is prevented from leaving a care setting. Incapacity, good intentions and relatives’ agreement do not supply general authority to detain.

The HSE National Consent Policy addresses deprivation of liberty and the need for legal advice and appropriate court involvement. Distinguish an ordinary care arrangement from detention, and distinguish a decision-support arrangement from authority for confinement. Do not start a new wardship process as though it remained the ordinary route after the decision-support reforms.

Local pathway:
Describe what happens if the person asks to leave and record their will and preferences.
Check capacity for the relevant decision without treating incapacity as a detention authorisation.
Use the current HSE Consent Policy and seek urgent legal advice where the person is held contrary to their wishes.
Identify the precise court or mental-health authority relied on, its limits and a plan to reduce restrictions.

Recording prompts:
1. Each restriction, setting, duration and actual effect
Notes:

2. The person’s wishes, understanding and objections
Notes:

3. Legal authority, decision-maker, limits and conditions
Notes:

4. Alternatives tried and the evidence about necessity
Notes:

5. Representation, review date, expiry and challenge
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Arrange independent support and access to legal advice where liberty is disputed. Court involvement and review must address the actual arrangement; a family meeting cannot confer the necessary power. Immediate action should not become indefinite confinement without review.

Sources:
https://www2.healthservice.hse.ie/organisation/national-pppgs/hse-national-consent-policy/

```

### Mental Health

```text
Mental Health
Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Mental Health Act 2026 was signed into law on 7 May 2026. Section 1 provides for commencement by ministerial order, potentially on different dates for different provisions. Enactment must not be treated as evidence that all new admission, treatment or review rules have replaced the 2001 framework.

For a real case, identify the operative provisions and current Mental Health Commission (MHC) guidance. The existing 2001 framework has separate application, medical recommendation and consultant-psychiatrist admission stages, with independent tribunal safeguards. Explain the route actually in force for the person rather than mixing stages from old and new legislation.

Local pathway:
Check the commencement record and current MHC operational guidance before choosing forms, criteria or time limits.
Identify voluntary alternatives and the purpose of the proposed assessment, admission or treatment.
Verify the authorised professionals and evidence required by the operative route.
Arrange the applicable legal representation, independent review and treatment safeguards, and record which legal version was used.

Recording prompts:
1. Mental and physical health evidence and the person’s account
Notes:

2. The local criteria and voluntary alternatives considered
Notes:

3. Separate authority for transport, admission and treatment
Notes:

4. Required notices, advocacy, representation and review
Notes:

5. Continuity, discharge responsibilities and crisis plan
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The person needs an accessible explanation of their status, legal support and the applicable tribunal or court process. A mental-health admission does not resolve every physical-health consent or accommodation decision. Check each intervention separately.

Sources:
https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2026/act/11/section/1/enacted/en/html
https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-health/press-releases/mental-health-act-2026-signed-into-law-by-president-connolly/
https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2001/act/25/enacted/en/html
https://www.mhcirl.ie/
```

### Adult Safeguarding

```text
Adult Safeguarding
Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Department of Health published the National Policy Framework for Adult Safeguarding in the Health and Social Care Sector in December 2025, with the publication page updated in February 2026. Read it alongside the operative HSE safeguarding procedures and the arrangements in the actual service. An older policy link alone does not describe the whole current policy picture.

Separate a safeguarding concern, a criminal matter, a provider-quality issue and a decision-support problem. HSE safeguarding services, An Garda Síochána, HIQA and the DSS have different remits. A safeguarding referral does not automatically create authority to override the adult’s decision.

Local pathway:
Identify the concern and safe contact arrangements, including coercion and dependency.
Use the service’s current safeguarding procedure and responsible HSE safeguarding route.
Refer criminal or urgent safety issues to the appropriate Garda or emergency response where needed.
Check consent, decision support and any legal authority separately from the protection plan.

Recording prompts:
1. Concern, source, chronology and the adult’s own account
Notes:

2. Immediate safety and a safe communication method
Notes:

3. The local reporting threshold, recipient and timing
Notes:

4. Consent, coercion and information-sharing basis
Notes:

5. Accepted responsibilities, outcomes and follow-up
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Ask about the adult’s desired outcomes and offer independent advocacy where appropriate. Explain the relevant service complaint, regulatory or DSS route. Record the policy version and whether a new national framework has been implemented through the service’s operative procedure.

Sources:
https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-health/publications/national-policy-framework-for-adult-safeguarding-in-the-health-and-social-care-sector/
https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-health/publications/adult-safeguarding/
```

# Practice Scenarios — Ireland — Ireland

Jurisdiction: Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/ireland/practice-scenarios.html

# Scenario Workouts — Ireland practice guide


All cases are fictional learning exercises. Explain your evidence and reasoning before reading the discussion.


## Professional Foundations — Ireland

A worker is asked to describe a client as refusing support, although the only offer conflicts with the client’s religious practice and transport needs.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Record the actual offer and the reasons it was unsuitable. Explore an accessible alternative and bring any unresolved resource issue to supervision. A professional formulation should make the barrier visible rather than treating the organisation’s first offer as the only reasonable option.


## Social Care and Support — Ireland

An older person is ready to leave hospital, but the family is told that approved home-support funding means daily visits are already in place.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Confirm the provider, tasks, hours and first visit. Assess whether an interim plan is safe and agreed if staffing is unavailable. Keep the person’s preference for home, the family’s actual availability and any unmet need in the discharge record.


## Decision-Making and Capacity — Ireland

A person has a decision-making assistance agreement and wants to refuse a proposed move. Staff ask the assistant to approve it instead.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Support the person to consider the actual options and record their wishes. Read the agreement: assistance is not replacement decision-making. If a separate assessment or court issue arises, identify it explicitly rather than expanding the assistant’s role.


## Restrictions and Liberty — Ireland

A residential service says an adult cannot leave because the family signed the admission form. The adult repeatedly asks to go home.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Hear the adult with suitable support, establish the actual restrictions and examine the legal basis. Family agreement is not enough. Explore a workable alternative and obtain timely legal advice under the current consent policy about the necessary court or other lawful route.


## Mental Health — Ireland

A team circulates a summary of the newly enacted Act and proposes to use its future procedures for an admission immediately.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Check whether the relevant provisions and forms have commenced. Use the operative law and current MHC instructions for the admission. Record the version check and keep preparation for reform separate from the person’s present legal safeguards.


## Adult Safeguarding — Ireland

An adult says a paid supporter controls their bank card but asks that the supporter not be dismissed because no replacement is available.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Explore coercion and immediate access to money, food and support. Make the appropriate safeguarding response while planning continuity of assistance. Consider whether a criminal, provider or decision-support concern also needs action; do not reduce the plan to removing one worker.


## Children, Families and Transitions — Ireland

A child describes repeated lack of food and supervision. A worker is told to wait until the next team meeting to establish proof.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Assess immediate safety and the evidence of harm, use the relevant Tusla reporting threshold and act without waiting to prove the allegation. Record the child’s account accurately and arrange practical support alongside the protection response.


## Rights, Culture and Recording — Ireland

An agency requests a complete family file to decide whether to offer a transport service.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Clarify the purpose and the minimum information actually required, the lawful basis and any sensitive-data condition. Discuss participation and confidentiality with the person where appropriate. Record what is shared and why, rather than sending the file simply because the requester is another public body.

- [National adult-safeguarding policy framework](https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-health/publications/national-policy-framework-for-adult-safeguarding-in-the-health-and-social-care-sector/)
- [Department of Health adult safeguarding updates](https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-health/publications/adult-safeguarding/)


### Children, Families and Transitions — Ireland

- [Tusla mandated reporting thresholds](https://www.tusla.ie/children-first/mandated-persons/what-are-the-thresholds-for-making-a-mandated-report/)
- [Children First guidance and legislation](https://www.tusla.ie/children-first/children-first-guidance-and-legislation/)
- [Children First Act 2015](https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2015/act/36/enacted/en/html)


### Rights, Culture and Recording — Ireland

- [Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission Act 2014: public bodies](https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2014/act/25/section/42/enacted/en/html)
- [Data Protection Act 2018](https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2018/act/7/enacted/en/html)
- [CORU social-worker Code](https://www.coru.ie/files-codes-of-conduct/swrb-code-of-professional-conduct-and-ethics-for-social-workers.pdf)


## How to verify a rule

Identify territorial scope, current consolidated text, amendments and commencement, then the applicable statutory guidance and service procedure. An enactment announcement or portal is not proof that every provision is in force.


## Editorial status

Final learning-guide release. Core lessons and linked learning tools were expanded on 8 September 2026. Independent practitioner review has not been recorded. Monthly monitoring flags source changes for editorial assessment and does not automatically rewrite legal guidance.

# Privacy Policy — Ireland

## Learning stored on your device

# Terms of Service — Ireland

## Purpose and scope

The Ireland guide is an educational resource for learning and supervision. It does not provide individual legal advice, determine a case outcome or certify professional competence. Use current official sources and the procedures applicable to your role.

## Responsible use

Practice scenarios are fictional. Downloads are learning prompts, not statutory forms. Do not enter identifiable case details into reflections or enquiries. Your browser stores local notes; export your own copy if you need a durable record.

## Sources and corrections

External sources may change. The source library records editorial scope; inclusion of a link or model does not imply endorsement by its publisher. Send corrections with the relevant source and section title through the contact route.

# Learning Map — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

# Learning Map — Aotearoa New Zealand

## A sequence for study

1. [Professional Foundations](/?jurisdiction=new-zealand&resource=foundations#learningWorkspace): Professional role, ethics, competence, supervision and accountable decisions.
2. [Social Care and Support](/?jurisdiction=new-zealand&resource=care-support#learningWorkspace): Needs, strengths, access to support, family responsibilities and service planning.
3. [Decision-Making and Capacity](/?jurisdiction=new-zealand&resource=mca#learningWorkspace): Decision support, consent and the authority for someone else to decide.
4. [Restrictions and Liberty](/?jurisdiction=new-zealand&resource=dols#learningWorkspace): Restrictions, legal authority, less restrictive options and review.
5. [Mental Health](/?jurisdiction=new-zealand&resource=mha#learningWorkspace): Mental-health support, crisis response, treatment and rights.
6. [Adult Safeguarding](/?jurisdiction=new-zealand&resource=safeguarding#learningWorkspace): Abuse, neglect, coercion, safe enquiry and the appropriate protective response.
7. [Children, Families and Transitions](/?jurisdiction=new-zealand&resource=children#learningWorkspace): Child participation, family support, child protection and transitions.
8. [Rights, Culture and Recording](/?jurisdiction=new-zealand&resource=rights#learningWorkspace): Participation, privacy, cultural safety and clear recording.

## Put learning into practice

Choose one fictional scenario. Record what is known, the person’s perspective and what still needs checking. Open the source library before answering a legal question. Use supervision to test alternative explanations and a reflection to record the next action.

# Case Route Finder — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/case-route-finder.html

# Case Route Finder — Aotearoa New Zealand

## Use the route finder

Select the concerns that fit a fictional case. More than one framework may be relevant. Open each suggested module and its sources; the tool selects learning topics and does not decide a legal threshold.

## Compare the routes

Separate support needs, decision-making, mental-health intervention, protective reporting and restrictions. Record the question each route answers, the source you checked and who needs to provide further advice.


## Route questions

### Care or carer support needs

Which needs and outcomes belong to the person and to carers?

Identify the responsible funder and referral route, including NASC or another applicable service. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### A decision-specific capacity question

What is the precise decision and why is ability to decide questioned?

Specify the treatment or other decision and provide the support needed for participation. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Restrictions or liberty concerns

What restrictions actually operate and how do they affect the person?

Describe actual restrictions and the person’s wishes, including what happens when they want to leave. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Mental health support or compulsion questions

What is the purpose of each proposed intervention?

Check whether the operative 1992 route or a subsequently commenced provision applies. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Abuse, neglect or safeguarding concerns

How can the person be heard safely and privately?

Identify immediate danger, the adult’s wishes and a safe way to communicate. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### A child, young carer or transition issue

What does the child say or show about safety and daily life?

Record the concern and use the appropriate Oranga Tamariki or police route where needed. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Language, participation or recording concerns

What makes participation accessible for this person?

Identify the consumer right, equality issue or public-function decision affecting the person. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Professional learning or supervision

What is the purpose and limit of your role?

Confirm registration, practising status, competence and the authority required for the task. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

# Learning Flashcards — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/learning-flashcards.html

# Learning Flashcards — Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide


Answer before revealing the response in the interactive workspace. These cards accompany the full local modules.


## Professional Foundations — Aotearoa New Zealand


### Which local framework anchors this topic in Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide?

The Social Workers Registration Act 2003, SWRB Code of Conduct and Core Competence Standards anchor professional practice in Aotearoa New Zealand. Registration and a current practising certificate should be distinguished from an employer’s allocation of duties. Specialist statutory roles have additional requirements.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

The competence framework includes practice with Māori and attention to Te Tiriti o Waitangi, culture, relationships and safe professional practice. Ask how the person wants whānau, hapū, iwi or other supporters involved. Cultural safety requires reflection on professional power and the person’s experience, rather than adding a cultural label to an unchanged assessment.


### What are the key local actions?

Confirm registration, practising status, competence and the authority required for the task. Discuss the person’s goals, language, cultural supports and preferred whānau involvement. Use supervision to test the effect of bias, colonisation, poverty and institutional barriers on the formulation. Connect CPD to feedback and the current SWRB requirements rather than assuming that attending a course proves competence.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

Explain the service complaint route and when a professional concern belongs with SWRB. Health and disability service concerns may also engage the Health and Disability Commissioner (HDC). Identify the actual issue and remedy rather than sending every concern to the same body.


### What common error should you avoid?

Treating whānau involvement as either automatically required in every decision or automatically excluded by individual consent.


## Social Care and Support — Aotearoa New Zealand


### Which local framework anchors this topic in Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide?

Disability Support Services (DSS), Needs Assessment and Service Coordination (NASC), Enabling Good Lives arrangements, health services and ACC have different eligibility and funding roles. Identify the scheme relevant to the person’s circumstances; injury-related support, disability support and older-person services should not be treated as one entitlement.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

DSS guidance describes referral to a NASC provider to understand needs and determine eligibility, with relevant supporting evidence. A needs assessment, allocation of funding and a service beginning are separate events. Check the current assessment and funding arrangements rather than relying on an old agency name or contract.


### What are the key local actions?

Identify the responsible funder and referral route, including NASC or another applicable service. Describe the person’s goals, daily support needs, environmental barriers and existing support. Check the evidence needed for eligibility and explain the decision and funding allocation separately. Confirm the provider, start date, whānau willingness and contingency for gaps or changing needs.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

Ask the relevant assessment or funding body for reasons and the applicable reassessment, review or complaint route. DSS publishes current assessment information. Track disputes with different funders separately and do not describe a referral to another agency as a resolved need.


### What common error should you avoid?

Assuming that one diagnosis, one assessment or one funding approval covers every service need.


## Decision-Making and Capacity — Aotearoa New Zealand


### Which local framework anchors this topic in Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide?

Right 7 of the Code of Health and Disability Services Consumers’ Rights addresses informed choice and consent, presumes competence and preserves choice to the extent of a person’s competence. The Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act 1988 (PPPR) provides routes including welfare guardianship, property orders and enduring powers of attorney.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

Where a consumer is not competent and no legally entitled representative is available, Right 7(4) has a specific framework. It is not a general rule that any relative may sign. Read the provision and the particular appointment before identifying who may act and what decision standard applies.


### What are the key local actions?

Specify the treatment or other decision and provide the support needed for participation. Identify the applicable consent or PPPR framework and record decision-specific evidence. Verify the scope and operation of any enduring power of attorney or court order. If relying on Right 7(4), check its conditions, efforts to ascertain the person’s views and consultation requirements.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

HDC and the independent advocacy service provide routes concerning consumer rights. PPPR court orders and representative disputes may require Family Court or other legal advice. The appropriate review depends on whether the issue is a service breach, capacity decision or representative’s authority.


### What common error should you avoid?

Treating diminished competence as loss of every choice or assuming financial authority includes healthcare.


## Restrictions and Liberty — Aotearoa New Zealand


### Which local framework anchors this topic in Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide?

Restrictions may engage the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990, the consumer Code, PPPR arrangements and, in specific circumstances, compulsory mental-health or intellectual-disability legislation. A welfare guardian or service plan is not an explanation for every measure used by staff.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

Identify whether the measure is an ordinary supported-care arrangement, restraint, seclusion or confinement under a specific statutory power. The Intellectual Disability (Compulsory Care and Rehabilitation) Act 2003 has a particular statutory scope; intellectual disability alone does not bring every person within it.


### What are the key local actions?

Describe actual restrictions and the person’s wishes, including what happens when they want to leave. Identify the applicable service standard and separate consent, representative authority and any compulsory-care power. Obtain specialist advice about the scope of the order or legal basis where confinement is proposed. Document alternatives, authorisation, monitoring, independent support and a plan to reduce restrictions.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

Consumer-rights complaints and advocacy are available through the HDC framework. Where a person is under the compulsory mental-health or intellectual-disability Acts, district inspectors have specific rights-protection functions. Identify the applicable court or tribunal review rather than assuming a single liberty procedure.


### What common error should you avoid?

Treating a care plan, guardian’s agreement or disability diagnosis as universal authority for confinement.


## Mental Health — Aotearoa New Zealand


### Which local framework anchors this topic in Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide?

The Ministry of Health states that the Mental Health Act 2026 received Royal Assent on 9 July 2026 and is to commence on 1 July 2028. Until replacement takes effect, the Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992 remains the operative framework. Preparation for the new system must be distinguished from present powers and rights.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

Under the 1992 framework, compulsory assessment and treatment require the statutory mental-disorder criteria and staged procedures. Clinical disagreement, unusual beliefs or a diagnosis alone do not establish all criteria. Use the current Ministry guidelines and authorised clinical roles for the particular stage.


### What are the key local actions?

Check whether the operative 1992 route or a subsequently commenced provision applies. Assess the actual mental-disorder and risk or self-care evidence against the relevant statutory criteria. Identify the required clinical assessment, notices, review stage and the person’s cultural and whānau support. Separate compulsory psychiatric treatment from unrelated healthcare consent and discharge-support decisions.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

District inspectors are independent lawyers who explain rights, investigate concerns and help with access to review. Judicial or Mental Health Review Tribunal processes depend on legal status. Explain the person’s current rights using the Ministry’s accessible materials and arrange legal support where needed.


### What common error should you avoid?

Treating the 2026 Act as fully operational before its commencement.


## Adult Safeguarding — Aotearoa New Zealand


### Which local framework anchors this topic in Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide?

Adult safety concerns can engage police, health or disability services, provider safeguarding arrangements, the HDC framework and specific criminal-law duties. There is no reason to assume that one overseas adult-protection procedure applies across these settings.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

The Crimes Act 1961 includes offences concerning ill-treatment or neglect and failure to protect a child or vulnerable adult in defined circumstances. Check the actual duty and the person’s role; do not simplify it into a universal reporting rule for every adult concern. DSS quality and safeguarding arrangements relate to the services within its remit.


### What are the key local actions?

Identify immediate danger, the adult’s wishes and a safe way to communicate. Choose the relevant police, provider, funder or health/disability complaint route for the facts and setting. Check any specific legal duty and act promptly where its conditions apply. Arrange practical support and follow-up alongside reporting, including continuity if a carer or worker is removed.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

HDC complaints and independent advocacy can address health and disability consumer rights. Police and the courts address different issues. Record which body has accepted responsibility and how the adult can raise concerns about the response.


### What common error should you avoid?

Assuming a provider incident report resolves all legal duties or covers safety outside the provider’s remit.


## Children, Families and Transitions — Aotearoa New Zealand


### Which local framework anchors this topic in Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide?

The Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 provides the care-and-protection framework, including reports of concern and family group conferences. Current Oranga Tamariki practice guidance explains assessment, referral, preparation, participation and implementation. A family group conference is a statutory process with defined roles, not simply an informal family meeting.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

Establish the child’s safety and views alongside whānau relationships, cultural identity and practical support. Use the current Act and policy for duties and powers; professional commitments to culturally safe practice should not be confused with an assumption that every historical statutory provision remains unchanged.


### What are the key local actions?

Record the concern and use the appropriate Oranga Tamariki or police route where needed. Distinguish the assessment, the basis for believing care or protection is needed and any referral for a family group conference. Prepare the child and whānau to understand the concern and participate, with the appropriate coordinator and supports. Record the agreed plan, responsible parties and review, and escalate when the plan is not meeting the child’s needs.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

Explain participation, support and any applicable court or complaint route. A plan should preserve the child’s voice and show who accepted each action. The statutory process and a practice model do not remove the need for evidence about actual safety.


### What common error should you avoid?

Treating agreement at a family meeting as proof that a safe, authorised and deliverable plan exists.


## Rights, Culture and Recording — Aotearoa New Zealand


### Which local framework anchors this topic in Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide?

The Code of Health and Disability Services Consumers’ Rights, Human Rights Act 1993, New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990 and professional standards answer different rights questions. Establish the provider and function involved before choosing the relevant route.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

The Privacy Act 2020 and Health Information Privacy Code govern information handling in their respective scope. The Privacy Commissioner publishes a version of the Health Information Privacy Code in force from 1 May 2026, reflecting the new indirect-collection requirements. Use that current version rather than an unchanged 2020 download.


### What are the key local actions?

Identify the consumer right, equality issue or public-function decision affecting the person. Ask about language, cultural safety, whānau involvement and accessible participation. Check the applicable privacy rules for collection, notification, use and disclosure; rule 11 governs health-information disclosure. Explain the relevant HDC, advocacy, privacy or other complaint and review route.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

A serious-threat exception to health-information confidentiality has conditions, including necessity and the applicable requirements concerning authorisation. Use the current Privacy Commissioner guidance and record the reasoning. A police request is not automatically a direction to release a whole file.


### What common error should you avoid?

Using an outdated privacy-code version or treating collection and disclosure as the same legal decision.

### Adult Safeguarding — Aotearoa New Zealand: What common error should you avoid?

Assuming a provider incident report resolves all legal duties or covers safety outside the provider’s remit.

### Children, Families and Transitions — Aotearoa New Zealand: Which local framework anchors this topic in Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide?

The Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 provides the care-and-protection framework, including reports of concern and family group conferences. Current Oranga Tamariki practice guidance explains assessment, referral, preparation, participation and implementation. A family group conference is a statutory process with defined roles, not simply an informal family meeting.

### Children, Families and Transitions — Aotearoa New Zealand: Which distinction must be kept clear?

Establish the child’s safety and views alongside whānau relationships, cultural identity and practical support. Use the current Act and policy for duties and powers; professional commitments to culturally safe practice should not be confused with an assumption that every historical statutory provision remains unchanged.

### Children, Families and Transitions — Aotearoa New Zealand: What are the key local actions?

Record the concern and use the appropriate Oranga Tamariki or police route where needed. Distinguish the assessment, the basis for believing care or protection is needed and any referral for a family group conference. Prepare the child and whānau to understand the concern and participate, with the appropriate coordinator and supports. Record the agreed plan, responsible parties and review, and escalate when the plan is not meeting the child’s needs.

### Children, Families and Transitions — Aotearoa New Zealand: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

Explain participation, support and any applicable court or complaint route. A plan should preserve the child’s voice and show who accepted each action. The statutory process and a practice model do not remove the need for evidence about actual safety.

### Children, Families and Transitions — Aotearoa New Zealand: What common error should you avoid?

Treating agreement at a family meeting as proof that a safe, authorised and deliverable plan exists.

### Rights, Culture and Recording — Aotearoa New Zealand: Which local framework anchors this topic in Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide?

The Code of Health and Disability Services Consumers’ Rights, Human Rights Act 1993, New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990 and professional standards answer different rights questions. Establish the provider and function involved before choosing the relevant route.

### Rights, Culture and Recording — Aotearoa New Zealand: Which distinction must be kept clear?

The Privacy Act 2020 and Health Information Privacy Code govern information handling in their respective scope. The Privacy Commissioner publishes a version of the Health Information Privacy Code in force from 1 May 2026, reflecting the new indirect-collection requirements. Use that current version rather than an unchanged 2020 download.

### Rights, Culture and Recording — Aotearoa New Zealand: What are the key local actions?

Identify the consumer right, equality issue or public-function decision affecting the person. Ask about language, cultural safety, whānau involvement and accessible participation. Check the applicable privacy rules for collection, notification, use and disclosure; rule 11 governs health-information disclosure. Explain the relevant HDC, advocacy, privacy or other complaint and review route.

### Rights, Culture and Recording — Aotearoa New Zealand: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

A serious-threat exception to health-information confidentiality has conditions, including necessity and the applicable requirements concerning authorisation. Use the current Privacy Commissioner guidance and record the reasoning. A police request is not automatically a direction to release a whole file.

### Rights, Culture and Recording — Aotearoa New Zealand: What common error should you avoid?

Using an outdated privacy-code version or treating collection and disclosure as the same legal decision.

# Practice Glossary — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

# Practice Glossary — Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide

Use each definition with its linked full lesson and official sources.

## Professional Foundations

The Social Workers Registration Act 2003, SWRB Code of Conduct and Core Competence Standards anchor professional practice in Aotearoa New Zealand. Registration and a current practising certificate should be distinguished from an employer’s allocation of duties. Specialist statutory roles have additional requirements.

## Social Care and Support

Disability Support Services (DSS), Needs Assessment and Service Coordination (NASC), Enabling Good Lives arrangements, health services and ACC have different eligibility and funding roles. Identify the scheme relevant to the person’s circumstances; injury-related support, disability support and older-person services should not be treated as one entitlement.

## Decision-Making and Capacity

Right 7 of the Code of Health and Disability Services Consumers’ Rights addresses informed choice and consent, presumes competence and preserves choice to the extent of a person’s competence. The Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act 1988 (PPPR) provides routes including welfare guardianship, property orders and enduring powers of attorney.

## Restrictions and Liberty

Restrictions may engage the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990, the consumer Code, PPPR arrangements and, in specific circumstances, compulsory mental-health or intellectual-disability legislation. A welfare guardian or service plan is not an explanation for every measure used by staff.

## Mental Health

The Ministry of Health states that the Mental Health Act 2026 received Royal Assent on 9 July 2026 and is to commence on 1 July 2028. Until replacement takes effect, the Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992 remains the operative framework. Preparation for the new system must be distinguished from present powers and rights.

## Adult Safeguarding

Adult safety concerns can engage police, health or disability services, provider safeguarding arrangements, the HDC framework and specific criminal-law duties. There is no reason to assume that one overseas adult-protection procedure applies across these settings.

## Children, Families and Transitions

The Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 provides the care-and-protection framework, including reports of concern and family group conferences. Current Oranga Tamariki practice guidance explains assessment, referral, preparation, participation and implementation. A family group conference is a statutory process with defined roles, not simply an informal family meeting.

## Rights, Culture and Recording

The Code of Health and Disability Services Consumers’ Rights, Human Rights Act 1993, New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990 and professional standards answer different rights questions. Establish the provider and function involved before choosing the relevant route.

## Social Workers Registration Board (SWRB)

The professional body identified for this guide. Check its remit and the requirements that apply to your role.

## Advocacy

Support to express views, understand choices and participate; statutory entitlements depend on the local framework.

## CPD

Continuing professional development: learning, reflection and evidence of improvement.

## Consent

Agreement to a specific action; check the applicable requirements for information, voluntariness and ability to consent.

## Coercion

Pressure or control that can affect expressed wishes and freedom to act.

## Eligibility

The criteria for a particular service or programme; distinct from a description of need.

## Capacity

Ability to make the relevant decision under the applicable legal framework; avoid a global label.

## Representative

Someone with a defined support or decision-making role; verify the source and scope of authority.

## Proportionality

A reasoned comparison of intended benefit, burdens, rights and alternatives.

## Cultural safety

Attention to power, identity and the person’s experience of a service, informed by their preferences.

## Data minimisation

Using or sharing only information needed for an identified lawful purpose.

## Confidentiality

Protecting information while understanding and explaining lawful exceptions.

## Safeguarding referral

Communicating a concern to the appropriate agency; confirm the applicable route and follow-up.

## Professional supervision

Structured discussion of decisions, ethics, skills, wellbeing and accountability.

## Formulation

A reasoned account connecting evidence and possible explanations to a plan.

## Family network

Relationships that may offer support; availability, safety and willingness need assessment.

## Transition

Planned change between services or life stages, with continuity and named responsibilities.

## Contingency

An agreed response if risks increase or the preferred plan cannot operate.

## Review

A planned check of outcomes, changing circumstances and whether actions remain appropriate.

## Least restrictive option

An option that can achieve the purpose with less interference in rights and freedom.

# Theory Into Practice — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/theory-into-practice-aotearoa-new-zealand.html

# Theory Into Practice — Aotearoa New Zealand

## Build a testable explanation

Use the theory finder to generate alternative explanations for a fictional case. Compare what each lens notices about relationships, environment, power, trauma and strengths. Record evidence that would support or challenge your explanation.

## Use models thoughtfully

Theories are shared learning lenses, not country-specific statutory rules. Their inclusion does not imply official adoption in Aotearoa New Zealand. Check suitability, training requirements, cultural context and the person’s account before applying a method.


## Interactive theory lenses

### Ecological Systems Theory

Person, family, housing, community, services, poverty, policy, culture, and environment.

Hypothesis: The presenting issue may be shaped by pressures around the person, not only by individual behaviour or choice.

- What changed in the environment before the concern escalated?
- Which systems are supporting the person, and which are adding pressure?
- Would risk reduce if housing, income, access, care, or community support changed?

### Strengths-Based Practice

Capabilities, identity, relationships, community, culture, hope, and what is already working.

Hypothesis: The person may have protective strategies or relationships that are hidden by a risk-heavy professional account.

- What has helped the person survive or cope so far?
- Who does the person trust, and what role could they safely play?
- Which strengths are real evidence, and which are optimistic assumptions?

### Trauma-Informed Practice

Safety, trust, choice, collaboration, empowerment, shame, threat responses, and control.

Hypothesis: Behaviour that looks like refusal, avoidance, anger, or disengagement may be a survival response to trauma, coercion, loss, or fear.

- What might feel unsafe or controlling from the person's perspective?
- What helps the person feel more choice and predictability?
- How can we avoid repeating patterns of powerlessness?

### Attachment Theory

Trust, separation, dependency, rejection, fear, care-seeking, and relationship patterns.

Hypothesis: Responses to professionals or carers may reflect previous experiences of care, loss, abandonment, or unsafe relationships.

- How does the person respond when support increases, reduces, or changes?
- Are there patterns of clinging, pushing away, testing, mistrust, or fear?
- What relationship approach is consistent, boundaried, and safe?

### Systems and Family Theory

Roles, rules, communication, repeated patterns, conflict, care dynamics, and network effects.

Hypothesis: The concern may be maintained by relationship patterns, family roles, service responses, or network conflict.

- Who gains or loses if the current pattern changes?
- What role has each person been placed in or taken on?
- How do professional responses affect the family or network pattern?

### Anti-Oppressive and Anti-Discriminatory Practice

Power, oppression, racism, disability, class, gender, sexuality, culture, age, stigma, and access.

Hypothesis: The presenting issue may be intensified by structural inequality, professional power, discrimination, or inaccessible services.

- What barriers has the person faced before we became involved?
- Whose account is being treated as most credible, and why?
- What reasonable adjustments, cultural humility, or advocacy are needed?

### Crisis Theory

Immediate stress, narrowed options, temporary disequilibrium, coping capacity, and stabilisation.

Hypothesis: The person or family may be temporarily overwhelmed and need stabilisation before longer-term planning is realistic.

- What immediate event or loss has exceeded usual coping?
- What needs to happen in the next 24 to 72 hours?
- What can wait until safety, sleep, food, medication, or support is more stable?

### Life Course Theory

Transitions, cumulative disadvantage, ageing, identity, loss, timing, and turning points.

Hypothesis: Current risk or distress may connect to earlier life events, cumulative exclusion, transition, bereavement, or changing identity.

- What transitions or losses are happening now?
- How has cumulative disadvantage shaped options and trust?
- What strengths, relationships, or identities from earlier life still matter?

### Task-Centred Practice

Specific problems, agreed goals, small steps, roles, review, and measurable change.

Hypothesis: The person may benefit from breaking an overwhelming issue into concrete, negotiated tasks with clear review.

- What problem does the person most want to work on first?
- What is the smallest useful next step?
- Who will do what, by when, and how will we know it helped?

## Model finder

Child protection mapping, danger statements, safety goals, family network work, scaling, and safety planning.

### Signs of Wellbeing, Success, and Belonging

Family support, children in care, permanency, reunification, stability, identity, and belonging work.

Domestic abuse-informed child welfare, perpetrator pattern mapping, protective parent strengths, and child impact.

Neglect assessment, evidence-based care mapping, physical care, safety, love and esteem, and developmental care.

### Restorative Practice

# Professional Foundations — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/professional-foundations.html

# Professional Foundations — Aotearoa New Zealand

## Learning outcomes

Explain your professional role, distinguish an ethical concern from a statutory power, and turn a formulation into an accountable plan.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

The Social Workers Registration Act 2003, SWRB Code of Conduct and Core Competence Standards anchor professional practice in Aotearoa New Zealand. Registration and a current practising certificate should be distinguished from an employer’s allocation of duties. Specialist statutory roles have additional requirements.

The competence framework includes practice with Māori and attention to Te Tiriti o Waitangi, culture, relationships and safe professional practice. Ask how the person wants whānau, hapū, iwi or other supporters involved. Cultural safety requires reflection on professional power and the person’s experience, rather than adding a cultural label to an unchanged assessment.

## From information to a professional formulation

A chronology says what happened. A formulation explains how the available evidence, the person's experience and their environment might connect. Start with the person's desired change. Map relationships, housing, income, health, discrimination and service barriers alongside individual strengths. A missed appointment may reflect fear, inaccessible transport or an unsafe household; it does not establish unwillingness to engage.

Use at least two possible explanations for a difficult situation. State what evidence supports each and what would challenge it. A strengths approach should identify actual resources the person can use, with their agreement. It should not turn an absent service into an assumed family responsibility. A trauma-informed conversation offers predictability, choice and control over pace while keeping necessary enquiries clear.

## Boundaries and supervision

Explain who employs you, the purpose of contact, how information will be used and the limits of confidentiality. Separate an invitation to accept support from an action the law permits without agreement. Ask for supervision when an instruction conflicts with professional duties or exceeds your authority. Record the issue, advice, action and unresolved concern; merely recording that a manager agreed does not explain the decision.

For a learning reflection, choose one decision you influenced. Describe what the person said, your initial assumption, what changed your understanding and what you will do differently. Seek feedback about the effect on the person, rather than counting training attendance as evidence of improved practice.

## Apply the local pathway

- Confirm registration, practising status, competence and the authority required for the task.
- Discuss the person’s goals, language, cultural supports and preferred whānau involvement.
- Use supervision to test the effect of bias, colonisation, poverty and institutional barriers on the formulation.
- Connect CPD to feedback and the current SWRB requirements rather than assuming that attending a course proves competence.

## Rights, challenge and review

Explain the service complaint route and when a professional concern belongs with SWRB. Health and disability service concerns may also engage the Health and Disability Commissioner (HDC). Identify the actual issue and remedy rather than sending every concern to the same body.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A service describes a Māori client as disengaged after arranging meetings without the support person they requested.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Ask what made the meetings unsafe or unhelpful and agree how participation should work. Review the earlier interpretation and record the person’s goals and chosen supports. Take the effect of professional and institutional power to supervision, with a concrete change to the next contact.

### Common error to avoid

Treating whānau involvement as either automatically required in every decision or automatically excluded by individual consent.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Your role and the legal or professional framework
- The person’s outcomes and communication preferences
- Evidence, competing explanations and missing perspectives
- Power, boundaries and any conflict of interest
- Agreed action, supervision, feedback and review

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [SWRB Core Competence Standards](https://swrb.govt.nz/practice/core-competence-standards/)
- [SWRB Code of Conduct](https://swrb.govt.nz/practice/code-of-conduct/)
- [Social Workers Registration Act 2003](https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2003/0017/latest/whole.html)

Editorial expansion: 8 September 2026. The sources support the distinctions taught here; check their current text, amendments, commencement and applicable local procedure before operational use. Independent practitioner review has not been recorded.

# Social Care and Support — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/social-care-and-support-aotearoa-new-zealand.html

# Social Care and Support — Aotearoa New Zealand

## Learning outcomes

Map assessment, eligibility, funding and delivery separately; include family support without assuming it; explain the local route for challenging a decision.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

Disability Support Services (DSS), Needs Assessment and Service Coordination (NASC), Enabling Good Lives arrangements, health services and ACC have different eligibility and funding roles. Identify the scheme relevant to the person’s circumstances; injury-related support, disability support and older-person services should not be treated as one entitlement.

DSS guidance describes referral to a NASC provider to understand needs and determine eligibility, with relevant supporting evidence. A needs assessment, allocation of funding and a service beginning are separate events. Check the current assessment and funding arrangements rather than relying on an old agency name or contract.

## Assess daily life, not just a list of services

Begin with what a good day would look like. Explore washing, dressing, nutrition, medicines, mobility, home safety, relationships, work or education and community participation. Ask about variation: what happens at night, on a bad day or when a regular supporter is unavailable? Establish what the person can do with appropriate equipment, accessible information or a different environment. Do not confuse performing a task once during a visit with being able to do it reliably in daily life.

Speak with family supporters about willingness, practical ability and sustainability. Their account belongs alongside the person's account, not in place of it. Record support that is actually offered and its limits. An adult child working overnight is not an available overnight care service. Where views differ, describe the disagreement and its consequences for the proposed plan.

## Turn the assessment into a deliverable plan

Keep four decisions visible: the needs identified; the applicable eligibility decision; the funding or charging decision; and the service that will actually start. A referral, waiting-list entry or funding approval is not proof that support has begun. Obtain the person's understanding of costs and responsibilities before recording agreement.

For each outcome, identify an action, a responsible service or person and a review trigger. Include what happens if the worker does not arrive, the person declines support, a carer becomes unavailable or needs change. Record unmet needs and interim arrangements explicitly. A budget dispute should not disappear into a description of the person as difficult or unrealistic.

## Apply the local pathway

- Identify the responsible funder and referral route, including NASC or another applicable service.
- Describe the person’s goals, daily support needs, environmental barriers and existing support.
- Check the evidence needed for eligibility and explain the decision and funding allocation separately.
- Confirm the provider, start date, whānau willingness and contingency for gaps or changing needs.

## Rights, challenge and review

Ask the relevant assessment or funding body for reasons and the applicable reassessment, review or complaint route. DSS publishes current assessment information. Track disputes with different funders separately and do not describe a referral to another agency as a resolved need.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A person with a longstanding disability develops additional support needs after an injury, and two services each suggest the other should pay.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Map the needs and the scope of each scheme, obtain the actual eligibility decisions and coordinate the interface. Record interim support and unresolved funding responsibility. Keep the person’s desired outcomes visible while the agencies resolve the dispute.

### Common error to avoid

Assuming that one diagnosis, one assessment or one funding approval covers every service need.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Daily-life evidence, fluctuation and desired outcomes
- The service, eligibility test and decision-maker
- Carer willingness and separately identified needs
- Funding, charges, decisions and reasons
- Start dates, unmet needs, contingency and challenge route

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

- [DSS access to support](https://www.disabilitysupport.govt.nz/disabled-people/assessment-and-funding/how-to-access-support)

# Decision-Making and Capacity — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/decision-making-and-capacity-aotearoa-new-zealand.html

# Decision-Making and Capacity — Aotearoa New Zealand

## Learning outcomes

Identify the precise decision, provide practical decision support, apply the local capacity or consent framework and verify a representative’s authority.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

Right 7 of the Code of Health and Disability Services Consumers’ Rights addresses informed choice and consent, presumes competence and preserves choice to the extent of a person’s competence. The Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act 1988 (PPPR) provides routes including welfare guardianship, property orders and enduring powers of attorney.

Where a consumer is not competent and no legally entitled representative is available, Right 7(4) has a specific framework. It is not a general rule that any relative may sign. Read the provision and the particular appointment before identifying who may act and what decision standard applies.

## Start with the decision and the support

Write the decision as a question the person could answer: accepting a particular treatment, choosing accommodation or authorising a financial transaction. These questions may engage different laws and decision-makers. A diagnosis, cognitive score or disagreement with professionals is not a complete capacity assessment. Describe the ability relevant to this decision and the evidence for any concern.

Prepare information about the real options, including doing nothing where relevant. Use an interpreter, accessible material, communication aids and suitable timing. Address pain, fatigue, sensory impairment, medication effects and anxiety. Ask the person to explain their understanding in their own way; repeating professional phrases is not the only way to demonstrate understanding. Record what support was tried and its effect, rather than simply writing that all support was offered.

## Keep authority and the decision itself separate

A relative may provide valuable information without holding authority to decide. Obtain the actual appointment, agreement, court order or statutory basis being relied upon. Check the decisions it covers, conditions, whether it is operative and whether another person has priority. Authority over property does not automatically include healthcare or accommodation.

Where a representative can lawfully act, identify the decision standard they must apply locally. Explore the person's wishes, values, previous statements and present participation. Record a disagreement rather than converting it into apparent agreement. Consider whether a reversible interim option allows more support or recovery before an irreversible decision. If authority remains disputed, obtain the appropriate clinical or legal advice and arrange the applicable review; a multidisciplinary meeting cannot create missing legal powers.

## Apply the local pathway

- Specify the treatment or other decision and provide the support needed for participation.
- Identify the applicable consent or PPPR framework and record decision-specific evidence.
- Verify the scope and operation of any enduring power of attorney or court order.
- If relying on Right 7(4), check its conditions, efforts to ascertain the person’s views and consultation requirements.

## Rights, challenge and review

HDC and the independent advocacy service provide routes concerning consumer rights. PPPR court orders and representative disputes may require Family Court or other legal advice. The appropriate review depends on whether the issue is a service breach, capacity decision or representative’s authority.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A woman can express a clear preference about treatment but needs information presented in short sessions. Her son says he should sign because he manages her bills.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Provide the communication support and assess the relevant decision. Financial help does not establish healthcare authority. Read any appointment and use the applicable consent framework, preserving the woman’s own choices to the extent she can make them.

### Common error to avoid

Treating diminished competence as loss of every choice or assuming financial authority includes healthcare.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Decision, options and time at which it is needed
- Communication support and observed responses
- Applicable legal test and evidence for each element
- Representative’s document, scope and decision standard
- Wishes, disagreement, review and any urgent action

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [HDC consent and competence guidance](https://www.hdc.org.nz/education/online-learning/consent-for-consumers-who-are-not-competent/)
- [Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act 1988](https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1988/0004/latest/whole.html)
