# Restrictions and Liberty — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/restrictions-and-liberty-aotearoa-new-zealand.html

# Restrictions and Liberty — Aotearoa New Zealand

## Learning outcomes

Describe actual restrictions, identify the setting-specific legal authority, test alternatives and make representation and review practical.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

Restrictions may engage the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990, the consumer Code, PPPR arrangements and, in specific circumstances, compulsory mental-health or intellectual-disability legislation. A welfare guardian or service plan is not an explanation for every measure used by staff.

Identify whether the measure is an ordinary supported-care arrangement, restraint, seclusion or confinement under a specific statutory power. The Intellectual Disability (Compulsory Care and Rehabilitation) Act 2003 has a particular statutory scope; intellectual disability alone does not bring every person within it.

## Describe what happens in everyday life

Look beyond the label used by the service. Describe locked doors, staff responses to a request to leave, supervision, physical interventions, isolation, medication used to control behaviour and restrictions on visitors, money or communication. State when each measure operates, who applies it, its duration and its cumulative effect. Distinguish a person's preferred routine from a rule enforced by staff.

Hear the person privately with suitable communication support. An absence of verbal objection is not a complete account of their wishes. Distress, repeated requests to go home or avoiding a particular worker may require further enquiry. Family agreement is relevant information but should not be treated as a substitute for the authority required by law.

## Connect necessity to a less restrictive plan

Identify the concrete harm a measure is intended to prevent. Explore environmental changes, pain relief, meaningful activity, different staffing, communication and practical support. Record which options were tried, their effects and why another option is proposed. Provider convenience or an unsigned risk assessment should not become the explanation for an ongoing restriction.

Separate emergency action from a continuing arrangement. An urgent response needs its own factual justification and follow-up; it should not silently become a standing plan. Check the scope of any order or authorisation, applicable conditions, expiry and who must review it. The person needs an accessible explanation and a usable way to object, obtain independent help and challenge the arrangement. Assign responsibility for acting on an objection rather than merely documenting it at the next routine meeting.

## Apply the local pathway

- Describe actual restrictions and the person’s wishes, including what happens when they want to leave.
- Identify the applicable service standard and separate consent, representative authority and any compulsory-care power.
- Obtain specialist advice about the scope of the order or legal basis where confinement is proposed.
- Document alternatives, authorisation, monitoring, independent support and a plan to reduce restrictions.

## Rights, challenge and review

Consumer-rights complaints and advocacy are available through the HDC framework. Where a person is under the compulsory mental-health or intellectual-disability Acts, district inspectors have specific rights-protection functions. Identify the applicable court or tribunal review rather than assuming a single liberty procedure.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A residential provider uses a locked room when a resident becomes distressed and says the welfare guardian approved the behaviour plan.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Assess immediate safety, the purpose and effect of isolation and the person’s experience. Check the guardian’s powers and the specific legal and service requirements for the measure. Explore communication, environmental and staffing changes, and escalate any missing authority or safeguard.

### Common error to avoid

Treating a care plan, guardian’s agreement or disability diagnosis as universal authority for confinement.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Each restriction, setting, duration and actual effect
- The person’s wishes, understanding and objections
- Legal authority, decision-maker, limits and conditions
- Alternatives tried and the evidence about necessity
- Representation, review date, expiry and challenge

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990](https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1990/0109/latest/whole.html)
- [PPPR Act 1988](https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1988/0004/latest/whole.html)
- [District inspectors and rights protection](https://www.health.govt.nz/regulation-legislation/mental-health-and-addiction/mental-health-act/mental-health-district-inspectors)

# Mental Health — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/mental-health-aotearoa-new-zealand.html

# Mental Health — Aotearoa New Zealand

## Learning outcomes

Distinguish voluntary care, compulsory assessment, detention and treatment; connect the local criteria to evidence and explain the person’s review rights.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

The Ministry of Health states that the Mental Health Act 2026 received Royal Assent on 9 July 2026 and is to commence on 1 July 2028. Until replacement takes effect, the Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992 remains the operative framework. Preparation for the new system must be distinguished from present powers and rights.

Under the 1992 framework, compulsory assessment and treatment require the statutory mental-disorder criteria and staged procedures. Clinical disagreement, unusual beliefs or a diagnosis alone do not establish all criteria. Use the current Ministry guidelines and authorised clinical roles for the particular stage.

## Assess the crisis in context

Attend to urgent physical health and immediate safety while creating space for the person's account. Explore sleep, medication, substance use, pain, relationships, housing, financial pressure and previous helpful or harmful experiences of services. Cultural or spiritual expression should be understood in context. Use an appropriate interpreter and ask which supporters the person wants involved.

Describe behaviour and its consequences rather than relying on labels such as non-compliant or high risk. Distinguish what you observed, what somebody reported and the inference being drawn. Consider information that challenges the proposed compulsory route as carefully as information that supports it. The existence of a legal power does not establish that its conditions are met in this case.

## Separate each intervention

Transport, assessment, admission, psychiatric treatment and treatment of an unrelated physical condition can involve different authorities. Check the exact route, the professional authorised to exercise it, required documentation and its time limits. Do not use a single statement that the person is detained to explain every intervention. Document attempts to arrange voluntary or less restrictive support and whether those services are actually available.

Rights information should be understandable at the time and revisited when the person can engage more fully. Explain independent support, legal representation and the applicable review process. During discharge planning, identify housing, medicines, follow-up, family responsibilities and crisis contacts. Confirm who accepts responsibility for each task. A person should not leave with an apparently complete plan consisting only of referrals that no receiving service has accepted.

## Apply the local pathway

- Check whether the operative 1992 route or a subsequently commenced provision applies.
- Assess the actual mental-disorder and risk or self-care evidence against the relevant statutory criteria.
- Identify the required clinical assessment, notices, review stage and the person’s cultural and whānau support.
- Separate compulsory psychiatric treatment from unrelated healthcare consent and discharge-support decisions.

## Rights, challenge and review

District inspectors are independent lawyers who explain rights, investigate concerns and help with access to review. Judicial or Mental Health Review Tribunal processes depend on legal status. Explain the person’s current rights using the Ministry’s accessible materials and arrange legal support where needed.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A team wants to apply a future provision of the 2026 Act because it has been included in a training presentation.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Confirm the commencement date and use the operative legislation and forms for the person’s present assessment. Explain current district-inspector and review rights. Record preparation for the new law as service development, not as the authority for today’s intervention.

### Common error to avoid

Treating the 2026 Act as fully operational before its commencement.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Mental and physical health evidence and the person’s account
- The local criteria and voluntary alternatives considered
- Separate authority for transport, admission and treatment
- Required notices, advocacy, representation and review
- Continuity, discharge responsibilities and crisis plan

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [Mental-health replacement and commencement](https://www.health.govt.nz/regulation-legislation/mental-health-and-addiction/repealing-and-replacing-the-mental-health-act)
- [Guidelines to the 1992 Act](https://www.health.govt.nz/publications/guidelines-to-the-mental-health-compulsory-assessment-and-treatment-act-1992)
- [Current mental-health rights](https://www.health.govt.nz/regulation-legislation/mental-health-and-addiction/mental-health-act/your-rights-under-the-mental-health-act)

# Adult Safeguarding — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/safeguarding-and-family-violence-aotearoa-new-zealand.html

# Adult Safeguarding — Aotearoa New Zealand

## Learning outcomes

Recognise abuse, neglect and coercion; choose the correct local reporting route; connect immediate protection to the adult’s wishes and continuing support.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

Adult safety concerns can engage police, health or disability services, provider safeguarding arrangements, the HDC framework and specific criminal-law duties. There is no reason to assume that one overseas adult-protection procedure applies across these settings.

The Crimes Act 1961 includes offences concerning ill-treatment or neglect and failure to protect a child or vulnerable adult in defined circumstances. Check the actual duty and the person’s role; do not simplify it into a universal reporting rule for every adult concern. DSS quality and safeguarding arrangements relate to the services within its remit.

## Enquire safely and proportionately

Start with immediate danger and the safest way to communicate. A private conversation may reveal concerns that cannot be expressed in front of a relative, carer or staff member. Check whether telephone calls, letters or messages could expose the person to retaliation. Use independent communication support where a proposed interpreter may have a conflict of interest.

Record the nature of the concern, its source, the person's own words and any observed injuries, living conditions or financial issues. Distinguish a disclosure, a suspicion and a confirmed finding. Do not wait to conduct your own investigation before acting on a reporting duty. Equally, avoid leading questions or repeated interviewing that may distress the person or compromise another agency's investigation.

## Combine protection with participation

Ask what the person wants to change and what they fear might happen after a report. Assess coercion, dependency and practical barriers alongside decision-making ability. A person may understand a risk yet be unable to obtain food, leave safely or resist somebody controlling their money. Support, reporting and authority to impose an intervention are separate questions.

Agree what information needs sharing, with whom and on what legal basis. Where sharing is required or justified without consent, record the reason and explain it to the person when safe and appropriate. Make a plan for immediate needs, follow-up contact and responsibility between agencies. A referral does not establish that somebody has accepted the concern. Confirm receipt, escalate unresolved danger and review whether the action has improved safety in the person's own terms.

## Apply the local pathway

- Identify immediate danger, the adult’s wishes and a safe way to communicate.
- Choose the relevant police, provider, funder or health/disability complaint route for the facts and setting.
- Check any specific legal duty and act promptly where its conditions apply.
- Arrange practical support and follow-up alongside reporting, including continuity if a carer or worker is removed.

## Rights, challenge and review

HDC complaints and independent advocacy can address health and disability consumer rights. Police and the courts address different issues. Record which body has accepted responsibility and how the adult can raise concerns about the response.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: An adult using funded support reports that a worker withholds meals as punishment but fears losing the service if they complain.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Establish immediate access to food and safe support, hear the adult privately and preserve the relevant facts. Follow the appropriate safeguarding and complaint routes and consider criminal duties or police involvement. Plan continuity so reporting does not leave the person without essential assistance.

### Common error to avoid

Assuming a provider incident report resolves all legal duties or covers safety outside the provider’s remit.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Concern, source, chronology and the adult’s own account
- Immediate safety and a safe communication method
- The local reporting threshold, recipient and timing
- Consent, coercion and information-sharing basis
- Accepted responsibilities, outcomes and follow-up

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [DSS quality and safeguarding responsibilities](https://www.disabilitysupport.govt.nz/providers/quality-and-safeguarding/we-can-all-contribute-to-quality-and-safeguarding)
- [Crimes Act 1961](https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1961/0043/latest/whole.html)

# Children, Families and Transitions — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/tamariki-rangatahi-and-wh-nau-aotearoa-new-zealand.html

# Children, Families and Transitions — Aotearoa New Zealand

## Learning outcomes

Separate family support from protection powers, apply the local reporting duty, involve the child and coordinate education, health and transition planning.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

The Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 provides the care-and-protection framework, including reports of concern and family group conferences. Current Oranga Tamariki practice guidance explains assessment, referral, preparation, participation and implementation. A family group conference is a statutory process with defined roles, not simply an informal family meeting.

Establish the child’s safety and views alongside whānau relationships, cultural identity and practical support. Use the current Act and policy for duties and powers; professional commitments to culturally safe practice should not be confused with an assumption that every historical statutory provision remains unchanged.

## Understand the child’s daily experience

Use age-appropriate communication, observation and accessible material. Ask about ordinary routines, trusted adults, worries, food, sleep, school and relationships. Record the child's words separately from adult interpretations. For a baby or a child who does not use speech, describe interactions and behaviour without claiming to know a view they have not expressed.

Assess harm, strengths and the practical conditions affecting care. Poverty, inaccessible services or overcrowded housing may require material help; they should not automatically be treated as evidence of parental indifference. At the same time, a family's strengths do not remove the need to act on a protection concern. Explore the experience of siblings and whether a proposed protective adult can actually provide the support being described.

## Keep support and compulsory intervention clear

Explain your role, the concern, confidentiality limits and the next step in language the family can understand. Establish the local reporting threshold and receiving authority. A practice model can organise enquiry but cannot determine a statutory threshold or authorise removal. Where you disagree with a decision, identify the evidence and use the relevant escalation process without delaying necessary immediate action.

Plan with education, health, disability and community services, identifying each person's responsibility. For a young person approaching adulthood, address accommodation, income, healthcare, relationships, education or work and decision support before a service ends. Confirm eligibility and acceptance by adult services rather than assuming that a childhood plan transfers automatically. Preserve cultural, family and community relationships in ways consistent with the child's safety and wishes.

## Apply the local pathway

- Record the concern and use the appropriate Oranga Tamariki or police route where needed.
- Distinguish the assessment, the basis for believing care or protection is needed and any referral for a family group conference.
- Prepare the child and whānau to understand the concern and participate, with the appropriate coordinator and supports.
- Record the agreed plan, responsible parties and review, and escalate when the plan is not meeting the child’s needs.

## Rights, challenge and review

Explain participation, support and any applicable court or complaint route. A plan should preserve the child’s voice and show who accepted each action. The statutory process and a practice model do not remove the need for evidence about actual safety.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A conference agrees that relatives will support a child, but nobody confirms transport, sleeping arrangements or who will supervise overnight.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Translate the broad agreement into a practical plan with named responsibilities and the child’s view. Verify that the arrangements are available and safe. Use the appropriate review or reconvening process if the plan does not meet the needs identified.

### Common error to avoid

Treating agreement at a family meeting as proof that a safe, authorised and deliverable plan exists.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Child’s account, communication and daily-life evidence
- Harm, strengths, needs and alternative explanations
- Reporting duty, recipient and action taken
- Family participation, culture and legal authority
- Named plan, education/health links and transition dates

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [Oranga Tamariki Act 1989](https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1989/0024/latest/whole.html)
- [Family group conference policy](https://practice.orangatamariki.govt.nz/policy/family-group-conferences-for-care-andor-protection-concerns)

# Rights, Culture and Recording — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/rights-culture-and-recording-aotearoa-new-zealand.html

# Rights, Culture and Recording — Aotearoa New Zealand

## Learning outcomes

Connect rights to an actual service decision, distinguish privacy from absolute secrecy and write a record that makes reasons and disagreement visible.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

The Code of Health and Disability Services Consumers’ Rights, Human Rights Act 1993, New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990 and professional standards answer different rights questions. Establish the provider and function involved before choosing the relevant route.

The Privacy Act 2020 and Health Information Privacy Code govern information handling in their respective scope. The Privacy Commissioner publishes a version of the Health Information Privacy Code in force from 1 May 2026, reflecting the new indirect-collection requirements. Use that current version rather than an unchanged 2020 download.

## Make rights practical

Identify the decision affecting the person: access to an assessment, a restriction, a disclosure, an inaccessible meeting or a refusal of support. Ask which right or duty is engaged and which organisation is responsible. A statement that a plan is rights-based does not explain whether the person could participate or how the effect on them was weighed.

Arrange interpretation, accessible formats and communication support suited to the person. Ask about cultural identity, discrimination and the supporters they wish to involve. Do not infer these preferences from appearance, surname or language. Consider whether a seemingly neutral rule disadvantages someone because of disability or another protected characteristic, and what accommodation or adjustment is available under the applicable law.

## Make disclosure and recording accountable

Identify the purpose, recipient and legal basis before sharing personal information. Determine whether the organisation is covered by health, public-sector, private-sector or another confidentiality regime. Consent is not the only possible basis for disclosure, but an organisational request is not a legal basis by itself. Share the information relevant to the permitted purpose and record any limits or objection.

A useful record separates observation, the person's account, information from others, analysis and action. Write what evidence led to the conclusion, which alternatives were considered and why a particular option was chosen. Preserve disagreement respectfully and correct factual errors through the appropriate process. Explain how the person can request access, seek correction, complain or obtain an independent review. Store learning reflections without identifiable case details and use approved systems for professional records.

## Apply the local pathway

- Identify the consumer right, equality issue or public-function decision affecting the person.
- Ask about language, cultural safety, whānau involvement and accessible participation.
- Check the applicable privacy rules for collection, notification, use and disclosure; rule 11 governs health-information disclosure.
- Explain the relevant HDC, advocacy, privacy or other complaint and review route.

## Rights, challenge and review

A serious-threat exception to health-information confidentiality has conditions, including necessity and the applicable requirements concerning authorisation. Use the current Privacy Commissioner guidance and record the reasoning. A police request is not automatically a direction to release a whole file.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A worker receives sensitive health information from a relative and later receives a police request for the entire record.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Check the current collection-notification requirements and any applicable exception, then assess disclosure separately. Establish the police request’s purpose and legal basis, share only what the applicable rule permits and document the person’s participation or why authorisation could not appropriately be sought.

### Common error to avoid

Using an outdated privacy-code version or treating collection and disclosure as the same legal decision.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Decision, affected rights and responsible organisation
- Accessibility, culture and participation arrangements
- Disclosure purpose, legal basis, recipient and limits
- Evidence, alternatives, reasons and disagreement
- Access, correction, complaints and review route

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [Current Health Information Privacy Code](https://www.privacy.org.nz/privacy-principles/codes-of-practice/hipc2020/)
- [Health-information disclosure guidance](https://www.privacy.org.nz/privacy-principles/codes-of-practice/hipc2020/hipc-factsheet-3/)
- [Requests from police and law enforcement](https://www.privacy.org.nz/responsibilities/releasing-personal-information-to-police-and-law-enforcement-agencies/)

# Quick Reference — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/quick-reference.html

# Practice reference — Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide


Use alongside the full modules and current official sources. Each entry separates the local framework, action and review.


## Professional Foundations — Aotearoa New Zealand

The Social Workers Registration Act 2003, SWRB Code of Conduct and Core Competence Standards anchor professional practice in Aotearoa New Zealand. Registration and a current practising certificate should be distinguished from an employer’s allocation of duties. Specialist statutory roles have additional requirements.

The competence framework includes practice with Māori and attention to Te Tiriti o Waitangi, culture, relationships and safe professional practice. Ask how the person wants whānau, hapū, iwi or other supporters involved. Cultural safety requires reflection on professional power and the person’s experience, rather than adding a cultural label to an unchanged assessment.


- Confirm registration, practising status, competence and the authority required for the task.
- Discuss the person’s goals, language, cultural supports and preferred whānau involvement.
- Use supervision to test the effect of bias, colonisation, poverty and institutional barriers on the formulation.
- Connect CPD to feedback and the current SWRB requirements rather than assuming that attending a course proves competence.


Explain the service complaint route and when a professional concern belongs with SWRB. Health and disability service concerns may also engage the Health and Disability Commissioner (HDC). Identify the actual issue and remedy rather than sending every concern to the same body.


- [SWRB Core Competence Standards](https://swrb.govt.nz/practice/core-competence-standards/)
- [SWRB Code of Conduct](https://swrb.govt.nz/practice/code-of-conduct/)
- [Social Workers Registration Act 2003](https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2003/0017/latest/whole.html)


## Social Care and Support — Aotearoa New Zealand

Disability Support Services (DSS), Needs Assessment and Service Coordination (NASC), Enabling Good Lives arrangements, health services and ACC have different eligibility and funding roles. Identify the scheme relevant to the person’s circumstances; injury-related support, disability support and older-person services should not be treated as one entitlement.

DSS guidance describes referral to a NASC provider to understand needs and determine eligibility, with relevant supporting evidence. A needs assessment, allocation of funding and a service beginning are separate events. Check the current assessment and funding arrangements rather than relying on an old agency name or contract.


- Identify the responsible funder and referral route, including NASC or another applicable service.
- Describe the person’s goals, daily support needs, environmental barriers and existing support.
- Check the evidence needed for eligibility and explain the decision and funding allocation separately.
- Confirm the provider, start date, whānau willingness and contingency for gaps or changing needs.


Ask the relevant assessment or funding body for reasons and the applicable reassessment, review or complaint route. DSS publishes current assessment information. Track disputes with different funders separately and do not describe a referral to another agency as a resolved need.


- [DSS needs assessment services](https://www.disabilitysupport.govt.nz/disabled-people/assessment-and-funding/needs-assessment-services)
- [DSS access to support](https://www.disabilitysupport.govt.nz/disabled-people/assessment-and-funding/how-to-access-support)


## Decision-Making and Capacity — Aotearoa New Zealand

Right 7 of the Code of Health and Disability Services Consumers’ Rights addresses informed choice and consent, presumes competence and preserves choice to the extent of a person’s competence. The Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act 1988 (PPPR) provides routes including welfare guardianship, property orders and enduring powers of attorney.

Where a consumer is not competent and no legally entitled representative is available, Right 7(4) has a specific framework. It is not a general rule that any relative may sign. Read the provision and the particular appointment before identifying who may act and what decision standard applies.


- Specify the treatment or other decision and provide the support needed for participation.
- Identify the applicable consent or PPPR framework and record decision-specific evidence.
- Verify the scope and operation of any enduring power of attorney or court order.
- If relying on Right 7(4), check its conditions, efforts to ascertain the person’s views and consultation requirements.


HDC and the independent advocacy service provide routes concerning consumer rights. PPPR court orders and representative disputes may require Family Court or other legal advice. The appropriate review depends on whether the issue is a service breach, capacity decision or representative’s authority.


- [HDC consent and competence guidance](https://www.hdc.org.nz/education/online-learning/consent-for-consumers-who-are-not-competent/)
- [Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act 1988](https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1988/0004/latest/whole.html)


## Restrictions and Liberty — Aotearoa New Zealand

Restrictions may engage the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990, the consumer Code, PPPR arrangements and, in specific circumstances, compulsory mental-health or intellectual-disability legislation. A welfare guardian or service plan is not an explanation for every measure used by staff.

Identify whether the measure is an ordinary supported-care arrangement, restraint, seclusion or confinement under a specific statutory power. The Intellectual Disability (Compulsory Care and Rehabilitation) Act 2003 has a particular statutory scope; intellectual disability alone does not bring every person within it.


- Describe actual restrictions and the person’s wishes, including what happens when they want to leave.
- Identify the applicable service standard and separate consent, representative authority and any compulsory-care power.
- Obtain specialist advice about the scope of the order or legal basis where confinement is proposed.
- Document alternatives, authorisation, monitoring, independent support and a plan to reduce restrictions.


Consumer-rights complaints and advocacy are available through the HDC framework. Where a person is under the compulsory mental-health or intellectual-disability Acts, district inspectors have specific rights-protection functions. Identify the applicable court or tribunal review rather than assuming a single liberty procedure.


- [New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990](https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1990/0109/latest/whole.html)
- [PPPR Act 1988](https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1988/0004/latest/whole.html)
- [District inspectors and rights protection](https://www.health.govt.nz/regulation-legislation/mental-health-and-addiction/mental-health-act/mental-health-district-inspectors)


## Mental Health — Aotearoa New Zealand

The Ministry of Health states that the Mental Health Act 2026 received Royal Assent on 9 July 2026 and is to commence on 1 July 2028. Until replacement takes effect, the Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992 remains the operative framework. Preparation for the new system must be distinguished from present powers and rights.

Under the 1992 framework, compulsory assessment and treatment require the statutory mental-disorder criteria and staged procedures. Clinical disagreement, unusual beliefs or a diagnosis alone do not establish all criteria. Use the current Ministry guidelines and authorised clinical roles for the particular stage.


- Check whether the operative 1992 route or a subsequently commenced provision applies.
- Assess the actual mental-disorder and risk or self-care evidence against the relevant statutory criteria.
- Identify the required clinical assessment, notices, review stage and the person’s cultural and whānau support.
- Separate compulsory psychiatric treatment from unrelated healthcare consent and discharge-support decisions.


District inspectors are independent lawyers who explain rights, investigate concerns and help with access to review. Judicial or Mental Health Review Tribunal processes depend on legal status. Explain the person’s current rights using the Ministry’s accessible materials and arrange legal support where needed.


- [Mental-health replacement and commencement](https://www.health.govt.nz/regulation-legislation/mental-health-and-addiction/repealing-and-replacing-the-mental-health-act)
- [Guidelines to the 1992 Act](https://www.health.govt.nz/publications/guidelines-to-the-mental-health-compulsory-assessment-and-treatment-act-1992)
- [Current mental-health rights](https://www.health.govt.nz/regulation-legislation/mental-health-and-addiction/mental-health-act/your-rights-under-the-mental-health-act)


## Adult Safeguarding — Aotearoa New Zealand

Adult safety concerns can engage police, health or disability services, provider safeguarding arrangements, the HDC framework and specific criminal-law duties. There is no reason to assume that one overseas adult-protection procedure applies across these settings.

The Crimes Act 1961 includes offences concerning ill-treatment or neglect and failure to protect a child or vulnerable adult in defined circumstances. Check the actual duty and the person’s role; do not simplify it into a universal reporting rule for every adult concern. DSS quality and safeguarding arrangements relate to the services within its remit.


- Identify immediate danger, the adult’s wishes and a safe way to communicate.
- Choose the relevant police, provider, funder or health/disability complaint route for the facts and setting.
- Check any specific legal duty and act promptly where its conditions apply.
- Arrange practical support and follow-up alongside reporting, including continuity if a carer or worker is removed.


HDC complaints and independent advocacy can address health and disability consumer rights. Police and the courts address different issues. Record which body has accepted responsibility and how the adult can raise concerns about the response.


- [DSS quality and safeguarding responsibilities](https://www.disabilitysupport.govt.nz/providers/quality-and-safeguarding/we-can-all-contribute-to-quality-and-safeguarding)
- [Crimes Act 1961](https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1961/0043/latest/whole.html)


## Children, Families and Transitions — Aotearoa New Zealand

The Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 provides the care-and-protection framework, including reports of concern and family group conferences. Current Oranga Tamariki practice guidance explains assessment, referral, preparation, participation and implementation. A family group conference is a statutory process with defined roles, not simply an informal family meeting.

Establish the child’s safety and views alongside whānau relationships, cultural identity and practical support. Use the current Act and policy for duties and powers; professional commitments to culturally safe practice should not be confused with an assumption that every historical statutory provision remains unchanged.


- Record the concern and use the appropriate Oranga Tamariki or police route where needed.
- Distinguish the assessment, the basis for believing care or protection is needed and any referral for a family group conference.
- Prepare the child and whānau to understand the concern and participate, with the appropriate coordinator and supports.
- Record the agreed plan, responsible parties and review, and escalate when the plan is not meeting the child’s needs.


Explain participation, support and any applicable court or complaint route. A plan should preserve the child’s voice and show who accepted each action. The statutory process and a practice model do not remove the need for evidence about actual safety.


- [Oranga Tamariki Act 1989](https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1989/0024/latest/whole.html)
- [Family group conference policy](https://practice.orangatamariki.govt.nz/policy/family-group-conferences-for-care-andor-protection-concerns)


## Rights, Culture and Recording — Aotearoa New Zealand

The Code of Health and Disability Services Consumers’ Rights, Human Rights Act 1993, New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990 and professional standards answer different rights questions. Establish the provider and function involved before choosing the relevant route.

The Privacy Act 2020 and Health Information Privacy Code govern information handling in their respective scope. The Privacy Commissioner publishes a version of the Health Information Privacy Code in force from 1 May 2026, reflecting the new indirect-collection requirements. Use that current version rather than an unchanged 2020 download.


- Identify the consumer right, equality issue or public-function decision affecting the person.
- Ask about language, cultural safety, whānau involvement and accessible participation.
- Check the applicable privacy rules for collection, notification, use and disclosure; rule 11 governs health-information disclosure.
- Explain the relevant HDC, advocacy, privacy or other complaint and review route.


A serious-threat exception to health-information confidentiality has conditions, including necessity and the applicable requirements concerning authorisation. Use the current Privacy Commissioner guidance and record the reasoning. A police request is not automatically a direction to release a whole file.


- [Current Health Information Privacy Code](https://www.privacy.org.nz/privacy-principles/codes-of-practice/hipc2020/)
- [Health-information disclosure guidance](https://www.privacy.org.nz/privacy-principles/codes-of-practice/hipc2020/hipc-factsheet-3/)
- [Requests from police and law enforcement](https://www.privacy.org.nz/responsibilities/releasing-personal-information-to-police-and-law-enforcement-agencies/)

Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Social Workers Registration Act 2003, SWRB Code of Conduct and Core Competence Standards anchor professional practice in Aotearoa New Zealand. Registration and a current practising certificate should be distinguished from an employer’s allocation of duties. Specialist statutory roles have additional requirements.

The competence framework includes practice with Māori and attention to Te Tiriti o Waitangi, culture, relationships and safe professional practice. Ask how the person wants whānau, hapū, iwi or other supporters involved. Cultural safety requires reflection on professional power and the person’s experience, rather than adding a cultural label to an unchanged assessment.

Local pathway:

Discuss the person’s goals, language, cultural supports and preferred whānau involvement.

# Practice Scenarios — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/practice-scenarios.html

# Scenario Workouts — Aotearoa New Zealand practice guide


All cases are fictional learning exercises. Explain your evidence and reasoning before reading the discussion.


## Professional Foundations — Aotearoa New Zealand

A service describes a Māori client as disengaged after arranging meetings without the support person they requested.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Ask what made the meetings unsafe or unhelpful and agree how participation should work. Review the earlier interpretation and record the person’s goals and chosen supports. Take the effect of professional and institutional power to supervision, with a concrete change to the next contact.


## Social Care and Support — Aotearoa New Zealand

A person with a longstanding disability develops additional support needs after an injury, and two services each suggest the other should pay.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Map the needs and the scope of each scheme, obtain the actual eligibility decisions and coordinate the interface. Record interim support and unresolved funding responsibility. Keep the person’s desired outcomes visible while the agencies resolve the dispute.


## Decision-Making and Capacity — Aotearoa New Zealand

A woman can express a clear preference about treatment but needs information presented in short sessions. Her son says he should sign because he manages her bills.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Provide the communication support and assess the relevant decision. Financial help does not establish healthcare authority. Read any appointment and use the applicable consent framework, preserving the woman’s own choices to the extent she can make them.


## Restrictions and Liberty — Aotearoa New Zealand

A residential provider uses a locked room when a resident becomes distressed and says the welfare guardian approved the behaviour plan.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Assess immediate safety, the purpose and effect of isolation and the person’s experience. Check the guardian’s powers and the specific legal and service requirements for the measure. Explore communication, environmental and staffing changes, and escalate any missing authority or safeguard.


## Mental Health — Aotearoa New Zealand

A team wants to apply a future provision of the 2026 Act because it has been included in a training presentation.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Confirm the commencement date and use the operative legislation and forms for the person’s present assessment. Explain current district-inspector and review rights. Record preparation for the new law as service development, not as the authority for today’s intervention.


## Adult Safeguarding — Aotearoa New Zealand

An adult using funded support reports that a worker withholds meals as punishment but fears losing the service if they complain.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Establish immediate access to food and safe support, hear the adult privately and preserve the relevant facts. Follow the appropriate safeguarding and complaint routes and consider criminal duties or police involvement. Plan continuity so reporting does not leave the person without essential assistance.


## Children, Families and Transitions — Aotearoa New Zealand

A conference agrees that relatives will support a child, but nobody confirms transport, sleeping arrangements or who will supervise overnight.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Translate the broad agreement into a practical plan with named responsibilities and the child’s view. Verify that the arrangements are available and safe. Use the appropriate review or reconvening process if the plan does not meet the needs identified.


## Rights, Culture and Recording — Aotearoa New Zealand

A worker receives sensitive health information from a relative and later receives a police request for the entire record.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?

- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Check the current collection-notification requirements and any applicable exception, then assess disclosure separately. Establish the police request’s purpose and legal basis, share only what the applicable rule permits and document the person’s participation or why authorisation could not appropriately be sought.


## Worked cases

### Professional Foundations — Aotearoa New Zealand

A service describes a Māori client as disengaged after arranging meetings without the support person they requested.

- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?

Discussion: Ask what made the meetings unsafe or unhelpful and agree how participation should work. Review the earlier interpretation and record the person’s goals and chosen supports. Take the effect of professional and institutional power to supervision, with a concrete change to the next contact.

### Social Care and Support — Aotearoa New Zealand

A person with a longstanding disability develops additional support needs after an injury, and two services each suggest the other should pay.

- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?

Discussion: Map the needs and the scope of each scheme, obtain the actual eligibility decisions and coordinate the interface. Record interim support and unresolved funding responsibility. Keep the person’s desired outcomes visible while the agencies resolve the dispute.

### Decision-Making and Capacity — Aotearoa New Zealand

A woman can express a clear preference about treatment but needs information presented in short sessions. Her son says he should sign because he manages her bills.

- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?

Discussion: Provide the communication support and assess the relevant decision. Financial help does not establish healthcare authority. Read any appointment and use the applicable consent framework, preserving the woman’s own choices to the extent she can make them.

# Case Route Finder — New South Wales

## Use the route finder

Select the concerns that fit a fictional case. More than one framework may be relevant. Open each suggested module and its sources; the tool selects learning topics and does not decide a legal threshold.

## Compare the routes

Separate support needs, decision-making, mental-health intervention, protective reporting and restrictions. Record the question each route answers, the source you checked and who needs to provide further advice.


## Route questions

### Care or carer support needs

Which needs and outcomes belong to the person and to carers?

Identify the scheme responsible for each need and the evidence required for its assessment. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### A decision-specific capacity question

What is the precise decision and why is ability to decide questioned?

Support the patient’s own decision and establish the precise treatment and capacity question. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Restrictions or liberty concerns

What restrictions actually operate and how do they affect the person?

Identify the practice, its purpose and whether it is a regulated restrictive practice in the actual setting. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Mental health support or compulsion questions

What is the purpose of each proposed intervention?

Identify the proposed route and connect the actual evidence to its criteria. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Abuse, neglect or safeguarding concerns

How can the person be heard safely and privately?

Arrange a safe conversation and identify immediate danger, dependency and the adult’s desired outcomes. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### A child, young carer or transition issue

What does the child say or show about safety and daily life?

Check the child’s age, your role and the applicable reporting threshold under the Act. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Language, participation or recording concerns

What makes participation accessible for this person?

Identify the state or Commonwealth duty relevant to access, discrimination or the proposed intervention. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Professional learning or supervision

What is the purpose and limit of your role?

Identify the employer, state, service setting and any appointment required for the task. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

# Learning Flashcards — New South Wales — New South Wales

Jurisdiction: New South Wales
