# Learning Flashcards — Victoria — Victoria

Jurisdiction: Victoria
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Victoria practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/australia-victoria/learning-flashcards-victoria.html

# Learning Flashcards — Victoria practice guide


Answer before revealing the response in the interactive workspace. These cards accompany the full local modules.


## Professional Foundations — Victoria


### Which local framework anchors this topic in Victoria practice guide?

The Australian Association of Social Workers (AASW) Code of Ethics and Practice Standards provide a professional framework. AASW membership or accreditation, an employer requirement and statutory authority are different matters. Check the requirements for the actual role and state rather than presenting the professional association as the source of every legal power.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

Practice should attend to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples’ self-determination, cultural safety and the effects of colonisation. Ask which community-controlled organisations or cultural supports the person wants involved. Professional values need to be connected to the state law governing the particular intervention.


### What are the key local actions?

Identify the employer, state, service setting and any appointment required for the task. Explain the professional role, consent and confidentiality limits before assessment. Consider power, racism, disability and material barriers alongside individual and family strengths. Use supervision and learning to test the effect of practice on the person, with the current AASW standards as a professional reference.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

Distinguish an employer complaint, a professional-association concern and a statutory regulator or tribunal route. The relevant health, disability, aged-care or child-protection body depends on the issue. A professional membership complaint is not an appeal against a state or Commonwealth funding decision.


### What common error should you avoid?

Equating association membership, clinical experience or a job title with every statutory appointment.


## Social Care and Support — Victoria


### Which local framework anchors this topic in Victoria practice guide?

Disability support through the NDIS, state health and housing services, and Commonwealth aged care have separate entry and funding rules. NDIS access involves age, residence and disability or early-intervention requirements; a diagnosis alone does not establish entitlement to a particular funded support. Check current NDIA rules for the actual application or plan.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

The Aged Care Act 2024 and Support at Home commenced on 1 November 2025. Do not describe the old Home Care Package arrangements as the only current system. The Commonwealth Home Support Programme has its own transition arrangements. Contributions and programme rules need a current check, including announced changes with later commencement dates.


### What are the key local actions?

Identify the scheme responsible for each need and the evidence required for its assessment. Keep access eligibility, plan funding, provider availability and any client contribution separate. Consider state health, housing and community support where a need is outside a particular funded scheme. Record the person’s goals, family willingness, actual start dates and the review route for each decision.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

For an NDIA decision, identify whether an internal review and subsequent Administrative Review Tribunal route are available and check the decision notice’s time limits. A provider complaint to the NDIS Commission is different from a funding review. Aged-care complaints and assessment reviews use their own routes.


### What common error should you avoid?

Treating NDIS eligibility as approval for every requested service, or using obsolete aged-care programme rules.


## Decision-Making and Capacity — Victoria


### Which local framework anchors this topic in Victoria practice guide?

The Medical Treatment Planning and Decisions Act 2016 governs important medical-consent and advance-care-directive questions. The Guardianship and Administration Act 2019 provides a separate framework for guardianship, administration and supported appointments. Specify whether the decision concerns treatment, personal matters or finances. Medical decision-making capacity concerns understanding the relevant information and effects, retaining it for the decision, considering it when choosing, and conveying the choice and related views or needs by any workable means. Provide practical support first; an apparently unwise choice does not establish incapacity.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

An advance care directive can include an instructional directive and a values directive, with different effects. Where the person cannot make the treatment decision, identify the lawful medical treatment decision maker. Their task concerns the decision the person would have made, informed by relevant preferences and values, rather than simply the representative’s preferred outcome.


### What are the key local actions?

Support the person to make the specific decision and assess the relevant decision-making ability. Check for a valid, applicable instructional directive and distinguish it from a values statement. Identify the medical treatment decision maker under the applicable appointment or hierarchy. For a separate personal or financial issue, verify the scope of the relevant guardian, administrator or other arrangement.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

The Office of the Public Advocate (OPA) explains healthcare decision-making and routes where no appropriate decision maker is available. VCAT has relevant guardianship and other statutory functions. Disputed authority or treatment requires the route applicable to that decision, not a general family vote.


### What common error should you avoid?

Treating an instructional directive as merely optional, or assuming financial administration includes medical consent.


## Restrictions and Liberty — Victoria


### Which local framework anchors this topic in Victoria practice guide?

The Disability Act 2006 and Victorian Senior Practitioner arrangements operate alongside the NDIS restrictive-practices framework where applicable. Authorised Program Officers, the Senior Practitioner, behaviour support practitioners and implementing providers have different responsibilities. A plan is not proof that every necessary authorisation or approval exists.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

The Senior Practitioner publishes directions and prohibitions, including a permanent-prohibition notice dated September 2025. Check the current rules for the particular practice and cohort before considering an application. A prohibited practice is not made permissible by including it in a behaviour support plan.


### What are the key local actions?

Identify the actual restriction, setting and whether the disability, mental-health or aged-care framework applies. For the disability route, check the Authorised Program Officer and Senior Practitioner requirements and current prohibitions. Check NDIS plan, authorisation and incident-reporting requirements separately where they apply. Record participation, alternatives, conditions, review and the strategy for reducing the restriction.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

OPA, advocacy services and the relevant regulator can assist with concerns within their remits. The person needs a usable way to object and seek the applicable legal or administrative review. A guardian’s agreement does not remove the statutory restrictions on restraint.


### What common error should you avoid?

Treating historical approval or a lodged plan as permanent permission, including for a prohibited practice.


## Mental Health — Victoria


### Which local framework anchors this topic in Victoria practice guide?

The Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 replaced the 2014 Act. It prefers voluntary assessment and treatment and provides separate assessment orders, temporary treatment orders and Mental Health Tribunal treatment orders. Each stage has its own authorised decision-maker and requirements.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

Compulsory treatment criteria include mental illness; immediate treatment needed to prevent serious deterioration in health or serious harm; that treatment being provided if the order is made; and no reasonably available less restrictive means. Evidence that a service is actually available matters. Assessment-order criteria should not be replaced with the treatment-order test.


### What are the key local actions?

Identify the stage, authorised practitioner and exact statutory criteria. Record the person’s preferences, available voluntary alternatives and why the proposed order is necessary. Check advance statements of preferences, nominated support persons and supported decision-making requirements. Separate treatment consent, any statutory treatment authority and additional safeguards for particular interventions.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

Explain the statement of rights, non-legal advocacy, second psychiatric opinion and Mental Health Tribunal routes. Current handbook guidance describes their application. A nominated support person assists participation; their role should not be treated as a general substitute-consent appointment.


### What common error should you avoid?

Using the assessment and treatment criteria interchangeably or treating a support person as the treatment decision-maker.


## Adult Safeguarding — Victoria


### Which local framework anchors this topic in Victoria practice guide?

Adult concerns may require family-violence services, police, OPA, disability safeguards, aged-care oversight or a provider complaint. Identify the relationship and service setting before selecting a route. The Family Violence Protection Act 2008 is relevant to violence and abuse within its defined relationships; not every adult concern is governed by that framework.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

The Orange Door provides access to family-violence and family-support services. NDIS and aged-care providers have their own incident and regulatory obligations. A referral for support, a reportable incident and an application for a protective order are different actions.


### What are the key local actions?

Hear the adult safely and identify immediate danger, coercion and practical dependence. Identify whether the concern involves family violence, a disability or aged-care provider, another service or crime. Use the relevant specialist, police and regulatory routes, checking any mandatory reporting duty. Plan safe contact, practical support and follow-up without assuming that a referral authorises coercive action.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

Explain the appropriate complaint, advocacy or court route for the issue. OPA can provide information about decision-making and rights within its remit. Keep the adult’s wishes and the legal authority for any intervention visible, including where agencies disagree.


### What common error should you avoid?

Treating all adult safeguarding as one statutory process or assuming a guardianship referral resolves family violence.


## Children, Families and Transitions — Victoria


### Which local framework anchors this topic in Victoria practice guide?

The Children, Youth and Families Act 2005 distinguishes protection grounds and mandatory reporting. The mandatory-reporter categories depend on the role: do not assume every person called a social worker is included solely by title. A social worker may fall within a listed role, such as school counselling or out-of-home care work.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

DFFH guidance requires listed reporters who form the relevant reasonable belief in their work to report protection concerns involving physical injury or sexual abuse. Other forms of significant harm may also be reported. The child’s harm and parental protection must be considered; the statutory reporting duty is not identical to every possible wellbeing concern.


### What are the key local actions?

Check the actual professional or employment category and the applicable reporting duty. Report to Child Protection as soon as practicable where the duty is engaged, including new grounds arising later. Consider a support referral to The Orange Door where appropriate, without substituting it for a required protection report. Check separate police and organisational duties, and plan child participation, cultural support and continuity.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

Explain the Child Protection process and the child’s and family’s access to support or legal advice. DFFH guidance distinguishes reporting routes from family-support referrals. Advice within an organisation should not delay an applicable personal reporting obligation.


### What common error should you avoid?

Assuming all social-work job titles create the same reporting duty, or confusing voluntary support with a mandatory report.


## Rights, Culture and Recording — Victoria


### Which local framework anchors this topic in Victoria practice guide?

The Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006 requires covered public authorities to act compatibly with Charter rights and give proper consideration to relevant rights, subject to statutory exceptions. Identify whether the provider is a public authority for the function involved. A Charter statement should explain the affected rights and reasoning, not simply declare compliance.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

The Equal Opportunity Act 2010, Health Records Act 2001 and Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 have different scopes. Commonwealth law may also apply. Determine the organisation and information involved before selecting a privacy or discrimination pathway.


### What are the key local actions?

Identify the relevant Charter rights and whether the decision-maker is a covered public authority. Consider the actual impact, alternatives and any lawful basis for limiting a right. Arrange accessible and culturally safe participation and address applicable equality obligations. Check the relevant privacy regime and explain access, correction, complaints and review.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

The Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission explains Charter duties and discrimination. Privacy and health complaints use their respective bodies and statutory routes. Obtain advice about the remedy for an alleged Charter breach rather than promising that every concern has a standalone Charter claim.


### What common error should you avoid?

Assuming every private provider has identical Charter duties or that naming rights establishes proper consideration.


## Revision cards

### Professional Foundations — Victoria: Which local framework anchors this topic in Victoria practice guide?

The Australian Association of Social Workers (AASW) Code of Ethics and Practice Standards provide a professional framework. AASW membership or accreditation, an employer requirement and statutory authority are different matters. Check the requirements for the actual role and state rather than presenting the professional association as the source of every legal power.

### Professional Foundations — Victoria: Which distinction must be kept clear?

Practice should attend to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples’ self-determination, cultural safety and the effects of colonisation. Ask which community-controlled organisations or cultural supports the person wants involved. Professional values need to be connected to the state law governing the particular intervention.

### Professional Foundations — Victoria: What are the key local actions?

Identify the employer, state, service setting and any appointment required for the task. Explain the professional role, consent and confidentiality limits before assessment. Consider power, racism, disability and material barriers alongside individual and family strengths. Use supervision and learning to test the effect of practice on the person, with the current AASW standards as a professional reference.

### Professional Foundations — Victoria: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

Distinguish an employer complaint, a professional-association concern and a statutory regulator or tribunal route. The relevant health, disability, aged-care or child-protection body depends on the issue. A professional membership complaint is not an appeal against a state or Commonwealth funding decision.

### Professional Foundations — Victoria: What common error should you avoid?

Equating association membership, clinical experience or a job title with every statutory appointment.

### Social Care and Support — Victoria: Which local framework anchors this topic in Victoria practice guide?

Disability support through the NDIS, state health and housing services, and Commonwealth aged care have separate entry and funding rules. NDIS access involves age, residence and disability or early-intervention requirements; a diagnosis alone does not establish entitlement to a particular funded support. Check current NDIA rules for the actual application or plan.

### Social Care and Support — Victoria: Which distinction must be kept clear?

The Aged Care Act 2024 and Support at Home commenced on 1 November 2025. Do not describe the old Home Care Package arrangements as the only current system. The Commonwealth Home Support Programme has its own transition arrangements. Contributions and programme rules need a current check, including announced changes with later commencement dates.

### Social Care and Support — Victoria: What are the key local actions?

Identify the scheme responsible for each need and the evidence required for its assessment. Keep access eligibility, plan funding, provider availability and any client contribution separate. Consider state health, housing and community support where a need is outside a particular funded scheme. Record the person’s goals, family willingness, actual start dates and the review route for each decision.

### Social Care and Support — Victoria: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

For an NDIA decision, identify whether an internal review and subsequent Administrative Review Tribunal route are available and check the decision notice’s time limits. A provider complaint to the NDIS Commission is different from a funding review. Aged-care complaints and assessment reviews use their own routes.

# Practice Glossary — Victoria practice guide

Use each definition with its linked full lesson and official sources.

## Professional Foundations

The Australian Association of Social Workers (AASW) Code of Ethics and Practice Standards provide a professional framework. AASW membership or accreditation, an employer requirement and statutory authority are different matters. Check the requirements for the actual role and state rather than presenting the professional association as the source of every legal power.

## Social Care and Support

Disability support through the NDIS, state health and housing services, and Commonwealth aged care have separate entry and funding rules. NDIS access involves age, residence and disability or early-intervention requirements; a diagnosis alone does not establish entitlement to a particular funded support. Check current NDIA rules for the actual application or plan.

## Decision-Making and Capacity

Provide practical support first; an apparently unwise choice does not establish incapacity.

## Restrictions and Liberty

The Disability Act 2006 and Victorian Senior Practitioner arrangements operate alongside the NDIS restrictive-practices framework where applicable. Authorised Program Officers, the Senior Practitioner, behaviour support practitioners and implementing providers have different responsibilities. A plan is not proof that every necessary authorisation or approval exists.

## Mental Health

## Adult Safeguarding

## Children, Families and Transitions

The Children, Youth and Families Act 2005 distinguishes protection grounds and mandatory reporting. The mandatory-reporter categories depend on the role: do not assume every person called a social worker is included solely by title. A social worker may fall within a listed role, such as school counselling or out-of-home care work.

## Rights, Culture and Recording

The Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006 requires covered public authorities to act compatibly with Charter rights and give proper consideration to relevant rights, subject to statutory exceptions. Identify whether the provider is a public authority for the function involved. A Charter statement should explain the affected rights and reasoning, not simply declare compliance.

## Australian Association of Social Workers (AASW)

The professional body identified for this guide. Check its remit and the requirements that apply to your role.

## Advocacy

Support to express views, understand choices and participate; statutory entitlements depend on the local framework.

## CPD

Continuing professional development: learning, reflection and evidence of improvement.

## Consent

Agreement to a specific action; check the applicable requirements for information, voluntariness and ability to consent.

## Coercion

Pressure or control that can affect expressed wishes and freedom to act.

## Eligibility

The criteria for a particular service or programme; distinct from a description of need.

## Capacity

Ability to make the relevant decision under the applicable legal framework; avoid a global label.

## Representative

Someone with a defined support or decision-making role; verify the source and scope of authority.

## Proportionality

A reasoned comparison of intended benefit, burdens, rights and alternatives.

## Cultural safety

Attention to power, identity and the person’s experience of a service, informed by their preferences.

## Data minimisation

Using or sharing only information needed for an identified lawful purpose.

## Confidentiality

Protecting information while understanding and explaining lawful exceptions.

## Safeguarding referral

Communicating a concern to the appropriate agency; confirm the applicable route and follow-up.

## Professional supervision

Structured discussion of decisions, ethics, skills, wellbeing and accountability.

## Formulation

A reasoned account connecting evidence and possible explanations to a plan.

## Family network

Relationships that may offer support; availability, safety and willingness need assessment.

## Transition

Planned change between services or life stages, with continuity and named responsibilities.

## Contingency

An agreed response if risks increase or the preferred plan cannot operate.

## Review

A planned check of outcomes, changing circumstances and whether actions remain appropriate.

## Least restrictive option

An option that can achieve the purpose with less interference in rights and freedom.

Continuing professional development: learning, reflection and evidence of improvement.

### Consent

Agreement to a specific action; check the applicable requirements for information, voluntariness and ability to consent.

### Coercion

Pressure or control that can affect expressed wishes and freedom to act.

### Eligibility

The criteria for a particular service or programme; distinct from a description of need.

### Capacity

Ability to make the relevant decision under the applicable legal framework; avoid a global label.

### Representative

Someone with a defined support or decision-making role; verify the source and scope of authority.

### Proportionality

A reasoned comparison of intended benefit, burdens, rights and alternatives.

### Cultural safety

Attention to power, identity and the person’s experience of a service, informed by their preferences.

### Data minimisation

Using or sharing only information needed for an identified lawful purpose.

### Confidentiality

Protecting information while understanding and explaining lawful exceptions.

### Safeguarding referral

Communicating a concern to the appropriate agency; confirm the applicable route and follow-up.

### Professional supervision

Structured discussion of decisions, ethics, skills, wellbeing and accountability.

### Formulation

A reasoned account connecting evidence and possible explanations to a plan.

### Family network

Relationships that may offer support; availability, safety and willingness need assessment.

### Transition

Planned change between services or life stages, with continuity and named responsibilities.

### Contingency

An agreed response if risks increase or the preferred plan cannot operate.

### Review

A planned check of outcomes, changing circumstances and whether actions remain appropriate.

### Least restrictive option

An option that can achieve the purpose with less interference in rights and freedom.

# Theory Into Practice — Victoria — Victoria

Jurisdiction: Victoria
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Victoria practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/australia-victoria/theory-into-practice-victoria-victoria.html

# Theory Into Practice — Victoria

## Build a testable explanation

Use the theory finder to generate alternative explanations for a fictional case. Compare what each lens notices about relationships, environment, power, trauma and strengths. Record evidence that would support or challenge your explanation.

## Use models thoughtfully

Theories are shared learning lenses, not country-specific statutory rules. Their inclusion does not imply official adoption in Victoria. Check suitability, training requirements, cultural context and the person’s account before applying a method.


## Interactive theory lenses

### Ecological Systems Theory

Person, family, housing, community, services, poverty, policy, culture, and environment.

Hypothesis: The presenting issue may be shaped by pressures around the person, not only by individual behaviour or choice.

- What changed in the environment before the concern escalated?
- Which systems are supporting the person, and which are adding pressure?
- Would risk reduce if housing, income, access, care, or community support changed?

### Strengths-Based Practice

Capabilities, identity, relationships, community, culture, hope, and what is already working.

Hypothesis: The person may have protective strategies or relationships that are hidden by a risk-heavy professional account.

- What has helped the person survive or cope so far?
- Who does the person trust, and what role could they safely play?
- Which strengths are real evidence, and which are optimistic assumptions?

### Trauma-Informed Practice

Safety, trust, choice, collaboration, empowerment, shame, threat responses, and control.

Hypothesis: Behaviour that looks like refusal, avoidance, anger, or disengagement may be a survival response to trauma, coercion, loss, or fear.

- What might feel unsafe or controlling from the person's perspective?
- What helps the person feel more choice and predictability?
- How can we avoid repeating patterns of powerlessness?

### Attachment Theory

Trust, separation, dependency, rejection, fear, care-seeking, and relationship patterns.

Hypothesis: Responses to professionals or carers may reflect previous experiences of care, loss, abandonment, or unsafe relationships.

- How does the person respond when support increases, reduces, or changes?
- Are there patterns of clinging, pushing away, testing, mistrust, or fear?
- What relationship approach is consistent, boundaried, and safe?

### Systems and Family Theory

Roles, rules, communication, repeated patterns, conflict, care dynamics, and network effects.

Hypothesis: The concern may be maintained by relationship patterns, family roles, service responses, or network conflict.

- Who gains or loses if the current pattern changes?
- What role has each person been placed in or taken on?
- How do professional responses affect the family or network pattern?

### Anti-Oppressive and Anti-Discriminatory Practice

Power, oppression, racism, disability, class, gender, sexuality, culture, age, stigma, and access.

Hypothesis: The presenting issue may be intensified by structural inequality, professional power, discrimination, or inaccessible services.

- What barriers has the person faced before we became involved?
- Whose account is being treated as most credible, and why?
- What reasonable adjustments, cultural humility, or advocacy are needed?

### Crisis Theory

Immediate stress, narrowed options, temporary disequilibrium, coping capacity, and stabilisation.

Hypothesis: The person or family may be temporarily overwhelmed and need stabilisation before longer-term planning is realistic.

- What immediate event or loss has exceeded usual coping?
- What needs to happen in the next 24 to 72 hours?
- What can wait until safety, sleep, food, medication, or support is more stable?

### Life Course Theory

Transitions, cumulative disadvantage, ageing, identity, loss, timing, and turning points.

Hypothesis: Current risk or distress may connect to earlier life events, cumulative exclusion, transition, bereavement, or changing identity.

- What transitions or losses are happening now?
- How has cumulative disadvantage shaped options and trust?
- What strengths, relationships, or identities from earlier life still matter?

### Task-Centred Practice

Specific problems, agreed goals, small steps, roles, review, and measurable change.

Hypothesis: The person may benefit from breaking an overwhelming issue into concrete, negotiated tasks with clear review.

- What problem does the person most want to work on first?
- What is the smallest useful next step?
- Who will do what, by when, and how will we know it helped?

# Children and Family Practice Models — Victoria

## Compare approaches to children and families

Use the model finder to explore enquiry, family relationships, support and safety planning. Begin with the child’s account and daily experience; distinguish observed evidence from adult interpretation.

## Local application

These shared models are educational examples, not a list of officially approved Victoria programmes. Check training, licensing, local adoption and cultural suitability. A model never replaces the applicable reporting duty or legal threshold.


## Model finder

### Signs of Safety

Child protection mapping, danger statements, safety goals, family network work, scaling, and safety planning.

### Signs of Wellbeing, Success, and Belonging

Family support, children in care, permanency, reunification, stability, identity, and belonging work.

### Family Safeguarding

Whole-family child protection where parental domestic abuse, mental health, substance misuse, trauma, or adult needs affect child safety.

### Contextual Safeguarding

Extra-familial harm, exploitation, peer group risk, school, neighbourhood, online spaces, and adolescent safeguarding.

### Family Group Conferencing

Family-led planning, kinship care, safety planning, pre-proceedings, reunification, and support network building.

### Systemic Practice

Family patterns, repeated cycles, communication, roles, meaning, conflict, and relationship-based formulation.

### Motivational Interviewing

Ambivalence, parental engagement, adolescent risk, substance use, resistance, and behaviour change conversations.

### Solution-Focused Practice

Goal-setting, exceptions, scaling, strengths, future-focused planning, and building on small signs of progress.

### PACE and DDP-Informed Practice

Children affected by trauma, attachment disruption, care experience, shame, mistrust, and blocked trust.

### Safe and Together

Domestic abuse-informed child welfare, perpetrator pattern mapping, protective parent strengths, and child impact.

### Graded Care Profile 2

Neglect assessment, evidence-based care mapping, physical care, safety, love and esteem, and developmental care.

### Restorative Practice

Repair, accountability, family meetings, school relationships, conflict, shame, and shared problem-solving.

# Professional Foundations — Victoria — Victoria

Jurisdiction: Victoria
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Victoria practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/australia-victoria/professional-foundations-victoria.html

# Professional Foundations — Victoria

## Learning outcomes

Explain your professional role, distinguish an ethical concern from a statutory power, and turn a formulation into an accountable plan.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

The Australian Association of Social Workers (AASW) Code of Ethics and Practice Standards provide a professional framework. AASW membership or accreditation, an employer requirement and statutory authority are different matters. Check the requirements for the actual role and state rather than presenting the professional association as the source of every legal power.

Practice should attend to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples’ self-determination, cultural safety and the effects of colonisation. Ask which community-controlled organisations or cultural supports the person wants involved. Professional values need to be connected to the state law governing the particular intervention.

## From information to a professional formulation

A chronology says what happened. A formulation explains how the available evidence, the person's experience and their environment might connect. Start with the person's desired change. Map relationships, housing, income, health, discrimination and service barriers alongside individual strengths. A missed appointment may reflect fear, inaccessible transport or an unsafe household; it does not establish unwillingness to engage.

Use at least two possible explanations for a difficult situation. State what evidence supports each and what would challenge it. A strengths approach should identify actual resources the person can use, with their agreement. It should not turn an absent service into an assumed family responsibility. A trauma-informed conversation offers predictability, choice and control over pace while keeping necessary enquiries clear.

## Boundaries and supervision

Explain who employs you, the purpose of contact, how information will be used and the limits of confidentiality. Separate an invitation to accept support from an action the law permits without agreement. Ask for supervision when an instruction conflicts with professional duties or exceeds your authority. Record the issue, advice, action and unresolved concern; merely recording that a manager agreed does not explain the decision.

For a learning reflection, choose one decision you influenced. Describe what the person said, your initial assumption, what changed your understanding and what you will do differently. Seek feedback about the effect on the person, rather than counting training attendance as evidence of improved practice.

## Apply the local pathway

- Identify the employer, state, service setting and any appointment required for the task.
- Explain the professional role, consent and confidentiality limits before assessment.
- Consider power, racism, disability and material barriers alongside individual and family strengths.
- Use supervision and learning to test the effect of practice on the person, with the current AASW standards as a professional reference.

## Rights, challenge and review

Distinguish an employer complaint, a professional-association concern and a statutory regulator or tribunal route. The relevant health, disability, aged-care or child-protection body depends on the issue. A professional membership complaint is not an appeal against a state or Commonwealth funding decision.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A practitioner is asked to sign a statutory assessment because they hold an AASW credential, without checking the specific appointment requirements.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Read the law and service procedure governing that assessment. Confirm qualifications, appointment and scope before signing. Bring any gap to the responsible manager and arrange an authorised practitioner while continuing work that is within your role.

### Common error to avoid

Equating association membership, clinical experience or a job title with every statutory appointment.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Your role and the legal or professional framework
- The person’s outcomes and communication preferences
- Evidence, competing explanations and missing perspectives
- Power, boundaries and any conflict of interest
- Agreed action, supervision, feedback and review

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [AASW Code of Ethics](https://www.aasw.asn.au/about-aasw/ethics-standards/code-of-ethics/)

Editorial expansion: 8 September 2026. The sources support the distinctions taught here; check their current text, amendments, commencement and applicable local procedure before operational use. Independent practitioner review has not been recorded.

# Social Care and Support — Victoria — Victoria

Jurisdiction: Victoria
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Victoria practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/australia-victoria/social-care-and-support-victoria-victoria.html

# Social Care and Support — Victoria

## Learning outcomes

Map assessment, eligibility, funding and delivery separately; include family support without assuming it; explain the local route for challenging a decision.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

Disability support through the NDIS, state health and housing services, and Commonwealth aged care have separate entry and funding rules. NDIS access involves age, residence and disability or early-intervention requirements; a diagnosis alone does not establish entitlement to a particular funded support. Check current NDIA rules for the actual application or plan.

The Aged Care Act 2024 and Support at Home commenced on 1 November 2025. Do not describe the old Home Care Package arrangements as the only current system. The Commonwealth Home Support Programme has its own transition arrangements. Contributions and programme rules need a current check, including announced changes with later commencement dates.

## Assess daily life, not just a list of services

Begin with what a good day would look like. Explore washing, dressing, nutrition, medicines, mobility, home safety, relationships, work or education and community participation. Ask about variation: what happens at night, on a bad day or when a regular supporter is unavailable? Establish what the person can do with appropriate equipment, accessible information or a different environment. Do not confuse performing a task once during a visit with being able to do it reliably in daily life.

Speak with family supporters about willingness, practical ability and sustainability. Their account belongs alongside the person's account, not in place of it. Record support that is actually offered and its limits. An adult child working overnight is not an available overnight care service. Where views differ, describe the disagreement and its consequences for the proposed plan.

## Turn the assessment into a deliverable plan

Keep four decisions visible: the needs identified; the applicable eligibility decision; the funding or charging decision; and the service that will actually start. A referral, waiting-list entry or funding approval is not proof that support has begun. Obtain the person's understanding of costs and responsibilities before recording agreement.

For each outcome, identify an action, a responsible service or person and a review trigger. Include what happens if the worker does not arrive, the person declines support, a carer becomes unavailable or needs change. Record unmet needs and interim arrangements explicitly. A budget dispute should not disappear into a description of the person as difficult or unrealistic.

## Apply the local pathway

- Identify the scheme responsible for each need and the evidence required for its assessment.
- Keep access eligibility, plan funding, provider availability and any client contribution separate.
- Consider state health, housing and community support where a need is outside a particular funded scheme.
- Record the person’s goals, family willingness, actual start dates and the review route for each decision.

## Rights, challenge and review

For an NDIA decision, identify whether an internal review and subsequent Administrative Review Tribunal route are available and check the decision notice’s time limits. A provider complaint to the NDIS Commission is different from a funding review. Aged-care complaints and assessment reviews use their own routes.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A person is told that their NDIS plan should pay for every need after a hospital admission, including treatment and unsuitable housing.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Map the actual support sought and the responsibility of each system. Obtain the relevant decisions and coordinate health, housing and disability support. Record unmet needs and interim arrangements rather than presenting an unfunded referral as a completed plan.

### Common error to avoid

Treating NDIS eligibility as approval for every requested service, or using obsolete aged-care programme rules.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Daily-life evidence, fluctuation and desired outcomes
- The service, eligibility test and decision-maker
- Carer willingness and separately identified needs
- Funding, charges, decisions and reasons
- Start dates, unmet needs, contingency and challenge route

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [NDIS access application and evidence](https://ndis.gov.au/applying/application-process/what-access-request-form)
- [NDIS legislative changes](https://ndis.gov.au/ndis-laws/getting-ndis-back-track/summary-legislation-changes)
- [Current aged-care provider rules and reforms](https://www.health.gov.au/our-work/aged-care-act/resources/providers)
- [CHSP transition arrangements](https://www.health.gov.au/our-work/chsp/reforms)

Editorial expansion: 8 September 2026. The sources support the distinctions taught here; check their current text, amendments, commencement and applicable local procedure before operational use. Independent practitioner review has not been recorded.

# Decision-Making and Capacity — Victoria — Victoria

Jurisdiction: Victoria
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Victoria practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/australia-victoria/decision-making-and-capacity-victoria-victoria.html

# Decision-Making and Capacity — Victoria

## Learning outcomes

Identify the precise decision, provide practical decision support, apply the local capacity or consent framework and verify a representative’s authority.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

The Medical Treatment Planning and Decisions Act 2016 governs important medical-consent and advance-care-directive questions. The Guardianship and Administration Act 2019 provides a separate framework for guardianship, administration and supported appointments. Specify whether the decision concerns treatment, personal matters or finances. Medical decision-making capacity concerns understanding the relevant information and effects, retaining it for the decision, considering it when choosing, and conveying the choice and related views or needs by any workable means. Provide practical support first; an apparently unwise choice does not establish incapacity.

An advance care directive can include an instructional directive and a values directive, with different effects. Where the person cannot make the treatment decision, identify the lawful medical treatment decision maker. Their task concerns the decision the person would have made, informed by relevant preferences and values, rather than simply the representative’s preferred outcome.

## Start with the decision and the support

Write the decision as a question the person could answer: accepting a particular treatment, choosing accommodation or authorising a financial transaction. These questions may engage different laws and decision-makers. A diagnosis, cognitive score or disagreement with professionals is not a complete capacity assessment. Describe the ability relevant to this decision and the evidence for any concern.

Prepare information about the real options, including doing nothing where relevant. Use an interpreter, accessible material, communication aids and suitable timing. Address pain, fatigue, sensory impairment, medication effects and anxiety. Ask the person to explain their understanding in their own way; repeating professional phrases is not the only way to demonstrate understanding. Record what support was tried and its effect, rather than simply writing that all support was offered.

## Keep authority and the decision itself separate

A relative may provide valuable information without holding authority to decide. Obtain the actual appointment, agreement, court order or statutory basis being relied upon. Check the decisions it covers, conditions, whether it is operative and whether another person has priority. Authority over property does not automatically include healthcare or accommodation.

Where a representative can lawfully act, identify the decision standard they must apply locally. Explore the person's wishes, values, previous statements and present participation. Record a disagreement rather than converting it into apparent agreement. Consider whether a reversible interim option allows more support or recovery before an irreversible decision. If authority remains disputed, obtain the appropriate clinical or legal advice and arrange the applicable review; a multidisciplinary meeting cannot create missing legal powers.

## Apply the local pathway

- Support the person to make the specific decision and assess the relevant decision-making ability.
- Check for a valid, applicable instructional directive and distinguish it from a values statement.
- Identify the medical treatment decision maker under the applicable appointment or hierarchy.
- For a separate personal or financial issue, verify the scope of the relevant guardian, administrator or other arrangement.

## Rights, challenge and review

The Office of the Public Advocate (OPA) explains healthcare decision-making and routes where no appropriate decision maker is available. VCAT has relevant guardianship and other statutory functions. Disputed authority or treatment requires the route applicable to that decision, not a general family vote.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A person’s advance directive refuses a particular treatment, but a relative asks the team to ignore it because they believe treatment would help.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Check validity, applicability and whether the statement is an instructional or values directive. Involve the responsible clinician and obtain advice where the position is disputed. Do not substitute the relative’s preference for the legal effect of the document or the person’s own decision.

### Common error to avoid

Treating an instructional directive as merely optional, or assuming financial administration includes medical consent.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Decision, options and time at which it is needed
- Communication support and observed responses
- Applicable legal test and evidence for each element
- Representative’s document, scope and decision standard
- Wishes, disagreement, review and any urgent action

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [OPA healthcare rights](https://www.publicadvocate.vic.gov.au/your-rights/your-healthcare)
- [Interpreting an instructional directive](https://www.publicadvocate.vic.gov.au/medical-treatment/patient-consent/interpreting-an-instructional-directive)
- [Medical Treatment Planning and Decisions Act 2016](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/medical-treatment-planning-and-decisions-act-2016)
- [Guardianship and Administration Act 2019](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/guardianship-and-administration-act-2019)
- [Patient capacity to consent](https://www.publicadvocate.vic.gov.au/medical-treatment/patient-consent/patient-capacity-to-consent)

# Restrictions and Liberty — Victoria — Victoria

Jurisdiction: Victoria
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Victoria practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/australia-victoria/restrictions-and-liberty-victoria-victoria.html

# Restrictions and Liberty — Victoria

## Learning outcomes

Describe actual restrictions, identify the setting-specific legal authority, test alternatives and make representation and review practical.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

The Disability Act 2006 and Victorian Senior Practitioner arrangements operate alongside the NDIS restrictive-practices framework where applicable. Authorised Program Officers, the Senior Practitioner, behaviour support practitioners and implementing providers have different responsibilities. A plan is not proof that every necessary authorisation or approval exists.

The Senior Practitioner publishes directions and prohibitions, including a permanent-prohibition notice dated September 2025. Check the current rules for the particular practice and cohort before considering an application. A prohibited practice is not made permissible by including it in a behaviour support plan.

## Describe what happens in everyday life

Look beyond the label used by the service. Describe locked doors, staff responses to a request to leave, supervision, physical interventions, isolation, medication used to control behaviour and restrictions on visitors, money or communication. State when each measure operates, who applies it, its duration and its cumulative effect. Distinguish a person's preferred routine from a rule enforced by staff.

Hear the person privately with suitable communication support. An absence of verbal objection is not a complete account of their wishes. Distress, repeated requests to go home or avoiding a particular worker may require further enquiry. Family agreement is relevant information but should not be treated as a substitute for the authority required by law.

## Connect necessity to a less restrictive plan

Identify the concrete harm a measure is intended to prevent. Explore environmental changes, pain relief, meaningful activity, different staffing, communication and practical support. Record which options were tried, their effects and why another option is proposed. Provider convenience or an unsigned risk assessment should not become the explanation for an ongoing restriction.

Separate emergency action from a continuing arrangement. An urgent response needs its own factual justification and follow-up; it should not silently become a standing plan. Check the scope of any order or authorisation, applicable conditions, expiry and who must review it. The person needs an accessible explanation and a usable way to object, obtain independent help and challenge the arrangement. Assign responsibility for acting on an objection rather than merely documenting it at the next routine meeting.

## Apply the local pathway

- Identify the actual restriction, setting and whether the disability, mental-health or aged-care framework applies.
- For the disability route, check the Authorised Program Officer and Senior Practitioner requirements and current prohibitions.
- Check NDIS plan, authorisation and incident-reporting requirements separately where they apply.
- Record participation, alternatives, conditions, review and the strategy for reducing the restriction.

## Rights, challenge and review

OPA, advocacy services and the relevant regulator can assist with concerns within their remits. The person needs a usable way to object and seek the applicable legal or administrative review. A guardian’s agreement does not remove the statutory restrictions on restraint.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A provider proposes a restraint copied from an old plan and assumes approval can be renewed without checking current directions.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Check whether the practice is now prohibited and whether the previous approval is relevant to the present circumstances. Assess alternatives and consult the responsible practitioner. Do not apply an obsolete approval to a new plan or bypass the Senior Practitioner’s requirements.

### Common error to avoid

Treating historical approval or a lodged plan as permanent permission, including for a prohibited practice.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Each restriction, setting, duration and actual effect
- The person’s wishes, understanding and objections
- Legal authority, decision-maker, limits and conditions
- Alternatives tried and the evidence about necessity
- Representation, review date, expiry and challenge

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [Victorian Senior Practitioner responsibilities](https://www.dffh.vic.gov.au/about-victorian-senior-practitioner)
- [Current directions and prohibitions](https://www.dffh.vic.gov.au/victorian-senior-practitioners-directions-and-prohibitions)
- [Disability Act 2006](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/disability-act-2006)
- [NDIS implementing-provider rules](https://www.ndiscommission.gov.au/rules-and-standards/behaviour-support-and-restrictive-practices/rules-implementing-providers)

Editorial expansion: 8 September 2026. The sources support the distinctions taught here; check their current text, amendments, commencement and applicable local procedure before operational use. Independent practitioner review has not been recorded.

# Mental Health — Victoria — Victoria

Jurisdiction: Victoria
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Victoria practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/australia-victoria/mental-health-victoria-victoria.html

# Mental Health — Victoria

## Learning outcomes

Distinguish voluntary care, compulsory assessment, detention and treatment; connect the local criteria to evidence and explain the person’s review rights.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

The Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 replaced the 2014 Act. It prefers voluntary assessment and treatment and provides separate assessment orders, temporary treatment orders and Mental Health Tribunal treatment orders. Each stage has its own authorised decision-maker and requirements.

Compulsory treatment criteria include mental illness; immediate treatment needed to prevent serious deterioration in health or serious harm; that treatment being provided if the order is made; and no reasonably available less restrictive means. Evidence that a service is actually available matters. Assessment-order criteria should not be replaced with the treatment-order test.

## Assess the crisis in context

Attend to urgent physical health and immediate safety while creating space for the person's account. Explore sleep, medication, substance use, pain, relationships, housing, financial pressure and previous helpful or harmful experiences of services. Cultural or spiritual expression should be understood in context. Use an appropriate interpreter and ask which supporters the person wants involved.

Describe behaviour and its consequences rather than relying on labels such as non-compliant or high risk. Distinguish what you observed, what somebody reported and the inference being drawn. Consider information that challenges the proposed compulsory route as carefully as information that supports it. The existence of a legal power does not establish that its conditions are met in this case.

## Separate each intervention

Transport, assessment, admission, psychiatric treatment and treatment of an unrelated physical condition can involve different authorities. Check the exact route, the professional authorised to exercise it, required documentation and its time limits. Do not use a single statement that the person is detained to explain every intervention. Document attempts to arrange voluntary or less restrictive support and whether those services are actually available.

Rights information should be understandable at the time and revisited when the person can engage more fully. Explain independent support, legal representation and the applicable review process. During discharge planning, identify housing, medicines, follow-up, family responsibilities and crisis contacts. Confirm who accepts responsibility for each task. A person should not leave with an apparently complete plan consisting only of referrals that no receiving service has accepted.

## Apply the local pathway

- Identify the stage, authorised practitioner and exact statutory criteria.
- Record the person’s preferences, available voluntary alternatives and why the proposed order is necessary.
- Check advance statements of preferences, nominated support persons and supported decision-making requirements.
- Separate treatment consent, any statutory treatment authority and additional safeguards for particular interventions.

## Rights, challenge and review

Explain the statement of rights, non-legal advocacy, second psychiatric opinion and Mental Health Tribunal routes. Current handbook guidance describes their application. A nominated support person assists participation; their role should not be treated as a general substitute-consent appointment.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A person is considered for a treatment order, but the proposed immediate treatment has not been arranged and a community alternative has not been explored.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Check all criteria, including that treatment will be provided and whether a less restrictive means is reasonably available. Obtain the person’s preferences and supports. The existence of illness and concern about deterioration alone does not explain the whole order decision.

### Common error to avoid

Using the assessment and treatment criteria interchangeably or treating a support person as the treatment decision-maker.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Mental and physical health evidence and the person’s account
- The local criteria and voluntary alternatives considered
- Separate authority for transport, admission and treatment
- Required notices, advocacy, representation and review
- Continuity, discharge responsibilities and crisis plan

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/mental-health-and-wellbeing-act-2022)
- [Compulsory assessment and treatment handbook](https://www.health.vic.gov.au/mental-health-and-wellbeing-act-handbook/compulsory-assessment-and-treament)
- [Treatment-order criteria and process](https://www.health.vic.gov.au/mental-health-and-wellbeing-act-handbook/treatments-and-interventions/treatment-orders)

# Adult Safeguarding — Victoria — Victoria

Jurisdiction: Victoria
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Victoria practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/australia-victoria/safeguarding-and-family-violence-victoria-victoria.html

# Adult Safeguarding — Victoria

## Learning outcomes

Recognise abuse, neglect and coercion; choose the correct local reporting route; connect immediate protection to the adult’s wishes and continuing support.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

Adult concerns may require family-violence services, police, OPA, disability safeguards, aged-care oversight or a provider complaint. Identify the relationship and service setting before selecting a route. The Family Violence Protection Act 2008 is relevant to violence and abuse within its defined relationships; not every adult concern is governed by that framework.

The Orange Door provides access to family-violence and family-support services. NDIS and aged-care providers have their own incident and regulatory obligations. A referral for support, a reportable incident and an application for a protective order are different actions.

## Enquire safely and proportionately

Start with immediate danger and the safest way to communicate. A private conversation may reveal concerns that cannot be expressed in front of a relative, carer or staff member. Check whether telephone calls, letters or messages could expose the person to retaliation. Use independent communication support where a proposed interpreter may have a conflict of interest.

Record the nature of the concern, its source, the person's own words and any observed injuries, living conditions or financial issues. Distinguish a disclosure, a suspicion and a confirmed finding. Do not wait to conduct your own investigation before acting on a reporting duty. Equally, avoid leading questions or repeated interviewing that may distress the person or compromise another agency's investigation.

## Combine protection with participation

Ask what the person wants to change and what they fear might happen after a report. Assess coercion, dependency and practical barriers alongside decision-making ability. A person may understand a risk yet be unable to obtain food, leave safely or resist somebody controlling their money. Support, reporting and authority to impose an intervention are separate questions.

Agree what information needs sharing, with whom and on what legal basis. Where sharing is required or justified without consent, record the reason and explain it to the person when safe and appropriate. Make a plan for immediate needs, follow-up contact and responsibility between agencies. A referral does not establish that somebody has accepted the concern. Confirm receipt, escalate unresolved danger and review whether the action has improved safety in the person's own terms.

## Apply the local pathway

- Hear the adult safely and identify immediate danger, coercion and practical dependence.
- Identify whether the concern involves family violence, a disability or aged-care provider, another service or crime.
- Use the relevant specialist, police and regulatory routes, checking any mandatory reporting duty.
- Plan safe contact, practical support and follow-up without assuming that a referral authorises coercive action.

## Rights, challenge and review

Explain the appropriate complaint, advocacy or court route for the issue. OPA can provide information about decision-making and rights within its remit. Keep the adult’s wishes and the legal authority for any intervention visible, including where agencies disagree.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: An adult with disability reports financial control by a partner and an unrelated failure by a support provider to deliver personal care.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Assess the family-violence concern and provider failure separately while coordinating safety. Consider the specialist family-violence route and the appropriate provider or NDIS response. Arrange continuity of care and safe contact rather than assuming one agency will handle both matters.

### Common error to avoid

Treating all adult safeguarding as one statutory process or assuming a guardianship referral resolves family violence.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Concern, source, chronology and the adult’s own account
- Immediate safety and a safe communication method
- The local reporting threshold, recipient and timing
- Consent, coercion and information-sharing basis
- Accepted responsibilities, outcomes and follow-up

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [Family Violence Protection Act 2008](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/family-violence-protection-act-2008)
- [The Orange Door](https://www.orangedoor.vic.gov.au/)
- [Office of the Public Advocate](https://www.publicadvocate.vic.gov.au/)

Editorial expansion: 8 September 2026. The sources support the distinctions taught here; check their current text, amendments, commencement and applicable local procedure before operational use. Independent practitioner review has not been recorded.

# Children, Families and Transitions — Victoria — Victoria

Jurisdiction: Victoria
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Victoria practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/australia-victoria/tamariki-rangatahi-and-wh-nau-victoria-victoria.html

# Children, Families and Transitions — Victoria

## Learning outcomes

Separate family support from protection powers, apply the local reporting duty, involve the child and coordinate education, health and transition planning.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

The Children, Youth and Families Act 2005 distinguishes protection grounds and mandatory reporting. The mandatory-reporter categories depend on the role: do not assume every person called a social worker is included solely by title. A social worker may fall within a listed role, such as school counselling or out-of-home care work.

DFFH guidance requires listed reporters who form the relevant reasonable belief in their work to report protection concerns involving physical injury or sexual abuse. Other forms of significant harm may also be reported. The child’s harm and parental protection must be considered; the statutory reporting duty is not identical to every possible wellbeing concern.

## Understand the child’s daily experience

Use age-appropriate communication, observation and accessible material. Ask about ordinary routines, trusted adults, worries, food, sleep, school and relationships. Record the child's words separately from adult interpretations. For a baby or a child who does not use speech, describe interactions and behaviour without claiming to know a view they have not expressed.

Assess harm, strengths and the practical conditions affecting care. Poverty, inaccessible services or overcrowded housing may require material help; they should not automatically be treated as evidence of parental indifference. At the same time, a family's strengths do not remove the need to act on a protection concern. Explore the experience of siblings and whether a proposed protective adult can actually provide the support being described.

## Keep support and compulsory intervention clear

Explain your role, the concern, confidentiality limits and the next step in language the family can understand. Establish the local reporting threshold and receiving authority. A practice model can organise enquiry but cannot determine a statutory threshold or authorise removal. Where you disagree with a decision, identify the evidence and use the relevant escalation process without delaying necessary immediate action.

Plan with education, health, disability and community services, identifying each person's responsibility. For a young person approaching adulthood, address accommodation, income, healthcare, relationships, education or work and decision support before a service ends. Confirm eligibility and acceptance by adult services rather than assuming that a childhood plan transfers automatically. Preserve cultural, family and community relationships in ways consistent with the child's safety and wishes.

## Apply the local pathway

- Check the actual professional or employment category and the applicable reporting duty.
- Report to Child Protection as soon as practicable where the duty is engaged, including new grounds arising later.
- Consider a support referral to The Orange Door where appropriate, without substituting it for a required protection report.
- Check separate police and organisational duties, and plan child participation, cultural support and continuity.

## Rights, challenge and review

Explain the Child Protection process and the child’s and family’s access to support or legal advice. DFFH guidance distinguishes reporting routes from family-support referrals. Advice within an organisation should not delay an applicable personal reporting obligation.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A school counsellor receives a disclosure of physical harm, while a colleague says the family should first be referred for voluntary parenting support.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Check the reasonable-belief and protection conditions and make the required report if met. Assess immediate safety and follow any separate police duty. Parenting support can run alongside the protection response; it does not replace it.

### Common error to avoid

Assuming all social-work job titles create the same reporting duty, or confusing voluntary support with a mandatory report.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Child’s account, communication and daily-life evidence
- Harm, strengths, needs and alternative explanations
- Reporting duty, recipient and action taken
- Family participation, culture and legal authority
- Named plan, education/health links and transition dates

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [DFFH mandatory reporting, updated August 2026](https://providers.dffh.vic.gov.au/mandatory-reporting)
- [Children, Youth and Families Act 2005](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/children-youth-and-families-act-2005)

Editorial expansion: 8 September 2026. The sources support the distinctions taught here; check their current text, amendments, commencement and applicable local procedure before operational use. Independent practitioner review has not been recorded.

# Rights, Culture and Recording — Victoria — Victoria

Jurisdiction: Victoria
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Victoria practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/australia-victoria/rights-culture-and-recording-victoria-victoria.html

# Rights, Culture and Recording — Victoria

## Learning outcomes

Connect rights to an actual service decision, distinguish privacy from absolute secrecy and write a record that makes reasons and disagreement visible.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

The Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006 requires covered public authorities to act compatibly with Charter rights and give proper consideration to relevant rights, subject to statutory exceptions. Identify whether the provider is a public authority for the function involved. A Charter statement should explain the affected rights and reasoning, not simply declare compliance.

The Equal Opportunity Act 2010, Health Records Act 2001 and Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 have different scopes. Commonwealth law may also apply. Determine the organisation and information involved before selecting a privacy or discrimination pathway.

## Make rights practical

Identify the decision affecting the person: access to an assessment, a restriction, a disclosure, an inaccessible meeting or a refusal of support. Ask which right or duty is engaged and which organisation is responsible. A statement that a plan is rights-based does not explain whether the person could participate or how the effect on them was weighed.

Arrange interpretation, accessible formats and communication support suited to the person. Ask about cultural identity, discrimination and the supporters they wish to involve. Do not infer these preferences from appearance, surname or language. Consider whether a seemingly neutral rule disadvantages someone because of disability or another protected characteristic, and what accommodation or adjustment is available under the applicable law.

## Make disclosure and recording accountable

Identify the purpose, recipient and legal basis before sharing personal information. Determine whether the organisation is covered by health, public-sector, private-sector or another confidentiality regime. Consent is not the only possible basis for disclosure, but an organisational request is not a legal basis by itself. Share the information relevant to the permitted purpose and record any limits or objection.

A useful record separates observation, the person's account, information from others, analysis and action. Write what evidence led to the conclusion, which alternatives were considered and why a particular option was chosen. Preserve disagreement respectfully and correct factual errors through the appropriate process. Explain how the person can request access, seek correction, complain or obtain an independent review. Store learning reflections without identifiable case details and use approved systems for professional records.

## Apply the local pathway

- Identify the relevant Charter rights and whether the decision-maker is a covered public authority.
- Consider the actual impact, alternatives and any lawful basis for limiting a right.
- Arrange accessible and culturally safe participation and address applicable equality obligations.
- Check the relevant privacy regime and explain access, correction, complaints and review.

## Rights, challenge and review

The Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission explains Charter duties and discrimination. Privacy and health complaints use their respective bodies and statutory routes. Obtain advice about the remedy for an alleged Charter breach rather than promising that every concern has a standalone Charter claim.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A public service restricts all family visits for administrative convenience without considering a resident’s cultural and family relationships.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Identify the rights affected, the purpose of the restriction and realistic alternatives. Hear the resident and supporters they choose, consider the applicable legal duties and record the reasoning. Review the blanket policy’s effect on the individual rather than relying only on its general wording.

### Common error to avoid

Assuming every private provider has identical Charter duties or that naming rights establishes proper consideration.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Decision, affected rights and responsible organisation
- Accessibility, culture and participation arrangements
- Disclosure purpose, legal basis, recipient and limits
- Evidence, alternatives, reasons and disagreement
- Access, correction, complaints and review route

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [Charter responsibilities of public authorities](https://www.humanrights.vic.gov.au/for-public-sector/charter-responsibilities/charter-and-the-government/)
- [Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/charter-human-rights-and-responsibilities-act-2006)
- [Health Records Act 2001](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/health-records-act-2001)

Editorial expansion: 8 September 2026. The sources support the distinctions taught here; check their current text, amendments, commencement and applicable local procedure before operational use. Independent practitioner review has not been recorded.
