# Quick Reference — Victoria — Victoria

Jurisdiction: Victoria
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Victoria practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/australia-victoria/quick-reference-victoria.html

# Practice reference — Victoria practice guide


Use alongside the full modules and current official sources. Each entry separates the local framework, action and review.


## Professional Foundations — Victoria

The Australian Association of Social Workers (AASW) Code of Ethics and Practice Standards provide a professional framework. AASW membership or accreditation, an employer requirement and statutory authority are different matters. Check the requirements for the actual role and state rather than presenting the professional association as the source of every legal power.

Practice should attend to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples’ self-determination, cultural safety and the effects of colonisation. Ask which community-controlled organisations or cultural supports the person wants involved. Professional values need to be connected to the state law governing the particular intervention.


- Identify the employer, state, service setting and any appointment required for the task.
- Explain the professional role, consent and confidentiality limits before assessment.
- Consider power, racism, disability and material barriers alongside individual and family strengths.
- Use supervision and learning to test the effect of practice on the person, with the current AASW standards as a professional reference.


Distinguish an employer complaint, a professional-association concern and a statutory regulator or tribunal route. The relevant health, disability, aged-care or child-protection body depends on the issue. A professional membership complaint is not an appeal against a state or Commonwealth funding decision.


- [AASW Code of Ethics](https://www.aasw.asn.au/about-aasw/ethics-standards/code-of-ethics/)


## Social Care and Support — Victoria

Disability support through the NDIS, state health and housing services, and Commonwealth aged care have separate entry and funding rules. NDIS access involves age, residence and disability or early-intervention requirements; a diagnosis alone does not establish entitlement to a particular funded support. Check current NDIA rules for the actual application or plan.

The Aged Care Act 2024 and Support at Home commenced on 1 November 2025. Do not describe the old Home Care Package arrangements as the only current system. The Commonwealth Home Support Programme has its own transition arrangements. Contributions and programme rules need a current check, including announced changes with later commencement dates.


- Identify the scheme responsible for each need and the evidence required for its assessment.
- Keep access eligibility, plan funding, provider availability and any client contribution separate.
- Consider state health, housing and community support where a need is outside a particular funded scheme.
- Record the person’s goals, family willingness, actual start dates and the review route for each decision.


For an NDIA decision, identify whether an internal review and subsequent Administrative Review Tribunal route are available and check the decision notice’s time limits. A provider complaint to the NDIS Commission is different from a funding review. Aged-care complaints and assessment reviews use their own routes.


- [NDIS access application and evidence](https://ndis.gov.au/applying/application-process/what-access-request-form)
- [NDIS legislative changes](https://ndis.gov.au/ndis-laws/getting-ndis-back-track/summary-legislation-changes)
- [Current aged-care provider rules and reforms](https://www.health.gov.au/our-work/aged-care-act/resources/providers)
- [CHSP transition arrangements](https://www.health.gov.au/our-work/chsp/reforms)


## Decision-Making and Capacity — Victoria

The Medical Treatment Planning and Decisions Act 2016 governs important medical-consent and advance-care-directive questions. The Guardianship and Administration Act 2019 provides a separate framework for guardianship, administration and supported appointments. Specify whether the decision concerns treatment, personal matters or finances. Medical decision-making capacity concerns understanding the relevant information and effects, retaining it for the decision, considering it when choosing, and conveying the choice and related views or needs by any workable means. Provide practical support first; an apparently unwise choice does not establish incapacity.

An advance care directive can include an instructional directive and a values directive, with different effects. Where the person cannot make the treatment decision, identify the lawful medical treatment decision maker. Their task concerns the decision the person would have made, informed by relevant preferences and values, rather than simply the representative’s preferred outcome.


- Support the person to make the specific decision and assess the relevant decision-making ability.
- Check for a valid, applicable instructional directive and distinguish it from a values statement.
- Identify the medical treatment decision maker under the applicable appointment or hierarchy.
- For a separate personal or financial issue, verify the scope of the relevant guardian, administrator or other arrangement.


The Office of the Public Advocate (OPA) explains healthcare decision-making and routes where no appropriate decision maker is available. VCAT has relevant guardianship and other statutory functions. Disputed authority or treatment requires the route applicable to that decision, not a general family vote.


- [OPA healthcare rights](https://www.publicadvocate.vic.gov.au/your-rights/your-healthcare)
- [Interpreting an instructional directive](https://www.publicadvocate.vic.gov.au/medical-treatment/patient-consent/interpreting-an-instructional-directive)
- [Medical Treatment Planning and Decisions Act 2016](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/medical-treatment-planning-and-decisions-act-2016)
- [Guardianship and Administration Act 2019](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/guardianship-and-administration-act-2019)
- [Patient capacity to consent](https://www.publicadvocate.vic.gov.au/medical-treatment/patient-consent/patient-capacity-to-consent)


## Restrictions and Liberty — Victoria

The Disability Act 2006 and Victorian Senior Practitioner arrangements operate alongside the NDIS restrictive-practices framework where applicable. Authorised Program Officers, the Senior Practitioner, behaviour support practitioners and implementing providers have different responsibilities. A plan is not proof that every necessary authorisation or approval exists.

The Senior Practitioner publishes directions and prohibitions, including a permanent-prohibition notice dated September 2025. Check the current rules for the particular practice and cohort before considering an application. A prohibited practice is not made permissible by including it in a behaviour support plan.


- Identify the actual restriction, setting and whether the disability, mental-health or aged-care framework applies.
- For the disability route, check the Authorised Program Officer and Senior Practitioner requirements and current prohibitions.
- Check NDIS plan, authorisation and incident-reporting requirements separately where they apply.
- Record participation, alternatives, conditions, review and the strategy for reducing the restriction.


OPA, advocacy services and the relevant regulator can assist with concerns within their remits. The person needs a usable way to object and seek the applicable legal or administrative review. A guardian’s agreement does not remove the statutory restrictions on restraint.


- [Victorian Senior Practitioner responsibilities](https://www.dffh.vic.gov.au/about-victorian-senior-practitioner)
- [Current directions and prohibitions](https://www.dffh.vic.gov.au/victorian-senior-practitioners-directions-and-prohibitions)
- [Disability Act 2006](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/disability-act-2006)
- [NDIS implementing-provider rules](https://www.ndiscommission.gov.au/rules-and-standards/behaviour-support-and-restrictive-practices/rules-implementing-providers)


## Mental Health — Victoria

The Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 replaced the 2014 Act. It prefers voluntary assessment and treatment and provides separate assessment orders, temporary treatment orders and Mental Health Tribunal treatment orders. Each stage has its own authorised decision-maker and requirements.

Compulsory treatment criteria include mental illness; immediate treatment needed to prevent serious deterioration in health or serious harm; that treatment being provided if the order is made; and no reasonably available less restrictive means. Evidence that a service is actually available matters. Assessment-order criteria should not be replaced with the treatment-order test.


- Identify the stage, authorised practitioner and exact statutory criteria.
- Record the person’s preferences, available voluntary alternatives and why the proposed order is necessary.
- Check advance statements of preferences, nominated support persons and supported decision-making requirements.
- Separate treatment consent, any statutory treatment authority and additional safeguards for particular interventions.


Explain the statement of rights, non-legal advocacy, second psychiatric opinion and Mental Health Tribunal routes. Current handbook guidance describes their application. A nominated support person assists participation; their role should not be treated as a general substitute-consent appointment.


- [Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/mental-health-and-wellbeing-act-2022)
- [Compulsory assessment and treatment handbook](https://www.health.vic.gov.au/mental-health-and-wellbeing-act-handbook/compulsory-assessment-and-treament)
- [Treatment-order criteria and process](https://www.health.vic.gov.au/mental-health-and-wellbeing-act-handbook/treatments-and-interventions/treatment-orders)

- [Family Violence Protection Act 2008](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/family-violence-protection-act-2008)
- [The Orange Door](https://www.orangedoor.vic.gov.au/)
- [Office of the Public Advocate](https://www.publicadvocate.vic.gov.au/)

```text
Disability support through the NDIS, state health and housing services, and Commonwealth aged care have separate entry and funding rules. NDIS access involves age, residence and disability or early-intervention requirements; a diagnosis alone does not establish entitlement to a particular funded support. Check current NDIA rules for the actual application or plan.

The Aged Care Act 2024 and Support at Home commenced on 1 November 2025. Do not describe the old Home Care Package arrangements as the only current system. The Commonwealth Home Support Programme has its own transition arrangements. Contributions and programme rules need a current check, including announced changes with later commencement dates.

Local pathway:
Identify the scheme responsible for each need and the evidence required for its assessment.
Keep access eligibility, plan funding, provider availability and any client contribution separate.
Consider state health, housing and community support where a need is outside a particular funded scheme.
Record the person’s goals, family willingness, actual start dates and the review route for each decision.

Recording prompts:
1. Daily-life evidence, fluctuation and desired outcomes
Notes:

2. The service, eligibility test and decision-maker
Notes:

3. Carer willingness and separately identified needs
Notes:

4. Funding, charges, decisions and reasons
Notes:

5. Start dates, unmet needs, contingency and challenge route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
For an NDIA decision, identify whether an internal review and subsequent Administrative Review Tribunal route are available and check the decision notice’s time limits. A provider complaint to the NDIS Commission is different from a funding review. Aged-care complaints and assessment reviews use their own routes.

Sources:
https://ndis.gov.au/applying/application-process/what-access-request-form
https://ndis.gov.au/ndis-laws/getting-ndis-back-track/summary-legislation-changes
https://www.health.gov.au/our-work/aged-care-act/resources/providers
https://www.health.gov.au/our-work/chsp/reforms

```

### Decision-Making and Capacity

```text
Decision-Making and Capacity
Victoria practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Medical Treatment Planning and Decisions Act 2016 governs important medical-consent and advance-care-directive questions. The Guardianship and Administration Act 2019 provides a separate framework for guardianship, administration and supported appointments. Specify whether the decision concerns treatment, personal matters or finances. Medical decision-making capacity concerns understanding the relevant information and effects, retaining it for the decision, considering it when choosing, and conveying the choice and related views or needs by any workable means. Provide practical support first; an apparently unwise choice does not establish incapacity.

An advance care directive can include an instructional directive and a values directive, with different effects. Where the person cannot make the treatment decision, identify the lawful medical treatment decision maker. Their task concerns the decision the person would have made, informed by relevant preferences and values, rather than simply the representative’s preferred outcome.

Local pathway:
Support the person to make the specific decision and assess the relevant decision-making ability.
Check for a valid, applicable instructional directive and distinguish it from a values statement.
Identify the medical treatment decision maker under the applicable appointment or hierarchy.
For a separate personal or financial issue, verify the scope of the relevant guardian, administrator or other arrangement.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, options and time at which it is needed
Notes:

2. Communication support and observed responses
Notes:

3. Applicable legal test and evidence for each element
Notes:

4. Representative’s document, scope and decision standard
Notes:

5. Wishes, disagreement, review and any urgent action
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The Office of the Public Advocate (OPA) explains healthcare decision-making and routes where no appropriate decision maker is available. VCAT has relevant guardianship and other statutory functions. Disputed authority or treatment requires the route applicable to that decision, not a general family vote.

Sources:
https://www.publicadvocate.vic.gov.au/your-rights/your-healthcare
https://www.publicadvocate.vic.gov.au/medical-treatment/patient-consent/interpreting-an-instructional-directive
https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/medical-treatment-planning-and-decisions-act-2016
https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/guardianship-and-administration-act-2019
https://www.publicadvocate.vic.gov.au/medical-treatment/patient-consent/patient-capacity-to-consent

```

### Restrictions and Liberty

```text
Restrictions and Liberty
Victoria practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Disability Act 2006 and Victorian Senior Practitioner arrangements operate alongside the NDIS restrictive-practices framework where applicable. Authorised Program Officers, the Senior Practitioner, behaviour support practitioners and implementing providers have different responsibilities. A plan is not proof that every necessary authorisation or approval exists.

The Senior Practitioner publishes directions and prohibitions, including a permanent-prohibition notice dated September 2025. Check the current rules for the particular practice and cohort before considering an application. A prohibited practice is not made permissible by including it in a behaviour support plan.

Local pathway:
Identify the actual restriction, setting and whether the disability, mental-health or aged-care framework applies.
For the disability route, check the Authorised Program Officer and Senior Practitioner requirements and current prohibitions.
Check NDIS plan, authorisation and incident-reporting requirements separately where they apply.
Record participation, alternatives, conditions, review and the strategy for reducing the restriction.

Recording prompts:
1. Each restriction, setting, duration and actual effect
Notes:

2. The person’s wishes, understanding and objections
Notes:

3. Legal authority, decision-maker, limits and conditions
Notes:

4. Alternatives tried and the evidence about necessity
Notes:

5. Representation, review date, expiry and challenge
Notes:

Challenge and review:
OPA, advocacy services and the relevant regulator can assist with concerns within their remits. The person needs a usable way to object and seek the applicable legal or administrative review. A guardian’s agreement does not remove the statutory restrictions on restraint.

Sources:
https://www.dffh.vic.gov.au/about-victorian-senior-practitioner
https://www.dffh.vic.gov.au/victorian-senior-practitioners-directions-and-prohibitions
https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/disability-act-2006
https://www.ndiscommission.gov.au/rules-and-standards/behaviour-support-and-restrictive-practices/rules-implementing-providers

```

### Mental Health

```text
Mental Health
Victoria practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 replaced the 2014 Act. It prefers voluntary assessment and treatment and provides separate assessment orders, temporary treatment orders and Mental Health Tribunal treatment orders. Each stage has its own authorised decision-maker and requirements.

Compulsory treatment criteria include mental illness; immediate treatment needed to prevent serious deterioration in health or serious harm; that treatment being provided if the order is made; and no reasonably available less restrictive means. Evidence that a service is actually available matters. Assessment-order criteria should not be replaced with the treatment-order test.

Local pathway:
Identify the stage, authorised practitioner and exact statutory criteria.
Record the person’s preferences, available voluntary alternatives and why the proposed order is necessary.
Check advance statements of preferences, nominated support persons and supported decision-making requirements.
Separate treatment consent, any statutory treatment authority and additional safeguards for particular interventions.

Recording prompts:
1. Mental and physical health evidence and the person’s account
Notes:

2. The local criteria and voluntary alternatives considered
Notes:

3. Separate authority for transport, admission and treatment
Notes:

4. Required notices, advocacy, representation and review
Notes:

5. Continuity, discharge responsibilities and crisis plan
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain the statement of rights, non-legal advocacy, second psychiatric opinion and Mental Health Tribunal routes. Current handbook guidance describes their application. A nominated support person assists participation; their role should not be treated as a general substitute-consent appointment.

Sources:
https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/mental-health-and-wellbeing-act-2022
https://www.health.vic.gov.au/mental-health-and-wellbeing-act-handbook/compulsory-assessment-and-treament
https://www.health.vic.gov.au/mental-health-and-wellbeing-act-handbook/treatments-and-interventions/treatment-orders

```

### Adult Safeguarding

```text
Adult Safeguarding
Victoria practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Adult concerns may require family-violence services, police, OPA, disability safeguards, aged-care oversight or a provider complaint. Identify the relationship and service setting before selecting a route. The Family Violence Protection Act 2008 is relevant to violence and abuse within its defined relationships; not every adult concern is governed by that framework.

The Orange Door provides access to family-violence and family-support services. NDIS and aged-care providers have their own incident and regulatory obligations. A referral for support, a reportable incident and an application for a protective order are different actions.

Local pathway:
Hear the adult safely and identify immediate danger, coercion and practical dependence.
Identify whether the concern involves family violence, a disability or aged-care provider, another service or crime.
Use the relevant specialist, police and regulatory routes, checking any mandatory reporting duty.
Plan safe contact, practical support and follow-up without assuming that a referral authorises coercive action.

Recording prompts:
1. Concern, source, chronology and the adult’s own account
Notes:

2. Immediate safety and a safe communication method
Notes:

3. The local reporting threshold, recipient and timing
Notes:

4. Consent, coercion and information-sharing basis
Notes:

5. Accepted responsibilities, outcomes and follow-up
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain the appropriate complaint, advocacy or court route for the issue. OPA can provide information about decision-making and rights within its remit. Keep the adult’s wishes and the legal authority for any intervention visible, including where agencies disagree.

Sources:
https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/family-violence-protection-act-2008
https://www.orangedoor.vic.gov.au/
https://www.publicadvocate.vic.gov.au/

```

### Children, Families and Transitions

```text
Children, Families and Transitions
Victoria practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Children, Youth and Families Act 2005 distinguishes protection grounds and mandatory reporting. The mandatory-reporter categories depend on the role: do not assume every person called a social worker is included solely by title. A social worker may fall within a listed role, such as school counselling or out-of-home care work.

DFFH guidance requires listed reporters who form the relevant reasonable belief in their work to report protection concerns involving physical injury or sexual abuse. Other forms of significant harm may also be reported. The child’s harm and parental protection must be considered; the statutory reporting duty is not identical to every possible wellbeing concern.

Local pathway:
Check the actual professional or employment category and the applicable reporting duty.
Report to Child Protection as soon as practicable where the duty is engaged, including new grounds arising later.
Consider a support referral to The Orange Door where appropriate, without substituting it for a required protection report.
Check separate police and organisational duties, and plan child participation, cultural support and continuity.

Recording prompts:
1. Child’s account, communication and daily-life evidence
Notes:

2. Harm, strengths, needs and alternative explanations
Notes:

3. Reporting duty, recipient and action taken
Notes:

4. Family participation, culture and legal authority
Notes:

5. Named plan, education/health links and transition dates
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain the Child Protection process and the child’s and family’s access to support or legal advice. DFFH guidance distinguishes reporting routes from family-support referrals. Advice within an organisation should not delay an applicable personal reporting obligation.

Sources:
https://providers.dffh.vic.gov.au/mandatory-reporting
https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/children-youth-and-families-act-2005

```

### Rights, Culture and Recording

```text
Rights, Culture and Recording
Victoria practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006 requires covered public authorities to act compatibly with Charter rights and give proper consideration to relevant rights, subject to statutory exceptions. Identify whether the provider is a public authority for the function involved. A Charter statement should explain the affected rights and reasoning, not simply declare compliance.

The Equal Opportunity Act 2010, Health Records Act 2001 and Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 have different scopes. Commonwealth law may also apply. Determine the organisation and information involved before selecting a privacy or discrimination pathway.

Local pathway:
Identify the relevant Charter rights and whether the decision-maker is a covered public authority.
Consider the actual impact, alternatives and any lawful basis for limiting a right.
Arrange accessible and culturally safe participation and address applicable equality obligations.
Check the relevant privacy regime and explain access, correction, complaints and review.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, affected rights and responsible organisation
Notes:

2. Accessibility, culture and participation arrangements
Notes:

3. Disclosure purpose, legal basis, recipient and limits
Notes:

4. Evidence, alternatives, reasons and disagreement
Notes:

5. Access, correction, complaints and review route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission explains Charter duties and discrimination. Privacy and health complaints use their respective bodies and statutory routes. Obtain advice about the remedy for an alleged Charter breach rather than promising that every concern has a standalone Charter claim.

Sources:
https://www.humanrights.vic.gov.au/for-public-sector/charter-responsibilities/charter-and-the-government/
https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/charter-human-rights-and-responsibilities-act-2006
https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/health-records-act-2001

```

# Practice Scenarios — Victoria — Victoria

Jurisdiction: Victoria
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Victoria practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/australia-victoria/practice-scenarios-victoria.html

# Scenario Workouts — Victoria practice guide


All cases are fictional learning exercises. Explain your evidence and reasoning before reading the discussion.


## Professional Foundations — Victoria

A practitioner is asked to sign a statutory assessment because they hold an AASW credential, without checking the specific appointment requirements.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Read the law and service procedure governing that assessment. Confirm qualifications, appointment and scope before signing. Bring any gap to the responsible manager and arrange an authorised practitioner while continuing work that is within your role.


## Social Care and Support — Victoria

A person is told that their NDIS plan should pay for every need after a hospital admission, including treatment and unsuitable housing.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Map the actual support sought and the responsibility of each system. Obtain the relevant decisions and coordinate health, housing and disability support. Record unmet needs and interim arrangements rather than presenting an unfunded referral as a completed plan.


## Decision-Making and Capacity — Victoria

A person’s advance directive refuses a particular treatment, but a relative asks the team to ignore it because they believe treatment would help.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Check validity, applicability and whether the statement is an instructional or values directive. Involve the responsible clinician and obtain advice where the position is disputed. Do not substitute the relative’s preference for the legal effect of the document or the person’s own decision.


## Restrictions and Liberty — Victoria

A provider proposes a restraint copied from an old plan and assumes approval can be renewed without checking current directions.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Check whether the practice is now prohibited and whether the previous approval is relevant to the present circumstances. Assess alternatives and consult the responsible practitioner. Do not apply an obsolete approval to a new plan or bypass the Senior Practitioner’s requirements.


## Mental Health — Victoria

A person is considered for a treatment order, but the proposed immediate treatment has not been arranged and a community alternative has not been explored.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Check all criteria, including that treatment will be provided and whether a less restrictive means is reasonably available. Obtain the person’s preferences and supports. The existence of illness and concern about deterioration alone does not explain the whole order decision.


## Adult Safeguarding — Victoria

An adult with disability reports financial control by a partner and an unrelated failure by a support provider to deliver personal care.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Assess the family-violence concern and provider failure separately while coordinating safety. Consider the specialist family-violence route and the appropriate provider or NDIS response. Arrange continuity of care and safe contact rather than assuming one agency will handle both matters.


## Children, Families and Transitions — Victoria

A school counsellor receives a disclosure of physical harm, while a colleague says the family should first be referred for voluntary parenting support.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Check the reasonable-belief and protection conditions and make the required report if met. Assess immediate safety and follow any separate police duty. Parenting support can run alongside the protection response; it does not replace it.


## Rights, Culture and Recording — Victoria

A public service restricts all family visits for administrative convenience without considering a resident’s cultural and family relationships.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Identify the rights affected, the purpose of the restriction and realistic alternatives. Hear the resident and supporters they choose, consider the applicable legal duties and record the reasoning. Review the blanket policy’s effect on the individual rather than relying only on its general wording.

# About Us — Victoria

## About this resource

Daily Mindset Moments CIC, founded by Raymond Hill, provides this structured social-work learning resource. It supports students, practitioners and supervisors with modules, fictional exercises, source links and private reflections.

## Victoria context

This guide separates the learning material for Victoria from the other practice locations. Shared theories support enquiry; laws, professional requirements and service pathways must be checked locally. Read the source library for scope and editorial status.

Jurisdiction: Victoria

# Privacy Policy — Victoria

## Learning stored on your device

The app stores your selected location, reading progress, confidence, saved reflections and unfinished reflection fields in this browser. Records are separated by location. They are not submitted to a professional body. Export or print a copy before clearing browser data or changing devices.

## Website enquiries

If you use the contact form, the details you submit are sent to the website’s form service and operator. Do not send confidential case information. External source websites have their own privacy policies.

## Your records

Use Delete reflection to remove saved entries. Clearing this site’s browser storage removes local progress and notes. Contact [Daily Mindset Moments CIC](mailto:info@daily-mindset-moments.com) about information sent through an enquiry.

# Terms of Service — Victoria

## Purpose and scope

The Victoria guide is an educational resource for learning and supervision. It does not provide individual legal advice, determine a case outcome or certify professional competence. Use current official sources and the procedures applicable to your role.

## Responsible use

Practice scenarios are fictional. Downloads are learning prompts, not statutory forms. Do not enter identifiable case details into reflections or enquiries. Your browser stores local notes; export your own copy if you need a durable record.

## Sources and corrections

External sources may change. The source library records editorial scope; inclusion of a link or model does not imply endorsement by its publisher. Send corrections with the relevant source and section title through the contact route.

# Start Here — British Columbia

## Your British Columbia learning guide

Use the location selector to choose among twelve separate guides. Your reading progress, confidence and reflections are stored separately for each location.

## Start learning

Read [Professional Foundations](/?jurisdiction=canada-british-columbia&resource=foundations#learningWorkspace), choose a topic from [Learning Map](/?jurisdiction=canada-british-columbia&resource=map#learningWorkspace), then practise with [Practice Scenarios](/?jurisdiction=canada-british-columbia&resource=scenarios#learningWorkspace). Test recall with flashcards and use the reflection log to identify a specific next action.

## Scope

Eight modules, forty flashcards, a glossary, eight fictional scenarios and ten recording prompts support revision and supervision. This is a final learning-guide release. It is not an exhaustive account of law, a statutory form or a regulator-approved training programme. The source library explains how to check the applicable version and local route.

# Learning Map — British Columbia — British Columbia

Jurisdiction: British Columbia
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent British Columbia practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/canada-british-columbia/learning-map-british-columbia.html

# Learning Map — British Columbia

## A sequence for study

1. [Professional Foundations](/?jurisdiction=canada-british-columbia&resource=foundations#learningWorkspace): Professional role, ethics, competence, supervision and accountable decisions.
2. [Social Care and Support](/?jurisdiction=canada-british-columbia&resource=care-support#learningWorkspace): Needs, strengths, access to support, family responsibilities and service planning.
3. [Decision-Making and Capacity](/?jurisdiction=canada-british-columbia&resource=mca#learningWorkspace): Decision support, consent and the authority for someone else to decide.
4. [Restrictions and Liberty](/?jurisdiction=canada-british-columbia&resource=dols#learningWorkspace): Restrictions, legal authority, less restrictive options and review.
5. [Mental Health](/?jurisdiction=canada-british-columbia&resource=mha#learningWorkspace): Mental-health support, crisis response, treatment and rights.
6. [Adult Safeguarding](/?jurisdiction=canada-british-columbia&resource=safeguarding#learningWorkspace): Abuse, neglect, coercion, safe enquiry and the appropriate protective response.
7. [Children, Families and Transitions](/?jurisdiction=canada-british-columbia&resource=children#learningWorkspace): Child participation, family support, child protection and transitions.
8. [Rights, Culture and Recording](/?jurisdiction=canada-british-columbia&resource=rights#learningWorkspace): Participation, privacy, cultural safety and clear recording.

## Put learning into practice

Choose one fictional scenario. Record what is known, the person’s perspective and what still needs checking. Open the source library before answering a legal question. Use supervision to test alternative explanations and a reflection to record the next action.

# Case Route Finder — British Columbia — British Columbia

Jurisdiction: British Columbia
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent British Columbia practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/canada-british-columbia/case-route-finder-british-columbia.html

# Case Route Finder — British Columbia

## Use the route finder

Select the concerns that fit a fictional case. More than one framework may be relevant. Open each suggested module and its sources; the tool selects learning topics and does not decide a legal threshold.

## Compare the routes

Separate support needs, decision-making, mental-health intervention, protective reporting and restrictions. Record the question each route answers, the source you checked and who needs to provide further advice.


## Route questions

### Care or carer support needs

Which needs and outcomes belong to the person and to carers?

Contact the appropriate health-authority home and community care service for eligibility and needs assessment. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### A decision-specific capacity question

What is the precise decision and why is ability to decide questioned?

Support the adult’s own decision and apply the relevant statutory incapability test. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Restrictions or liberty concerns

What restrictions actually operate and how do they affect the person?

Describe the restriction, who enforces it and the adult’s wishes or objections. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Mental health support or compulsion questions

What is the purpose of each proposed intervention?

Identify the route and evidence for each applicable criterion, including voluntary alternatives. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Abuse, neglect or safeguarding concerns

How can the person be heard safely and privately?

Identify the alleged harm and why the adult may be unable to seek assistance themselves. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### A child, young carer or transition issue

What does the child say or show about safety and daily life?

Identify the concern and the child’s age, using the CFCSA reporting threshold. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Language, participation or recording concerns

What makes participation accessible for this person?

Identify the service decision, relevant right and responsible organisation. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Professional learning or supervision

What is the purpose and limit of your role?

Confirm the practitioner’s role, regulatory position and any specific statutory designation. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

# Learning Flashcards — British Columbia — British Columbia

Jurisdiction: British Columbia
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent British Columbia practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/canada-british-columbia/learning-flashcards-british-columbia.html

# Learning Flashcards — British Columbia practice guide


Answer before revealing the response in the interactive workspace. These cards accompany the full local modules.


## Professional Foundations — British Columbia


### Which local framework anchors this topic in British Columbia practice guide?

The British Columbia College of Social Workers (BCCSW) Code of Ethics and Standards of Practice and the Social Workers Act provide the professional framework. Check the registration category, scope and any applicable statutory exemption or special role; a job title alone does not explain a practitioner’s regulatory position.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

Health authorities, Community Living BC (CLBC), child and family services, Indigenous authorities and community organisations have different remits. Identify the organisation exercising the function and the law governing it. Cultural safety includes attention to Indigenous self-determination, racism and the person’s chosen community relationships.


### What are the key local actions?

Confirm the practitioner’s role, regulatory position and any specific statutory designation. Explain the purpose of involvement, participation and confidentiality limits. Map the responsible health, community, child-service or Indigenous authority rather than treating all services as one system. Use supervision and continuing learning to test evidence, bias and the practical effect of decisions.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

Distinguish a BCCSW professional complaint from a health-authority, service, privacy or statutory decision review. Help the person identify which body can address the action or remedy in question.


### What common error should you avoid?

Assuming every social-work role has identical registration requirements or investigative powers.


## Social Care and Support — British Columbia


### Which local framework anchors this topic in British Columbia practice guide?

Publicly subsidised home and community care involves health-authority assessment, general eligibility and service-specific criteria. Provincial guidance addresses status, residence, age and health-related need, with exceptions to some general conditions. Do not convert a general criterion into an absolute exclusion without checking those exceptions.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

Home support, long-term care, assisted living, CLBC supports and income assistance are different programmes. Needs assessment, access priority, client contribution and actual provision must be distinguished. The responsible office should explain which programme and policy support the decision.


### What are the key local actions?

Contact the appropriate health-authority home and community care service for eligibility and needs assessment. Check general and service-specific criteria, including any relevant exception. Record assessed needs, family willingness, priority, costs and when support will actually begin. Obtain reasons and the applicable health-authority review or complaint process if access or service levels are disputed.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

Provincial guidance distinguishes complaints about care from appeals of home and community care service decisions. Use the current health-authority process and decision notice. A provider complaint will not necessarily review a funding or eligibility decision.


### What common error should you avoid?

Applying general eligibility criteria without checking exceptions or treating an assessment as guaranteed service delivery.


## Decision-Making and Capacity — British Columbia


### Which local framework anchors this topic in British Columbia practice guide?

The Health Care (Consent) and Care Facility (Admission) Act has separate health-care and facility-admission provisions. The Representation Agreement Act and Patients Property Act provide other forms of authority. Identify the decision and the relevant document before deciding which route applies. For healthcare, the provider assesses whether the adult understands the relevant treatment information and its application to their own situation. Adapt communication to the adult’s abilities; a communication difference alone does not establish incapability.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

Where temporary substitute consent for healthcare is needed, the healthcare provider selects the first available qualified person in the statutory list. The person’s prior capable instructions or wishes and the Act’s decision standard matter. An available relative is not automatically entitled to displace an authorised representative or another person with priority.


### What are the key local actions?

Support the adult’s own decision and apply the relevant statutory incapability test. Check any advance directive, representation agreement or committee order and its scope. Where the temporary substitute route applies, use the statutory priority and qualification requirements. Separate healthcare consent from admission and from personal or financial decisions under another framework.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

The Public Guardian and Trustee has relevant functions when a suitable substitute is unavailable or authority is disputed. Court or other statutory review may be needed depending on the issue. Explain the specific route and preserve the adult’s participation.


### What common error should you avoid?

Using the temporary substitute list without checking an existing representative, or treating an agreement as unlimited authority.


## Restrictions and Liberty — British Columbia


### Which local framework anchors this topic in British Columbia practice guide?

Care-facility admission consent, treatment consent and authority for restraint or detention are distinct. The Health Care (Consent) and Care Facility (Admission) Act, facility licensing rules and Mental Health Act may apply in different circumstances. Read the actual measure and legal setting rather than treating admission as permission for every restriction.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

Part 3 of the Adult Guardianship Act includes limited protective and emergency powers for designated agencies in defined circumstances. Those powers are not a general standing authority for a provider to confine an adult. The least intrusive response and the person’s wishes remain central to the assessment.


### What are the key local actions?

Describe the restriction, who enforces it and the adult’s wishes or objections. Identify the applicable facility, mental-health or designated-agency framework and the precise authority. Check any order, emergency condition, monitoring duty and limit on duration or scope. Explore alternatives and arrange the relevant independent support, complaint or legal review.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

Mental-health detention has review-panel and court routes; other disputed restrictions may require different legal advice or service-regulation responses. A healthcare substitute or a family member cannot be assumed to authorise every liberty restriction.


### What common error should you avoid?

Treating a protection referral or admission consent as authority for ongoing confinement.


## Mental Health — British Columbia


### Which local framework anchors this topic in British Columbia practice guide?

The Mental Health Act provides involuntary admission through medical certification and other defined routes. Section 22 addresses mental disorder requiring treatment, need for treatment in or through a designated facility, need for care, supervision and control to prevent substantial deterioration or protect the person or others, and inability to be suitably admitted voluntarily.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

The statutory framework includes treatment authority for detained patients, which differs from ordinary substitute-consent healthcare. Do not import another province’s treatment-consent rule. The person’s status, required certificates and the particular treatment must all be checked.


### What are the key local actions?

Identify the route and evidence for each applicable criterion, including voluntary alternatives. Check certificates, dates, notices and renewal or review requirements. Identify the legal basis for psychiatric treatment and distinguish unrelated healthcare decisions. Arrange rights advice, access to a review panel or court process and the applicable second-opinion route.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

The Act includes rights advice, notice, review panels, court discharge applications and a second-medical-opinion provision. These mechanisms address different questions. Explain the route that fits the person’s concern rather than presenting a treatment complaint as identical to detention review.


### What common error should you avoid?

Reducing certification to immediate dangerousness alone or importing another province’s consent rules.


## Adult Safeguarding — British Columbia


### Which local framework anchors this topic in British Columbia practice guide?

Part 3 of the Adult Guardianship Act concerns abuse, neglect or self-neglect where an adult cannot seek support and assistance because of the specified restraint, disability, illness, injury or decision-related conditions. Designated agencies must look into relevant reports. The statutory threshold and agency role should be stated explicitly.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

Designated agencies include regional health bodies and, within defined remits, CLBC and Providence Health Care. The Public Guardian and Trustee has different functions. An adult need not already be a service user for a relevant concern to be considered.


### What are the key local actions?

Identify the alleged harm and why the adult may be unable to seek assistance themselves. Refer to the designated agency appropriate to the person and setting. Arrange immediate safety and consider police or other statutory duties where needed. Separate voluntary support, investigation, emergency action and a court-backed support-and-assistance plan.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

Preserve the adult’s participation and use the Act’s principles concerning autonomy and effective, least intrusive support. A designated-agency investigation is not the same as appointing a substitute decision-maker. Obtain advice where an imposed plan or emergency power is proposed.


### What common error should you avoid?

Treating decisional incapability as the only reason an adult may qualify for assistance.


## Children, Families and Transitions — British Columbia


### Which local framework anchors this topic in British Columbia practice guide?

The Child, Family and Community Service Act (CFCSA) defines a child as a person under 19 and creates a duty to report where its protection conditions are engaged. Do not apply another province’s age boundary. A report should reach the appropriate child-protection authority; telling a supervisor alone is insufficient.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

Indigenous child and family service laws may apply, with provincial guidance explaining referral to an Indigenous authority where relevant. Establish the child’s legal and service context rather than assuming the provincial process is the only possible authority.


### What are the key local actions?

Identify the concern and the child’s age, using the CFCSA reporting threshold. Make the report through the appropriate provincial or Indigenous-authority arrangements and address immediate danger. Record the child’s words, evidence, cultural relationships and actions taken. Coordinate support and participation while distinguishing a report, investigation, agreement and court measure.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

Explain who is responding and how the child and family can obtain advocacy, legal advice or a complaint review. Respect the applicable Indigenous jurisdiction and do not delay an urgent safety report while assuming that another organisation will act.


### What common error should you avoid?

Using another province’s reporting age or assuming that every Indigenous child’s case follows an identical provincial route.


## Rights, Culture and Recording — British Columbia


### Which local framework anchors this topic in British Columbia practice guide?

The BC Human Rights Code applies to discrimination in its covered areas, while the Canadian Charter has a distinct scope. Indigenous rights and applicable Indigenous laws must be considered in the actual function, alongside professional cultural-safety responsibilities.


### Which distinction must be kept clear?

The Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act (FIPPA) generally concerns public bodies, while the Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA) governs covered private organisations. Determine the organisation’s legal status and the information involved before applying collection, disclosure or access rules.


### What are the key local actions?

Identify the service decision, relevant right and responsible organisation. Consider accommodation, language, cultural safety and the person’s chosen supports. Check whether FIPPA, PIPA or another specific rule applies to the record and disclosure. Record the lawful purpose, necessary information, reasons and the access, correction or complaint route.


### How can the person participate or challenge the decision?

The Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner for BC addresses matters within FIPPA and PIPA; the Human Rights Tribunal addresses Code complaints. Professional and service complaints are separate. Help the person select the route that can address their concern.


### What common error should you avoid?

Assuming public-body and private-organisation privacy rules are interchangeable.

### Restrictions and Liberty

Describe the restriction, who enforces it and the adult’s wishes or objections. Work through the fictional case and explain: Treating a protection referral or admission consent as authority for ongoing confinement.

### Mental Health

Identify the route and evidence for each applicable criterion, including voluntary alternatives. Work through the fictional case and explain: Reducing certification to immediate dangerousness alone or importing another province’s consent rules.

### Adult Safeguarding

Identify the alleged harm and why the adult may be unable to seek assistance themselves. Work through the fictional case and explain: Treating decisional incapability as the only reason an adult may qualify for assistance.

### Children, Families and Transitions

Identify the concern and the child’s age, using the CFCSA reporting threshold. Work through the fictional case and explain: Using another province’s reporting age or assuming that every Indigenous child’s case follows an identical provincial route.

### Rights, Culture and Recording

Identify the service decision, relevant right and responsible organisation. Work through the fictional case and explain: Assuming public-body and private-organisation privacy rules are interchangeable.

# Practice Glossary — British Columbia practice guide

Use each definition with its linked full lesson and official sources.

## Professional Foundations

The British Columbia College of Social Workers (BCCSW) Code of Ethics and Standards of Practice and the Social Workers Act provide the professional framework. Check the registration category, scope and any applicable statutory exemption or special role; a job title alone does not explain a practitioner’s regulatory position.

## Social Care and Support

Publicly subsidised home and community care involves health-authority assessment, general eligibility and service-specific criteria. Provincial guidance addresses status, residence, age and health-related need, with exceptions to some general conditions. Do not convert a general criterion into an absolute exclusion without checking those exceptions.

## Decision-Making and Capacity

The Health Care (Consent) and Care Facility (Admission) Act has separate health-care and facility-admission provisions. The Representation Agreement Act and Patients Property Act provide other forms of authority. Identify the decision and the relevant document before deciding which route applies. For healthcare, the provider assesses whether the adult understands the relevant treatment information and its application to their own situation. Adapt communication to the adult’s abilities; a communication difference alone does not establish incapability.

## Restrictions and Liberty

Care-facility admission consent, treatment consent and authority for restraint or detention are distinct. The Health Care (Consent) and Care Facility (Admission) Act, facility licensing rules and Mental Health Act may apply in different circumstances. Read the actual measure and legal setting rather than treating admission as permission for every restriction.

## Mental Health

The Mental Health Act provides involuntary admission through medical certification and other defined routes. Section 22 addresses mental disorder requiring treatment, need for treatment in or through a designated facility, need for care, supervision and control to prevent substantial deterioration or protect the person or others, and inability to be suitably admitted voluntarily.

## Adult Safeguarding

Part 3 of the Adult Guardianship Act concerns abuse, neglect or self-neglect where an adult cannot seek support and assistance because of the specified restraint, disability, illness, injury or decision-related conditions. Designated agencies must look into relevant reports. The statutory threshold and agency role should be stated explicitly.

## Children, Families and Transitions

The Child, Family and Community Service Act (CFCSA) defines a child as a person under 19 and creates a duty to report where its protection conditions are engaged. Do not apply another province’s age boundary. A report should reach the appropriate child-protection authority; telling a supervisor alone is insufficient.

## Rights, Culture and Recording

The BC Human Rights Code applies to discrimination in its covered areas, while the Canadian Charter has a distinct scope. Indigenous rights and applicable Indigenous laws must be considered in the actual function, alongside professional cultural-safety responsibilities.

## British Columbia College of Social Workers (BCCSW)

The professional body identified for this guide. Check its remit and the requirements that apply to your role.

## Advocacy

Support to express views, understand choices and participate; statutory entitlements depend on the local framework.

## CPD

Continuing professional development: learning, reflection and evidence of improvement.

## Consent

Agreement to a specific action; check the applicable requirements for information, voluntariness and ability to consent.

## Coercion

Pressure or control that can affect expressed wishes and freedom to act.

## Eligibility

The criteria for a particular service or programme; distinct from a description of need.

## Capacity

Ability to make the relevant decision under the applicable legal framework; avoid a global label.

## Representative

Someone with a defined support or decision-making role; verify the source and scope of authority.

## Proportionality

A reasoned comparison of intended benefit, burdens, rights and alternatives.

## Cultural safety

Attention to power, identity and the person’s experience of a service, informed by their preferences.

## Data minimisation

Using or sharing only information needed for an identified lawful purpose.

## Confidentiality

Protecting information while understanding and explaining lawful exceptions.

## Safeguarding referral

Communicating a concern to the appropriate agency; confirm the applicable route and follow-up.

## Professional supervision

Structured discussion of decisions, ethics, skills, wellbeing and accountability.

## Formulation

A reasoned account connecting evidence and possible explanations to a plan.

## Family network

Relationships that may offer support; availability, safety and willingness need assessment.

## Transition

Planned change between services or life stages, with continuity and named responsibilities.

## Contingency

An agreed response if risks increase or the preferred plan cannot operate.

## Review

A planned check of outcomes, changing circumstances and whether actions remain appropriate.

## Least restrictive option

An option that can achieve the purpose with less interference in rights and freedom.

# Theory Into Practice — British Columbia — British Columbia

Jurisdiction: British Columbia
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent British Columbia practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/canada-british-columbia/theory-into-practice-british-columbia-british-columbia.html

# Theory Into Practice — British Columbia

## Build a testable explanation

Use the theory finder to generate alternative explanations for a fictional case. Compare what each lens notices about relationships, environment, power, trauma and strengths. Record evidence that would support or challenge your explanation.

## Use models thoughtfully

Theories are shared learning lenses, not country-specific statutory rules. Their inclusion does not imply official adoption in British Columbia. Check suitability, training requirements, cultural context and the person’s account before applying a method.


## Interactive theory lenses

### Ecological Systems Theory

Person, family, housing, community, services, poverty, policy, culture, and environment.

Hypothesis: The presenting issue may be shaped by pressures around the person, not only by individual behaviour or choice.

- What changed in the environment before the concern escalated?
- Which systems are supporting the person, and which are adding pressure?
- Would risk reduce if housing, income, access, care, or community support changed?

### Strengths-Based Practice

Capabilities, identity, relationships, community, culture, hope, and what is already working.

Hypothesis: The person may have protective strategies or relationships that are hidden by a risk-heavy professional account.

- What has helped the person survive or cope so far?
- Who does the person trust, and what role could they safely play?
- Which strengths are real evidence, and which are optimistic assumptions?

### Trauma-Informed Practice

Safety, trust, choice, collaboration, empowerment, shame, threat responses, and control.

Hypothesis: Behaviour that looks like refusal, avoidance, anger, or disengagement may be a survival response to trauma, coercion, loss, or fear.

- What might feel unsafe or controlling from the person's perspective?
- What helps the person feel more choice and predictability?
- How can we avoid repeating patterns of powerlessness?

### Attachment Theory

Trust, separation, dependency, rejection, fear, care-seeking, and relationship patterns.

Hypothesis: Responses to professionals or carers may reflect previous experiences of care, loss, abandonment, or unsafe relationships.

- How does the person respond when support increases, reduces, or changes?
- Are there patterns of clinging, pushing away, testing, mistrust, or fear?
- What relationship approach is consistent, boundaried, and safe?

### Systems and Family Theory

Roles, rules, communication, repeated patterns, conflict, care dynamics, and network effects.

Hypothesis: The concern may be maintained by relationship patterns, family roles, service responses, or network conflict.

- Who gains or loses if the current pattern changes?
- What role has each person been placed in or taken on?
- How do professional responses affect the family or network pattern?

### Anti-Oppressive and Anti-Discriminatory Practice

Power, oppression, racism, disability, class, gender, sexuality, culture, age, stigma, and access.

Hypothesis: The presenting issue may be intensified by structural inequality, professional power, discrimination, or inaccessible services.

- What barriers has the person faced before we became involved?
- Whose account is being treated as most credible, and why?
- What reasonable adjustments, cultural humility, or advocacy are needed?

### Crisis Theory

Immediate stress, narrowed options, temporary disequilibrium, coping capacity, and stabilisation.

Hypothesis: The person or family may be temporarily overwhelmed and need stabilisation before longer-term planning is realistic.

- What immediate event or loss has exceeded usual coping?
- What needs to happen in the next 24 to 72 hours?
- What can wait until safety, sleep, food, medication, or support is more stable?

### Life Course Theory

Transitions, cumulative disadvantage, ageing, identity, loss, timing, and turning points.

Hypothesis: Current risk or distress may connect to earlier life events, cumulative exclusion, transition, bereavement, or changing identity.

- What transitions or losses are happening now?
- How has cumulative disadvantage shaped options and trust?
- What strengths, relationships, or identities from earlier life still matter?

### Task-Centred Practice

Specific problems, agreed goals, small steps, roles, review, and measurable change.

Hypothesis: The person may benefit from breaking an overwhelming issue into concrete, negotiated tasks with clear review.

- What problem does the person most want to work on first?
- What is the smallest useful next step?
- Who will do what, by when, and how will we know it helped?

### Signs of Wellbeing, Success, and Belonging

Family support, children in care, permanency, reunification, stability, identity, and belonging work.

### Contextual Safeguarding

Extra-familial harm, exploitation, peer group risk, school, neighbourhood, online spaces, and adolescent safeguarding.

Children affected by trauma, attachment disruption, care experience, shame, mistrust, and blocked trust.

Domestic abuse-informed child welfare, perpetrator pattern mapping, protective parent strengths, and child impact.

Neglect assessment, evidence-based care mapping, physical care, safety, love and esteem, and developmental care.

### Restorative Practice

Repair, accountability, family meetings, school relationships, conflict, shame, and shared problem-solving.

# Professional Foundations — British Columbia — British Columbia

Jurisdiction: British Columbia
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent British Columbia practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/canada-british-columbia/professional-foundations-british-columbia.html

# Professional Foundations — British Columbia

## Learning outcomes

Explain your professional role, distinguish an ethical concern from a statutory power, and turn a formulation into an accountable plan.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

The British Columbia College of Social Workers (BCCSW) Code of Ethics and Standards of Practice and the Social Workers Act provide the professional framework. Check the registration category, scope and any applicable statutory exemption or special role; a job title alone does not explain a practitioner’s regulatory position.

Health authorities, Community Living BC (CLBC), child and family services, Indigenous authorities and community organisations have different remits. Identify the organisation exercising the function and the law governing it. Cultural safety includes attention to Indigenous self-determination, racism and the person’s chosen community relationships.

## From information to a professional formulation

A chronology says what happened. A formulation explains how the available evidence, the person's experience and their environment might connect. Start with the person's desired change. Map relationships, housing, income, health, discrimination and service barriers alongside individual strengths. A missed appointment may reflect fear, inaccessible transport or an unsafe household; it does not establish unwillingness to engage.

Use at least two possible explanations for a difficult situation. State what evidence supports each and what would challenge it. A strengths approach should identify actual resources the person can use, with their agreement. It should not turn an absent service into an assumed family responsibility. A trauma-informed conversation offers predictability, choice and control over pace while keeping necessary enquiries clear.

## Boundaries and supervision

Explain who employs you, the purpose of contact, how information will be used and the limits of confidentiality. Separate an invitation to accept support from an action the law permits without agreement. Ask for supervision when an instruction conflicts with professional duties or exceeds your authority. Record the issue, advice, action and unresolved concern; merely recording that a manager agreed does not explain the decision.

For a learning reflection, choose one decision you influenced. Describe what the person said, your initial assumption, what changed your understanding and what you will do differently. Seek feedback about the effect on the person, rather than counting training attendance as evidence of improved practice.

## Apply the local pathway

- Confirm the practitioner’s role, regulatory position and any specific statutory designation.
- Explain the purpose of involvement, participation and confidentiality limits.
- Map the responsible health, community, child-service or Indigenous authority rather than treating all services as one system.
- Use supervision and continuing learning to test evidence, bias and the practical effect of decisions.

## Rights, challenge and review

Distinguish a BCCSW professional complaint from a health-authority, service, privacy or statutory decision review. Help the person identify which body can address the action or remedy in question.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A worker assumes that employment by a health authority automatically gives them the powers of a designated adult-protection investigator.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Check the organisation’s designation and the worker’s actual role, authority and procedure. Gather relevant social evidence within scope and arrange the appropriate designated-agency response. Employment and statutory investigative authority should not be conflated.

### Common error to avoid

Assuming every social-work role has identical registration requirements or investigative powers.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Your role and the legal or professional framework
- The person’s outcomes and communication preferences
- Evidence, competing explanations and missing perspectives
- Power, boundaries and any conflict of interest
- Agreed action, supervision, feedback and review

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [BCCSW Standards and Scope of Practice](https://bccsw.ca/for-registrants/standards-scope-of-practice/)
- [Social Workers Act](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/08031_01)

# Social Care and Support — British Columbia — British Columbia

Jurisdiction: British Columbia
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent British Columbia practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/canada-british-columbia/social-care-and-support-british-columbia-british-columbia.html

# Social Care and Support — British Columbia

## Learning outcomes

Map assessment, eligibility, funding and delivery separately; include family support without assuming it; explain the local route for challenging a decision.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

Publicly subsidised home and community care involves health-authority assessment, general eligibility and service-specific criteria. Provincial guidance addresses status, residence, age and health-related need, with exceptions to some general conditions. Do not convert a general criterion into an absolute exclusion without checking those exceptions.

Home support, long-term care, assisted living, CLBC supports and income assistance are different programmes. Needs assessment, access priority, client contribution and actual provision must be distinguished. The responsible office should explain which programme and policy support the decision.

## Assess daily life, not just a list of services

Begin with what a good day would look like. Explore washing, dressing, nutrition, medicines, mobility, home safety, relationships, work or education and community participation. Ask about variation: what happens at night, on a bad day or when a regular supporter is unavailable? Establish what the person can do with appropriate equipment, accessible information or a different environment. Do not confuse performing a task once during a visit with being able to do it reliably in daily life.

Speak with family supporters about willingness, practical ability and sustainability. Their account belongs alongside the person's account, not in place of it. Record support that is actually offered and its limits. An adult child working overnight is not an available overnight care service. Where views differ, describe the disagreement and its consequences for the proposed plan.

## Turn the assessment into a deliverable plan

Keep four decisions visible: the needs identified; the applicable eligibility decision; the funding or charging decision; and the service that will actually start. A referral, waiting-list entry or funding approval is not proof that support has begun. Obtain the person's understanding of costs and responsibilities before recording agreement.

For each outcome, identify an action, a responsible service or person and a review trigger. Include what happens if the worker does not arrive, the person declines support, a carer becomes unavailable or needs change. Record unmet needs and interim arrangements explicitly. A budget dispute should not disappear into a description of the person as difficult or unrealistic.

## Apply the local pathway

- Contact the appropriate health-authority home and community care service for eligibility and needs assessment.
- Check general and service-specific criteria, including any relevant exception.
- Record assessed needs, family willingness, priority, costs and when support will actually begin.
- Obtain reasons and the applicable health-authority review or complaint process if access or service levels are disputed.

## Rights, challenge and review

Provincial guidance distinguishes complaints about care from appeals of home and community care service decisions. Use the current health-authority process and decision notice. A provider complaint will not necessarily review a funding or eligibility decision.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A recently arrived older adult is told that a general residence requirement means no assessment or alternative support can be considered.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Check the published exceptions and the person’s actual health needs and circumstances. Identify any other relevant service while the eligibility question is resolved. Record reasons, interim support and the route for challenging the decision.

### Common error to avoid

Applying general eligibility criteria without checking exceptions or treating an assessment as guaranteed service delivery.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Daily-life evidence, fluctuation and desired outcomes
- The service, eligibility test and decision-maker
- Carer willingness and separately identified needs
- Funding, charges, decisions and reasons
- Start dates, unmet needs, contingency and challenge route

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [Home and community care eligibility](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/health/accessing-health-care/home-community-care/are-you-eligible)
- [Arranging care and assessment](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/health/accessing-health-care/home-community-care/how-to-arrange-for-care)
- [Home and community care concerns and complaints](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/health/accessing-health-care/home-community-care/concerns-and-complaints)
