# Decision-Making and Capacity — British Columbia — British Columbia

Jurisdiction: British Columbia
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent British Columbia practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/canada-british-columbia/decision-making-and-capacity-british-columbia-british-columbia.html

# Decision-Making and Capacity — British Columbia

## Learning outcomes

Identify the precise decision, provide practical decision support, apply the local capacity or consent framework and verify a representative’s authority.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

The Health Care (Consent) and Care Facility (Admission) Act has separate health-care and facility-admission provisions. The Representation Agreement Act and Patients Property Act provide other forms of authority. Identify the decision and the relevant document before deciding which route applies. For healthcare, the provider assesses whether the adult understands the relevant treatment information and its application to their own situation. Adapt communication to the adult’s abilities; a communication difference alone does not establish incapability.

Where temporary substitute consent for healthcare is needed, the healthcare provider selects the first available qualified person in the statutory list. The person’s prior capable instructions or wishes and the Act’s decision standard matter. An available relative is not automatically entitled to displace an authorised representative or another person with priority.

## Start with the decision and the support

Write the decision as a question the person could answer: accepting a particular treatment, choosing accommodation or authorising a financial transaction. These questions may engage different laws and decision-makers. A diagnosis, cognitive score or disagreement with professionals is not a complete capacity assessment. Describe the ability relevant to this decision and the evidence for any concern.

Prepare information about the real options, including doing nothing where relevant. Use an interpreter, accessible material, communication aids and suitable timing. Address pain, fatigue, sensory impairment, medication effects and anxiety. Ask the person to explain their understanding in their own way; repeating professional phrases is not the only way to demonstrate understanding. Record what support was tried and its effect, rather than simply writing that all support was offered.

## Keep authority and the decision itself separate

A relative may provide valuable information without holding authority to decide. Obtain the actual appointment, agreement, court order or statutory basis being relied upon. Check the decisions it covers, conditions, whether it is operative and whether another person has priority. Authority over property does not automatically include healthcare or accommodation.

Where a representative can lawfully act, identify the decision standard they must apply locally. Explore the person's wishes, values, previous statements and present participation. Record a disagreement rather than converting it into apparent agreement. Consider whether a reversible interim option allows more support or recovery before an irreversible decision. If authority remains disputed, obtain the appropriate clinical or legal advice and arrange the applicable review; a multidisciplinary meeting cannot create missing legal powers.

## Apply the local pathway

- Support the adult’s own decision and apply the relevant statutory incapability test.
- Check any advance directive, representation agreement or committee order and its scope.
- Where the temporary substitute route applies, use the statutory priority and qualification requirements.
- Separate healthcare consent from admission and from personal or financial decisions under another framework.

## Rights, challenge and review

The Public Guardian and Trustee has relevant functions when a suitable substitute is unavailable or authority is disputed. Court or other statutory review may be needed depending on the issue. Explain the specific route and preserve the adult’s participation.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A friend offers to consent to treatment because they visit most often, although a valid representation agreement may appoint somebody else.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Assess the adult’s own ability and read the agreement. Determine the appropriate healthcare-consent route and priority before seeking consent. Frequent contact is useful evidence about wishes but does not by itself establish authority.

### Common error to avoid

Using the temporary substitute list without checking an existing representative, or treating an agreement as unlimited authority.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Decision, options and time at which it is needed
- Communication support and observed responses
- Applicable legal test and evidence for each element
- Representative’s document, scope and decision standard
- Wishes, disagreement, review and any urgent action

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [Health Care (Consent) and Care Facility (Admission) Act](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96181_01)
- [Representation Agreement Act](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96405_01)

# Restrictions and Liberty — British Columbia — British Columbia

Jurisdiction: British Columbia
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent British Columbia practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/canada-british-columbia/restrictions-and-liberty-british-columbia-british-columbia.html

# Restrictions and Liberty — British Columbia

## Learning outcomes

Describe actual restrictions, identify the setting-specific legal authority, test alternatives and make representation and review practical.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

Care-facility admission consent, treatment consent and authority for restraint or detention are distinct. The Health Care (Consent) and Care Facility (Admission) Act, facility licensing rules and Mental Health Act may apply in different circumstances. Read the actual measure and legal setting rather than treating admission as permission for every restriction.

Part 3 of the Adult Guardianship Act includes limited protective and emergency powers for designated agencies in defined circumstances. Those powers are not a general standing authority for a provider to confine an adult. The least intrusive response and the person’s wishes remain central to the assessment.

## Describe what happens in everyday life

Look beyond the label used by the service. Describe locked doors, staff responses to a request to leave, supervision, physical interventions, isolation, medication used to control behaviour and restrictions on visitors, money or communication. State when each measure operates, who applies it, its duration and its cumulative effect. Distinguish a person's preferred routine from a rule enforced by staff.

Hear the person privately with suitable communication support. An absence of verbal objection is not a complete account of their wishes. Distress, repeated requests to go home or avoiding a particular worker may require further enquiry. Family agreement is relevant information but should not be treated as a substitute for the authority required by law.

## Connect necessity to a less restrictive plan

Identify the concrete harm a measure is intended to prevent. Explore environmental changes, pain relief, meaningful activity, different staffing, communication and practical support. Record which options were tried, their effects and why another option is proposed. Provider convenience or an unsigned risk assessment should not become the explanation for an ongoing restriction.

Separate emergency action from a continuing arrangement. An urgent response needs its own factual justification and follow-up; it should not silently become a standing plan. Check the scope of any order or authorisation, applicable conditions, expiry and who must review it. The person needs an accessible explanation and a usable way to object, obtain independent help and challenge the arrangement. Assign responsibility for acting on an objection rather than merely documenting it at the next routine meeting.

## Apply the local pathway

- Describe the restriction, who enforces it and the adult’s wishes or objections.
- Identify the applicable facility, mental-health or designated-agency framework and the precise authority.
- Check any order, emergency condition, monitoring duty and limit on duration or scope.
- Explore alternatives and arrange the relevant independent support, complaint or legal review.

## Rights, challenge and review

Mental-health detention has review-panel and court routes; other disputed restrictions may require different legal advice or service-regulation responses. A healthcare substitute or a family member cannot be assumed to authorise every liberty restriction.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A care facility locks a resident’s door after an adult-protection referral and says the referral gives it authority to continue indefinitely.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Clarify whether any lawful emergency or court measure exists and its limits. Review the actual restriction and the adult’s wishes, arrange safer alternatives and obtain the appropriate legal or designated-agency advice. A referral itself confers no indefinite detention power.

### Common error to avoid

Treating a protection referral or admission consent as authority for ongoing confinement.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Each restriction, setting, duration and actual effect
- The person’s wishes, understanding and objections
- Legal authority, decision-maker, limits and conditions
- Alternatives tried and the evidence about necessity
- Representation, review date, expiry and challenge

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [Adult Guardianship Act](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96006_01)
- [Health Care (Consent) and Care Facility (Admission) Act](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96181_01)
- [Mental Health Act](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96288_01)

# Mental Health — British Columbia — British Columbia

Jurisdiction: British Columbia
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent British Columbia practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/canada-british-columbia/mental-health-british-columbia-british-columbia.html

# Mental Health — British Columbia

## Learning outcomes

Distinguish voluntary care, compulsory assessment, detention and treatment; connect the local criteria to evidence and explain the person’s review rights.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

The Mental Health Act provides involuntary admission through medical certification and other defined routes. Section 22 addresses mental disorder requiring treatment, need for treatment in or through a designated facility, need for care, supervision and control to prevent substantial deterioration or protect the person or others, and inability to be suitably admitted voluntarily.

The statutory framework includes treatment authority for detained patients, which differs from ordinary substitute-consent healthcare. Do not import another province’s treatment-consent rule. The person’s status, required certificates and the particular treatment must all be checked.

## Assess the crisis in context

Attend to urgent physical health and immediate safety while creating space for the person's account. Explore sleep, medication, substance use, pain, relationships, housing, financial pressure and previous helpful or harmful experiences of services. Cultural or spiritual expression should be understood in context. Use an appropriate interpreter and ask which supporters the person wants involved.

Describe behaviour and its consequences rather than relying on labels such as non-compliant or high risk. Distinguish what you observed, what somebody reported and the inference being drawn. Consider information that challenges the proposed compulsory route as carefully as information that supports it. The existence of a legal power does not establish that its conditions are met in this case.

## Separate each intervention

Transport, assessment, admission, psychiatric treatment and treatment of an unrelated physical condition can involve different authorities. Check the exact route, the professional authorised to exercise it, required documentation and its time limits. Do not use a single statement that the person is detained to explain every intervention. Document attempts to arrange voluntary or less restrictive support and whether those services are actually available.

Rights information should be understandable at the time and revisited when the person can engage more fully. Explain independent support, legal representation and the applicable review process. During discharge planning, identify housing, medicines, follow-up, family responsibilities and crisis contacts. Confirm who accepts responsibility for each task. A person should not leave with an apparently complete plan consisting only of referrals that no receiving service has accepted.

## Apply the local pathway

- Identify the route and evidence for each applicable criterion, including voluntary alternatives.
- Check certificates, dates, notices and renewal or review requirements.
- Identify the legal basis for psychiatric treatment and distinguish unrelated healthcare decisions.
- Arrange rights advice, access to a review panel or court process and the applicable second-opinion route.

## Rights, challenge and review

The Act includes rights advice, notice, review panels, court discharge applications and a second-medical-opinion provision. These mechanisms address different questions. Explain the route that fits the person’s concern rather than presenting a treatment complaint as identical to detention review.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A person is detained and a worker assumes the treatment-consent process must be identical to the one used in a neighbouring province.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Read the BC provisions governing the person’s actual status and proposed treatment. Explain the specific review and second-opinion rights, and assess unrelated physical healthcare under its own framework. Avoid substituting a familiar out-of-province process.

### Common error to avoid

Reducing certification to immediate dangerousness alone or importing another province’s consent rules.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Mental and physical health evidence and the person’s account
- The local criteria and voluntary alternatives considered
- Separate authority for transport, admission and treatment
- Required notices, advocacy, representation and review
- Continuity, discharge responsibilities and crisis plan

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [BC Mental Health Act, current consolidation](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96288_01)

# Adult Safeguarding — British Columbia — British Columbia

Jurisdiction: British Columbia
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent British Columbia practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/canada-british-columbia/safeguarding-and-family-violence-british-columbia-british-columbia.html

# Adult Safeguarding — British Columbia

## Learning outcomes

Recognise abuse, neglect and coercion; choose the correct local reporting route; connect immediate protection to the adult’s wishes and continuing support.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

Part 3 of the Adult Guardianship Act concerns abuse, neglect or self-neglect where an adult cannot seek support and assistance because of the specified restraint, disability, illness, injury or decision-related conditions. Designated agencies must look into relevant reports. The statutory threshold and agency role should be stated explicitly.

Designated agencies include regional health bodies and, within defined remits, CLBC and Providence Health Care. The Public Guardian and Trustee has different functions. An adult need not already be a service user for a relevant concern to be considered.

## Enquire safely and proportionately

Start with immediate danger and the safest way to communicate. A private conversation may reveal concerns that cannot be expressed in front of a relative, carer or staff member. Check whether telephone calls, letters or messages could expose the person to retaliation. Use independent communication support where a proposed interpreter may have a conflict of interest.

Record the nature of the concern, its source, the person's own words and any observed injuries, living conditions or financial issues. Distinguish a disclosure, a suspicion and a confirmed finding. Do not wait to conduct your own investigation before acting on a reporting duty. Equally, avoid leading questions or repeated interviewing that may distress the person or compromise another agency's investigation.

## Combine protection with participation

Ask what the person wants to change and what they fear might happen after a report. Assess coercion, dependency and practical barriers alongside decision-making ability. A person may understand a risk yet be unable to obtain food, leave safely or resist somebody controlling their money. Support, reporting and authority to impose an intervention are separate questions.

Agree what information needs sharing, with whom and on what legal basis. Where sharing is required or justified without consent, record the reason and explain it to the person when safe and appropriate. Make a plan for immediate needs, follow-up contact and responsibility between agencies. A referral does not establish that somebody has accepted the concern. Confirm receipt, escalate unresolved danger and review whether the action has improved safety in the person's own terms.

## Apply the local pathway

- Identify the alleged harm and why the adult may be unable to seek assistance themselves.
- Refer to the designated agency appropriate to the person and setting.
- Arrange immediate safety and consider police or other statutory duties where needed.
- Separate voluntary support, investigation, emergency action and a court-backed support-and-assistance plan.

## Rights, challenge and review

Preserve the adult’s participation and use the Act’s principles concerning autonomy and effective, least intrusive support. A designated-agency investigation is not the same as appointing a substitute decision-maker. Obtain advice where an imposed plan or emergency power is proposed.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A person understands that a family member is taking money but is physically prevented from leaving home or contacting services.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Consider the inability to seek assistance and the relevant designated-agency route rather than rejecting the concern because the person understands the abuse. Arrange safe communication, practical protection and any police response, with the adult’s wishes clearly recorded.

### Common error to avoid

Treating decisional incapability as the only reason an adult may qualify for assistance.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Concern, source, chronology and the adult’s own account
- Immediate safety and a safe communication method
- The local reporting threshold, recipient and timing
- Consent, coercion and information-sharing basis
- Accepted responsibilities, outcomes and follow-up

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [PGT: protecting an adult from abuse or neglect](https://www.trustee.bc.ca/adults/protecting-vulnerable-adult-abuse-neglect-or-self-neglect)
- [Adult Guardianship Act](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96006_01)
- [Designated Agencies Regulation](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/11_19_2002)

# Children, Families and Transitions — British Columbia — British Columbia

Jurisdiction: British Columbia
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent British Columbia practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/canada-british-columbia/tamariki-rangatahi-and-wh-nau-british-columbia-british-columbia.html

# Children, Families and Transitions — British Columbia

## Learning outcomes

Separate family support from protection powers, apply the local reporting duty, involve the child and coordinate education, health and transition planning.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

The Child, Family and Community Service Act (CFCSA) defines a child as a person under 19 and creates a duty to report where its protection conditions are engaged. Do not apply another province’s age boundary. A report should reach the appropriate child-protection authority; telling a supervisor alone is insufficient.

Indigenous child and family service laws may apply, with provincial guidance explaining referral to an Indigenous authority where relevant. Establish the child’s legal and service context rather than assuming the provincial process is the only possible authority.

## Understand the child’s daily experience

Use age-appropriate communication, observation and accessible material. Ask about ordinary routines, trusted adults, worries, food, sleep, school and relationships. Record the child's words separately from adult interpretations. For a baby or a child who does not use speech, describe interactions and behaviour without claiming to know a view they have not expressed.

Assess harm, strengths and the practical conditions affecting care. Poverty, inaccessible services or overcrowded housing may require material help; they should not automatically be treated as evidence of parental indifference. At the same time, a family's strengths do not remove the need to act on a protection concern. Explore the experience of siblings and whether a proposed protective adult can actually provide the support being described.

## Keep support and compulsory intervention clear

Explain your role, the concern, confidentiality limits and the next step in language the family can understand. Establish the local reporting threshold and receiving authority. A practice model can organise enquiry but cannot determine a statutory threshold or authorise removal. Where you disagree with a decision, identify the evidence and use the relevant escalation process without delaying necessary immediate action.

Plan with education, health, disability and community services, identifying each person's responsibility. For a young person approaching adulthood, address accommodation, income, healthcare, relationships, education or work and decision support before a service ends. Confirm eligibility and acceptance by adult services rather than assuming that a childhood plan transfers automatically. Preserve cultural, family and community relationships in ways consistent with the child's safety and wishes.

## Apply the local pathway

- Identify the concern and the child’s age, using the CFCSA reporting threshold.
- Make the report through the appropriate provincial or Indigenous-authority arrangements and address immediate danger.
- Record the child’s words, evidence, cultural relationships and actions taken.
- Coordinate support and participation while distinguishing a report, investigation, agreement and court measure.

## Rights, challenge and review

Explain who is responding and how the child and family can obtain advocacy, legal advice or a complaint review. Respect the applicable Indigenous jurisdiction and do not delay an urgent safety report while assuming that another organisation will act.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A worker hears a serious concern about an 18-year-old and dismisses it because the worker previously practised where adult services began earlier.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Check the BC age definition and applicable protection conditions. Make the appropriate report and coordinate support with the young person’s participation. Identify any relevant Indigenous authority and transition arrangements rather than importing the former jurisdiction’s boundary.

### Common error to avoid

Using another province’s reporting age or assuming that every Indigenous child’s case follows an identical provincial route.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Child’s account, communication and daily-life evidence
- Harm, strengths, needs and alternative explanations
- Reporting duty, recipient and action taken
- Family participation, culture and legal authority
- Named plan, education/health links and transition dates

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [BC reporting child abuse](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/safety/public-safety/protecting-children/reporting-child-abuse)
- [Child, Family and Community Service Act](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96046_01)

# Rights, Culture and Recording — British Columbia — British Columbia

Jurisdiction: British Columbia
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent British Columbia practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/canada-british-columbia/rights-culture-and-recording-british-columbia-british-columbia.html

# Rights, Culture and Recording — British Columbia

## Learning outcomes

Connect rights to an actual service decision, distinguish privacy from absolute secrecy and write a record that makes reasons and disagreement visible.

## Local legislation, policy and professional framework

The BC Human Rights Code applies to discrimination in its covered areas, while the Canadian Charter has a distinct scope. Indigenous rights and applicable Indigenous laws must be considered in the actual function, alongside professional cultural-safety responsibilities.

The Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act (FIPPA) generally concerns public bodies, while the Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA) governs covered private organisations. Determine the organisation’s legal status and the information involved before applying collection, disclosure or access rules.

## Make rights practical

Identify the decision affecting the person: access to an assessment, a restriction, a disclosure, an inaccessible meeting or a refusal of support. Ask which right or duty is engaged and which organisation is responsible. A statement that a plan is rights-based does not explain whether the person could participate or how the effect on them was weighed.

Arrange interpretation, accessible formats and communication support suited to the person. Ask about cultural identity, discrimination and the supporters they wish to involve. Do not infer these preferences from appearance, surname or language. Consider whether a seemingly neutral rule disadvantages someone because of disability or another protected characteristic, and what accommodation or adjustment is available under the applicable law.

## Make disclosure and recording accountable

Identify the purpose, recipient and legal basis before sharing personal information. Determine whether the organisation is covered by health, public-sector, private-sector or another confidentiality regime. Consent is not the only possible basis for disclosure, but an organisational request is not a legal basis by itself. Share the information relevant to the permitted purpose and record any limits or objection.

A useful record separates observation, the person's account, information from others, analysis and action. Write what evidence led to the conclusion, which alternatives were considered and why a particular option was chosen. Preserve disagreement respectfully and correct factual errors through the appropriate process. Explain how the person can request access, seek correction, complain or obtain an independent review. Store learning reflections without identifiable case details and use approved systems for professional records.

## Apply the local pathway

- Identify the service decision, relevant right and responsible organisation.
- Consider accommodation, language, cultural safety and the person’s chosen supports.
- Check whether FIPPA, PIPA or another specific rule applies to the record and disclosure.
- Record the lawful purpose, necessary information, reasons and the access, correction or complaint route.

## Rights, challenge and review

The Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner for BC addresses matters within FIPPA and PIPA; the Human Rights Tribunal addresses Code complaints. Professional and service complaints are separate. Help the person select the route that can address their concern.

## Worked learning example

Fictional case: A private community provider copies a public health authority’s privacy form and assumes that the same disclosure powers apply.

Before reading the discussion, identify the relevant decision, the missing evidence and the person who can lawfully act.

### Discussion and reasoning

Determine the provider’s actual legal obligations and purpose of sharing. Revise the consent and information process to fit the applicable law, and record what the person was told. Similar work does not establish identical statutory powers.

### Common error to avoid

Assuming public-body and private-organisation privacy rules are interchangeable.

## Recording and supervision exercise

Use the matching printable prompt to make a short record for this case. Include:

- Decision, affected rights and responsible organisation
- Accessibility, culture and participation arrangements
- Disclosure purpose, legal basis, recipient and limits
- Evidence, alternatives, reasons and disagreement
- Access, correction, complaints and review route

Ask a supervisor to identify a missing fact that could change your conclusion. Revise the plan to show who will obtain that fact and what happens while it remains uncertain.

## Official sources and currency

- [BC Human Rights Code](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96210_01)
- [Personal Information Protection Act](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/03063_01)
- [FIPPA](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96165_00)

# Practice reference — British Columbia practice guide


Use alongside the full modules and current official sources. Each entry separates the local framework, action and review.


## Professional Foundations — British Columbia

The British Columbia College of Social Workers (BCCSW) Code of Ethics and Standards of Practice and the Social Workers Act provide the professional framework. Check the registration category, scope and any applicable statutory exemption or special role; a job title alone does not explain a practitioner’s regulatory position.

Health authorities, Community Living BC (CLBC), child and family services, Indigenous authorities and community organisations have different remits. Identify the organisation exercising the function and the law governing it. Cultural safety includes attention to Indigenous self-determination, racism and the person’s chosen community relationships.


- Confirm the practitioner’s role, regulatory position and any specific statutory designation.
- Explain the purpose of involvement, participation and confidentiality limits.
- Map the responsible health, community, child-service or Indigenous authority rather than treating all services as one system.
- Use supervision and continuing learning to test evidence, bias and the practical effect of decisions.


Distinguish a BCCSW professional complaint from a health-authority, service, privacy or statutory decision review. Help the person identify which body can address the action or remedy in question.


- [BCCSW Standards and Scope of Practice](https://bccsw.ca/for-registrants/standards-scope-of-practice/)
- [Social Workers Act](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/08031_01)


## Social Care and Support — British Columbia

Publicly subsidised home and community care involves health-authority assessment, general eligibility and service-specific criteria. Provincial guidance addresses status, residence, age and health-related need, with exceptions to some general conditions. Do not convert a general criterion into an absolute exclusion without checking those exceptions.

Home support, long-term care, assisted living, CLBC supports and income assistance are different programmes. Needs assessment, access priority, client contribution and actual provision must be distinguished. The responsible office should explain which programme and policy support the decision.


- Contact the appropriate health-authority home and community care service for eligibility and needs assessment.
- Check general and service-specific criteria, including any relevant exception.
- Record assessed needs, family willingness, priority, costs and when support will actually begin.
- Obtain reasons and the applicable health-authority review or complaint process if access or service levels are disputed.


Provincial guidance distinguishes complaints about care from appeals of home and community care service decisions. Use the current health-authority process and decision notice. A provider complaint will not necessarily review a funding or eligibility decision.


- [Home and community care eligibility](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/health/accessing-health-care/home-community-care/are-you-eligible)

## Decision-Making and Capacity — British Columbia

The Health Care (Consent) and Care Facility (Admission) Act has separate health-care and facility-admission provisions. The Representation Agreement Act and Patients Property Act provide other forms of authority. Identify the decision and the relevant document before deciding which route applies. For healthcare, the provider assesses whether the adult understands the relevant treatment information and its application to their own situation. Adapt communication to the adult’s abilities; a communication difference alone does not establish incapability.

Where temporary substitute consent for healthcare is needed, the healthcare provider selects the first available qualified person in the statutory list. The person’s prior capable instructions or wishes and the Act’s decision standard matter. An available relative is not automatically entitled to displace an authorised representative or another person with priority.


- Support the adult’s own decision and apply the relevant statutory incapability test.
- Check any advance directive, representation agreement or committee order and its scope.
- Where the temporary substitute route applies, use the statutory priority and qualification requirements.
- Separate healthcare consent from admission and from personal or financial decisions under another framework.


The Public Guardian and Trustee has relevant functions when a suitable substitute is unavailable or authority is disputed. Court or other statutory review may be needed depending on the issue. Explain the specific route and preserve the adult’s participation.

## Children, Families and Transitions — British Columbia

Do not apply another province’s age boundary. A report should reach the appropriate child-protection authority; telling a supervisor alone is insufficient.

Indigenous child and family service laws may apply, with provincial guidance explaining referral to an Indigenous authority where relevant. Establish the child’s legal and service context rather than assuming the provincial process is the only possible authority.


- Identify the concern and the child’s age, using the CFCSA reporting threshold.
- Make the report through the appropriate provincial or Indigenous-authority arrangements and address immediate danger.
- Record the child’s words, evidence, cultural relationships and actions taken.
- Coordinate support and participation while distinguishing a report, investigation, agreement and court measure.


Explain who is responding and how the child and family can obtain advocacy, legal advice or a complaint review. Respect the applicable Indigenous jurisdiction and do not delay an urgent safety report while assuming that another organisation will act.


- [BC reporting child abuse](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/safety/public-safety/protecting-children/reporting-child-abuse)
- [Child, Family and Community Service Act](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96046_01)


## Rights, Culture and Recording — British Columbia

The BC Human Rights Code applies to discrimination in its covered areas, while the Canadian Charter has a distinct scope. Indigenous rights and applicable Indigenous laws must be considered in the actual function, alongside professional cultural-safety responsibilities.

The Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act (FIPPA) generally concerns public bodies, while the Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA) governs covered private organisations. Determine the organisation’s legal status and the information involved before applying collection, disclosure or access rules.


- Identify the service decision, relevant right and responsible organisation.
- Consider accommodation, language, cultural safety and the person’s chosen supports.
- Check whether FIPPA, PIPA or another specific rule applies to the record and disclosure.
- Record the lawful purpose, necessary information, reasons and the access, correction or complaint route.


The Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner for BC addresses matters within FIPPA and PIPA; the Human Rights Tribunal addresses Code complaints. Professional and service complaints are separate. Help the person select the route that can address their concern.


- [BC Human Rights Code](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96210_01)
- [Personal Information Protection Act](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/03063_01)
- [FIPPA](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96165_00)

### Professional Foundations

```text
Professional Foundations
British Columbia practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The British Columbia College of Social Workers (BCCSW) Code of Ethics and Standards of Practice and the Social Workers Act provide the professional framework. Check the registration category, scope and any applicable statutory exemption or special role; a job title alone does not explain a practitioner’s regulatory position.

Health authorities, Community Living BC (CLBC), child and family services, Indigenous authorities and community organisations have different remits. Identify the organisation exercising the function and the law governing it. Cultural safety includes attention to Indigenous self-determination, racism and the person’s chosen community relationships.

Local pathway:
Confirm the practitioner’s role, regulatory position and any specific statutory designation.
Explain the purpose of involvement, participation and confidentiality limits.
Map the responsible health, community, child-service or Indigenous authority rather than treating all services as one system.
Use supervision and continuing learning to test evidence, bias and the practical effect of decisions.

Notes:

Notes:

5. Agreed action, supervision, feedback and review
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Distinguish a BCCSW professional complaint from a health-authority, service, privacy or statutory decision review. Help the person identify which body can address the action or remedy in question.
```

### Social Care and Support

```text
Social Care and Support
British Columbia practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Publicly subsidised home and community care involves health-authority assessment, general eligibility and service-specific criteria. Provincial guidance addresses status, residence, age and health-related need, with exceptions to some general conditions. Do not convert a general criterion into an absolute exclusion without checking those exceptions.

Home support, long-term care, assisted living, CLBC supports and income assistance are different programmes. Needs assessment, access priority, client contribution and actual provision must be distinguished. The responsible office should explain which programme and policy support the decision.

Local pathway:
Contact the appropriate health-authority home and community care service for eligibility and needs assessment.
Check general and service-specific criteria, including any relevant exception.
Record assessed needs, family willingness, priority, costs and when support will actually begin.
Obtain reasons and the applicable health-authority review or complaint process if access or service levels are disputed.

Recording prompts:
1. Daily-life evidence, fluctuation and desired outcomes
Notes:

2. The service, eligibility test and decision-maker
Notes:

3. Carer willingness and separately identified needs
Notes:

4. Funding, charges, decisions and reasons
Notes:

5. Start dates, unmet needs, contingency and challenge route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Provincial guidance distinguishes complaints about care from appeals of home and community care service decisions. Use the current health-authority process and decision notice. A provider complaint will not necessarily review a funding or eligibility decision.

Sources:
https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/health/accessing-health-care/home-community-care/are-you-eligible
```

### Decision-Making and Capacity

```text
Decision-Making and Capacity
British Columbia practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Health Care (Consent) and Care Facility (Admission) Act has separate health-care and facility-admission provisions. The Representation Agreement Act and Patients Property Act provide other forms of authority. Identify the decision and the relevant document before deciding which route applies. For healthcare, the provider assesses whether the adult understands the relevant treatment information and its application to their own situation. Adapt communication to the adult’s abilities; a communication difference alone does not establish incapability.

Where temporary substitute consent for healthcare is needed, the healthcare provider selects the first available qualified person in the statutory list. The person’s prior capable instructions or wishes and the Act’s decision standard matter. An available relative is not automatically entitled to displace an authorised representative or another person with priority.

Local pathway:
Support the adult’s own decision and apply the relevant statutory incapability test.
Check any advance directive, representation agreement or committee order and its scope.
Where the temporary substitute route applies, use the statutory priority and qualification requirements.
Separate healthcare consent from admission and from personal or financial decisions under another framework.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, options and time at which it is needed
Notes:

2. Communication support and observed responses
Notes:

3. Applicable legal test and evidence for each element
Notes:

4. Representative’s document, scope and decision standard
Notes:

5. Wishes, disagreement, review and any urgent action
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The Public Guardian and Trustee has relevant functions when a suitable substitute is unavailable or authority is disputed. Court or other statutory review may be needed depending on the issue. Explain the specific route and preserve the adult’s participation.

Sources:
https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96181_01
https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96405_01

```

### Restrictions and Liberty

```text
Restrictions and Liberty
British Columbia practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Care-facility admission consent, treatment consent and authority for restraint or detention are distinct. The Health Care (Consent) and Care Facility (Admission) Act, facility licensing rules and Mental Health Act may apply in different circumstances. Read the actual measure and legal setting rather than treating admission as permission for every restriction.

Part 3 of the Adult Guardianship Act includes limited protective and emergency powers for designated agencies in defined circumstances. Those powers are not a general standing authority for a provider to confine an adult. The least intrusive response and the person’s wishes remain central to the assessment.

Local pathway:
Describe the restriction, who enforces it and the adult’s wishes or objections.
Identify the applicable facility, mental-health or designated-agency framework and the precise authority.
Check any order, emergency condition, monitoring duty and limit on duration or scope.
Explore alternatives and arrange the relevant independent support, complaint or legal review.

Recording prompts:
1. Each restriction, setting, duration and actual effect
Notes:

2. The person’s wishes, understanding and objections
Notes:

3. Legal authority, decision-maker, limits and conditions
Notes:

4. Alternatives tried and the evidence about necessity
Notes:

5. Representation, review date, expiry and challenge
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Mental-health detention has review-panel and court routes; other disputed restrictions may require different legal advice or service-regulation responses. A healthcare substitute or a family member cannot be assumed to authorise every liberty restriction.

Sources:
https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96006_01
https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96181_01
https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96288_01

```

### Mental Health

```text
Mental Health
British Columbia practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Mental Health Act provides involuntary admission through medical certification and other defined routes. Section 22 addresses mental disorder requiring treatment, need for treatment in or through a designated facility, need for care, supervision and control to prevent substantial deterioration or protect the person or others, and inability to be suitably admitted voluntarily.

The statutory framework includes treatment authority for detained patients, which differs from ordinary substitute-consent healthcare. Do not import another province’s treatment-consent rule. The person’s status, required certificates and the particular treatment must all be checked.

Local pathway:
Identify the route and evidence for each applicable criterion, including voluntary alternatives.
Check certificates, dates, notices and renewal or review requirements.
Identify the legal basis for psychiatric treatment and distinguish unrelated healthcare decisions.
Arrange rights advice, access to a review panel or court process and the applicable second-opinion route.

Recording prompts:
1. Mental and physical health evidence and the person’s account
Notes:

2. The local criteria and voluntary alternatives considered
Notes:

3. Separate authority for transport, admission and treatment
Notes:

4. Required notices, advocacy, representation and review
Notes:

5. Continuity, discharge responsibilities and crisis plan
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The Act includes rights advice, notice, review panels, court discharge applications and a second-medical-opinion provision. These mechanisms address different questions. Explain the route that fits the person’s concern rather than presenting a treatment complaint as identical to detention review.

Sources:
https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96288_01

```

### Adult Safeguarding

```text
Adult Safeguarding
British Columbia practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Part 3 of the Adult Guardianship Act concerns abuse, neglect or self-neglect where an adult cannot seek support and assistance because of the specified restraint, disability, illness, injury or decision-related conditions. Designated agencies must look into relevant reports. The statutory threshold and agency role should be stated explicitly.

Designated agencies include regional health bodies and, within defined remits, CLBC and Providence Health Care. The Public Guardian and Trustee has different functions. An adult need not already be a service user for a relevant concern to be considered.

Local pathway:
Identify the alleged harm and why the adult may be unable to seek assistance themselves.
Refer to the designated agency appropriate to the person and setting.
Arrange immediate safety and consider police or other statutory duties where needed.
Separate voluntary support, investigation, emergency action and a court-backed support-and-assistance plan.

Recording prompts:
1. Concern, source, chronology and the adult’s own account
Notes:

2. Immediate safety and a safe communication method
Notes:

3. The local reporting threshold, recipient and timing
Notes:

4. Consent, coercion and information-sharing basis
Notes:

5. Accepted responsibilities, outcomes and follow-up
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Preserve the adult’s participation and use the Act’s principles concerning autonomy and effective, least intrusive support. A designated-agency investigation is not the same as appointing a substitute decision-maker. Obtain advice where an imposed plan or emergency power is proposed.

Sources:
https://www.trustee.bc.ca/adults/protecting-vulnerable-adult-abuse-neglect-or-self-neglect
https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96006_01
https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/11_19_2002
```

# Practice Scenarios — British Columbia — British Columbia

Jurisdiction: British Columbia
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent British Columbia practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/canada-british-columbia/practice-scenarios-british-columbia.html

# Scenario Workouts — British Columbia practice guide


All cases are fictional learning exercises. Explain your evidence and reasoning before reading the discussion.


## Professional Foundations — British Columbia

A worker assumes that employment by a health authority automatically gives them the powers of a designated adult-protection investigator.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Check the organisation’s designation and the worker’s actual role, authority and procedure. Gather relevant social evidence within scope and arrange the appropriate designated-agency response. Employment and statutory investigative authority should not be conflated.


## Social Care and Support — British Columbia

A recently arrived older adult is told that a general residence requirement means no assessment or alternative support can be considered.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Check the published exceptions and the person’s actual health needs and circumstances. Identify any other relevant service while the eligibility question is resolved. Record reasons, interim support and the route for challenging the decision.


## Decision-Making and Capacity — British Columbia

A friend offers to consent to treatment because they visit most often, although a valid representation agreement may appoint somebody else.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Assess the adult’s own ability and read the agreement. Determine the appropriate healthcare-consent route and priority before seeking consent. Frequent contact is useful evidence about wishes but does not by itself establish authority.


## Restrictions and Liberty — British Columbia

A care facility locks a resident’s door after an adult-protection referral and says the referral gives it authority to continue indefinitely.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Clarify whether any lawful emergency or court measure exists and its limits. Review the actual restriction and the adult’s wishes, arrange safer alternatives and obtain the appropriate legal or designated-agency advice. A referral itself confers no indefinite detention power.


## Mental Health — British Columbia

A person is detained and a worker assumes the treatment-consent process must be identical to the one used in a neighbouring province.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Read the BC provisions governing the person’s actual status and proposed treatment. Explain the specific review and second-opinion rights, and assess unrelated physical healthcare under its own framework. Avoid substituting a familiar out-of-province process.


## Adult Safeguarding — British Columbia

A person understands that a family member is taking money but is physically prevented from leaving home or contacting services.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Consider the inability to seek assistance and the relevant designated-agency route rather than rejecting the concern because the person understands the abuse. Arrange safe communication, practical protection and any police response, with the adult’s wishes clearly recorded.


## Children, Families and Transitions — British Columbia

A worker hears a serious concern about an 18-year-old and dismisses it because the worker previously practised where adult services began earlier.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Check the BC age definition and applicable protection conditions. Make the appropriate report and coordinate support with the young person’s participation. Identify any relevant Indigenous authority and transition arrangements rather than importing the former jurisdiction’s boundary.


## Rights, Culture and Recording — British Columbia

A private community provider copies a public health authority’s privacy form and assumes that the same disclosure powers apply.


- Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
- What evidence and support could change the next step?
- How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?


### Discussion

Determine the provider’s actual legal obligations and purpose of sharing. Revise the consent and information process to fit the applicable law, and record what the person was told. Similar work does not establish identical statutory powers.

### Children, Families and Transitions — British Columbia

- [BC reporting child abuse](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/safety/public-safety/protecting-children/reporting-child-abuse)
- [Child, Family and Community Service Act](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96046_01)


### Rights, Culture and Recording — British Columbia

- [BC Human Rights Code](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96210_01)
- [Personal Information Protection Act](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/03063_01)
- [FIPPA](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96165_00)


## How to verify a rule

Identify territorial scope, current consolidated text, amendments and commencement, then the applicable statutory guidance and service procedure. An enactment announcement or portal is not proof that every provision is in force.


## Editorial status

Final learning-guide release. Core lessons and linked learning tools were expanded on 8 September 2026. Independent practitioner review has not been recorded. Monthly monitoring flags source changes for editorial assessment and does not automatically rewrite legal guidance.

# About Us — British Columbia

## About this resource

Daily Mindset Moments CIC, founded by Raymond Hill, provides this structured social-work learning resource. It supports students, practitioners and supervisors with modules, fictional exercises, source links and private reflections.

## British Columbia context

This guide separates the learning material for British Columbia from the other practice locations. Shared theories support enquiry; laws, professional requirements and service pathways must be checked locally. Read the source library for scope and editorial status.

# Privacy Policy — British Columbia

## Learning stored on your device

The app stores your selected location, reading progress, confidence, saved reflections and unfinished reflection fields in this browser. Records are separated by location. They are not submitted to a professional body. Export or print a copy before clearing browser data or changing devices.

## Website enquiries

If you use the contact form, the details you submit are sent to the website’s form service and operator. Do not send confidential case information. External source websites have their own privacy policies.

## Your records

Use Delete reflection to remove saved entries. Clearing this site’s browser storage removes local progress and notes. Contact [Daily Mindset Moments CIC](mailto:info@daily-mindset-moments.com) about information sent through an enquiry.

# Terms of Service — British Columbia — British Columbia

# Terms of Service — British Columbia

## Purpose and scope

The British Columbia guide is an educational resource for learning and supervision. It does not provide individual legal advice, determine a case outcome or certify professional competence. Use current official sources and the procedures applicable to your role.

## Responsible use

Practice scenarios are fictional. Downloads are learning prompts, not statutory forms. Do not enter identifiable case details into reflections or enquiries. Your browser stores local notes; export your own copy if you need a durable record.

## Sources and corrections

External sources may change. The source library records editorial scope; inclusion of a link or model does not imply endorsement by its publisher. Send corrections with the relevant source and section title through the contact route.

# Learning Map — New York — New York

Jurisdiction: New York
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent New York practitioner review is not recorded.

# Learning Map — New York

## A sequence for study

1. [Professional Foundations](/?jurisdiction=united-states-new-york&resource=foundations#learningWorkspace): Professional role, ethics, competence, supervision and accountable decisions.
2. [Social Care and Support](/?jurisdiction=united-states-new-york&resource=care-support#learningWorkspace): Needs, strengths, access to support, family responsibilities and service planning.
3. [Decision-Making and Capacity](/?jurisdiction=united-states-new-york&resource=mca#learningWorkspace): Decision support, consent and the authority for someone else to decide.
4. [Restrictions and Liberty](/?jurisdiction=united-states-new-york&resource=dols#learningWorkspace): Restrictions, legal authority, less restrictive options and review.
5. [Mental Health](/?jurisdiction=united-states-new-york&resource=mha#learningWorkspace): Mental-health support, crisis response, treatment and rights.
6. [Adult Safeguarding](/?jurisdiction=united-states-new-york&resource=safeguarding#learningWorkspace): Abuse, neglect, coercion, safe enquiry and the appropriate protective response.
7. [Children, Families and Transitions](/?jurisdiction=united-states-new-york&resource=children#learningWorkspace): Child participation, family support, child protection and transitions.
8. [Rights, Culture and Recording](/?jurisdiction=united-states-new-york&resource=rights#learningWorkspace): Participation, privacy, cultural safety and clear recording.

## Put learning into practice

Choose one fictional scenario. Record what is known, the person’s perspective and what still needs checking. Open the source library before answering a legal question. Use supervision to test alternative explanations and a reflection to record the next action.

# Case Route Finder — New York — New York

Jurisdiction: New York
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent New York practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/united-states-new-york/case-route-finder-new-york.html

# Case Route Finder — New York

## Use the route finder

Select the concerns that fit a fictional case. More than one framework may be relevant. Open each suggested module and its sources; the tool selects learning topics and does not decide a legal threshold.

## Compare the routes

Separate support needs, decision-making, mental-health intervention, protective reporting and restrictions. Record the question each route answers, the source you checked and who needs to provide further advice.


## Route questions

### Care or carer support needs

Which needs and outcomes belong to the person and to carers?

Identify Medicaid eligibility, the service requested and the responsible assessment and authorisation bodies. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### A decision-specific capacity question

What is the precise decision and why is ability to decide questioned?

Specify the decision, support the person and identify the applicable healthcare or guardianship framework. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Restrictions or liberty concerns

What restrictions actually operate and how do they affect the person?

Describe the restriction, setting, person’s wishes and current legal status. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Mental health support or compulsion questions

What is the purpose of each proposed intervention?

Identify the exact Article 9 route and evidence for its current criteria. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Abuse, neglect or safeguarding concerns

How can the person be heard safely and privately?

Identify the harm, functional difficulties and whether responsible assistance is actually available. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### A child, young carer or transition issue

What does the child say or show about safety and daily life?

Identify the reporter role, child’s age, alleged responsible person and facts supporting reasonable cause. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Language, participation or recording concerns

What makes participation accessible for this person?

Identify the organisation, record and state or federal privacy provisions involved. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.

### Professional learning or supervision

What is the purpose and limit of your role?

Confirm the licence, current registration, scope and supervision required for the actual work. Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.
